item.title: Bills news: What motivates head coach Joe Brady?
item.description: Joe Brady considers himself a players’ coach and he is emphasizing strong relationships, high energy and authenticity.
item.content:encoded:
Heading into the 2026 NFL season, Joe Brady is the NFL’s youngest head coach at the ripe old age of 36. And while he has spent the past few years working with Josh Allen and directing one of the league’s highest scoring offenses, Brady says his primary focus has always been on connecting with his players through his authentic, energetic approach to leadership.

“I never thought my identity was, ‘I want to be a head coach,'” Brady told BuffaloBills.com. “I just wanted to call plays.”

After spending time as Buffalo’s quarterbacks coach (2022-23), interim offensive coordinator (2023) and offensive coordinator (2024-25), Brady realized he was ready to take on the challenge of being a head coach.

Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by breaking down Brady’s leadership and coaching style, discussing what motivates Brady and finding out how Brady is bringing a new energy to the Bills.

Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts in the comments section.

How Joe Brady is preparing for his head coaching debut

Head coach Joe Brady is preparing for his first meaningful game leading the Buffalo Bills, but as he’s leading the preparations for Sunday’s season opener against the Houston Texans, Brady admits he’s not focusing at all on the fact that this will be his head coaching debut.

“I’m run different. I don’t ever take those seconds and appreciate that,” said Brady ahead of Wednesday’s practice in Orchard Park. “I know we have a huge test for our guys this week, and I’ve got to be whatever they need me to be. That’s the most important thing.”

“He’s the first one in, the last one out,” quarterback Josh Allen said. “When he says he loves to work, he truly loves to work,” Allen said. “He loves football, he loves this game.”

We also explore how new offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael Jr. and new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard are embracing their first NFL coordinator roles; check in on the status of several injured Bills players; and find out how starting left tackle Dion Dawkins is preparing for the start of his 10th season in Buffalo.

item.title: 5 Titans who need to step up vs. Jets in Week 1
item.description: The following five Tennessee Titans players need to step up versus the New York Jets in Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
After minicamp, OTAs, training camp and the preseason, the Tennessee Titans finally begin their 2026 NFL campaign on Sunday. They’ll host the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium in Week 1. Head coach Robert Saleh will officially make his debut, marking the start of a new era in Tennessee.

Coach Saleh needs multiple players to step up versus the Jets, his former team, in Week 1. We’ve identified five in particular.

Jeffery Simmons, DT

Jeffery Simmons is the best defensive tackle in the NFL. He needs to apply pressure to Jets quarterback Geno Smith, who is a mistake-prone quarterback when under duress. Smith leads the NFL in interceptions across the 2024-25 seasons combined.

Cam Ward, QB

This entire fanbase will be monitoring Cam Ward’s progress as a sophomore quarterback. After a pair of lackluster showings in the preseason, fans want a heat-check on Ward as a quarterback. A big-time showing versus the Jets would ease any lingering concerns.

Carnell Tate, WR

Rookie No. 4 overall pick Carnell Tate will make his official regular season debut. The Titans drafted Tate for him to be Ward’s go-to playmaker. After failing to register a catch in the preseason, Titans fans want to see Ward pepper him with targets.

Alontae Taylor, CB

The Titans paid Alontae Taylor roughly $20 million per season to be the defense’s No. 1 cornerback. Taylor and the entire first-team unit struggled in the preseason, allowing multiple explosive touchdowns. He needs a better showing versus Garrett Wilson and the Jets’ potentially underrated passing attack.

Tony Pollard, RB

Tony Pollard has enjoyed four consecutive 1,000 yard seasons. The Titans’ reliable bellcow is both underrated and underappreciated. Pollard appears primed for another big season in Tennessee as the lead ball carrier. Tyjae Spears will spell him, and both backs are expected to catch more passes in Brian Daboll’s offense.

item.title: Week 1 NFL odds, picks, predictions: Our best bets, including a play in Cowboys-Giants
item.description: Our NFL handicappers give out their favorite bets for Week 1 games.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 of the NFL began with a 13-10 Seattle Seahawks win over the New England Patriots and continued on Thursday night with the NFL's first-ever regular season game played in Australia — a 27-7 victory by the San Francisco 49ers over the Los Angeles Rams.

What will the rest of the weekend have in store for bettors?

Our NFL handicapping team of Corbie Craig, Matt Jacob, Jeremy Pond and Matt Russell combine to give their best bets for Week 1 of the NFL season.

Odds subject to change.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Cincinnati Bengals (-3.5, 50.5)

Jacob: The highest total on the Week 1 NFL slate comes from Cincinnati — and it makes complete sense. After all, the Bengals' defense leaked like a broken water main all last season, while Tampa Bay's stop unit was well below average. Also, the two quarterbacks in this contest — Baker Mayfield and Joe Burrow — are big-armed veterans who combined for 43 touchdown passes in just 25 games in 2025.

Here's what you may not know: Burrow is a notorious slow starter. He has one total touchdown pass in the last three season openers. And for his career, he has many interceptions (five) as TD throws in Week 1. 

Now check out Cincinnati's points production in its six openers this decade: 17 (vs. Cleveland last year); 10 (vs. New England in 2024); 3 (at Cleveland in 2023); 20 (vs. Pittsburgh in overtime in 2022); 27 (vs. Minnesota in overtime in 2021); 13 (vs. the Chargers in 2020). Only the game against the Vikings (27-24 final) hurdled 43 combined points. 

To be fair, Mayfield has been spectacular in his three openers with Tampa Bay (nine TDs, zero INTs). However, only one of the Buccaneers' last four Week 1 games has cleared 43 points.

Then there's this: Since 2022, seven Week 1 contests have closed with a total of at least 50 points. Only twice did the over cash.

Bet: Under 50.5

Green Bay Packers at Minnesota Vikings (-1.5, 46.5)

Jacob: Minnesota followed up its stunning 14-3 record in 2024 with a miserable start to last season, dropping eight of the first dozen games. Rather than throw in the towel, though, the Vikings regrouped and closed on a five-game winning streak to finish one game above .500. And they did it with J.J. McCarthy — now the team's third-string QB — starting four of the five contests.

Meanwhile, the 2025 Packers went the complete opposite direction, dropping their final four games after a 9-3-1 start to miss the playoffs for just the second time in seven years.

Bet the Minnesota Vikings to cover the spread at sportsbooks

Obviously, there's no certainty that late-season momentum — either positive or negative — will carry over to this year. But at least the Vikings' roster is in better shape: Minnesota enters the season without a single starter on the injured list. Conversely, Green Bay won't have ineligible running back Josh Jacobs (whose backups are completely unproven); three starting offensive lineman are banged up (and that unit lost two of last year's starters to free agency); star pass-rusher Micah Parsons (torn Achilles) is on IR; and two starting defensive linemen are questionable.

What about new Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray? I believe he'll be a huge upgrade over McCarthy — in large part because I expect head coach Kevin O'Connell to resurrect Murray in the same way he did Sam Darnold two years ago.

Bet: Vikings -1.5 

Pond: We are about to experience the Justin Jefferson bounce-back season and it starts against the Packers in this NFC North showdown. 

The two-time, First-team All-Pro wide receiver is coming off a campaign he'd surely like to forget. Jefferson finished with career lows in yards (1,048), average yards per catch (12.5) and touchdowns (two) for a Minnesota team that went 9-8 and missed the playoffs.

A season removed from that disappointment, Jefferson will get things cooking with Murray under center against a Green Bay defense missing Parsons.

Jump on this ladder play featuring four wagers, and which includes three at plus money. You can tack on over 110 yards (+310) if you're looking to go even deeper on these bets.

Bet: Jefferson alt receiving yards — 70+ Yards (-136) | 80+ Yards (+110) | 90+ Yards (+158) | 100+ Yards (+225) at FanDuel

Denver Broncos at Kansas City Chiefs (-2.5, 43.5)

Craig: KennethWalker III is walking into a crowded room in a new offense, in September, with a quarterback who has never handed him the ball in a game that counted. He ran for 1,027 yards on 221 carries across all 17 games for Seattle last season, which comes out to 60.4 yards a game, and the market has posted 61.5. That is last year's rate copied forward with a rounding error on top, and last year Walker was splitting a backfield in Seattle. He is not doing that now.

Kansas City signed him on March 12 to a three-year deal worth up to $45 million with $28.7 million guaranteed, and the Chiefs signed him to replace both Isiah Pacheco and Kareem Hunt. You don't pay a running back like that to hand him the same workload he had somewhere else.

Our projection lands at 67.9 yards and the case is volume rather than efficiency. A back getting 13 carries a game in a duo now should be getting more than that as the highest-paid piece of a Kansas City backfield that has lost its two most-used players.

Bet: Kenneth Walker III over 61.5 rushing yards (-109)

Buffalo Bills (-1.5, 44.5) at Houston Texans

Craig: James Cook carried the ball 309 times in the regular season last year (18.2 attempts per game). He has been one of the most durable high-volume backs in football, and the market has him at 17.5 carries, which is a perfectly reasonable place to put a number for a back nobody has any reason to doubt. The problem with copying that number forward is that the man who called those plays is now the man running the team.

Offensive coordinator Joe Brady was promoted to head coach on Jan. 27 after Sean McDermott was fired, and Brady has already said publicly that Cook's workload was high and that the backfield needs to share it, with Ray Davis lined up behind him. That is not a beat writer's speculation — it's the head coach describing his own plan.

Then look at the opponent, because Houston fielded the best defense in football last season and then spent the whole offseason making the front even harder to run at, signing Logan Hall in free agency and trading up in the second round for Ohio State defensive tackle Kayden McDonald.

The last time these two teams played, Cook broke a 45-yard touchdown in the first quarter and then spent the rest of the afternoon grinding out 71 yards on his other 16 carries in a 23-19 Houston win, finishing with 17 attempts, which is under the number the market is asking you to lay today.

Bet: Cook under 17.5 rush attempts (-111)

Atlanta Falcons at Pittsburgh Steelers (-4.5, 41.5)

Russell: It's Week 1, and we've already seen a star quarterback not make it out of the first series of the game, but the Falcons' quarterback situation looks to have that beat. Here are Atlanta's options to start at QB for a road game on Sunday:

  1. Michael Penix — not ready to return from an ACL injury.

  2. Tua Tagovailoa — already rumored to be on the chopping block barring epic performance, tumbled to the ground with a back issue in Thursday's practice.

  3. Cooper Rush — four interceptions, no touchdowns on 52 attempts last season.

  4. Jack Strand — undrafted free agent from Division II, Minnesota State-Moorhead.

Not to sound overly dramatic, but if the Steelers can't win this game by a touchdown or more, they should be eliminated from playoff contention. 

The Falcons come into the season rated in the market as a below-average team (40 out of 100 in THE WINDOW's estimated market ratings), but teams with quarterback debacles often see their rating for that week fall into the 20s. That would equate to a new line of Steelers -7, at least. 

Bet: Steelers -4.5

Dallas Cowboys (-3, 48.5) at New York Giants

Pond: I'm expecting fireworks in this matchup of NFC East rivals who will shine on offense and struggle mightily on defense.

Dallas averaged 27.7 points per game a season ago, finishing second in total offense (6,663 yards) and seventh in points. In contrast, the Cowboys were downright atrocious on defense. They conceded a league-worst 30.1 PPG and wound up third in yards allowed (6,409) during a 7-9-1 campaign.

As for the Giants, they weren't much better on the defensive front. They finished 26th in team defense and yielded the fifth-worst yards (6,112) overall a season ago.

Sure, both franchises are optimistic they'll be able to turn things around, but I'm not buying it. These are teams that will be hard to stop when they have the ball and poor trying to defend.

Dallas and New York combined for a whopping 77 points in Week 2 of the 2025 campaign and 51 points in the rematch. I don't think we hit that gaudy number here, but clearing this total shouldn't be an issue.

Bet: Over 47.5 (-128 at DraftKings)

item.title: Vikings vs Packers Week 1: Kyler Murray’s Debut, Love’s Data, and Keys to Victory
item.description: Murray's debut, Love's elite numbers, and a battered Packers defense — everything for Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
Murray could throw 400 or 180 Sunday. Forno maps Vikings–Packers keys. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano of The Real Forno Show (Vikings 1st & SKOL / Bleav) preview Minnesota’s Week 1 home opener against Green Bay at 3:25 p.m. CT. The hook is the unknown: a Kyler Murray debut against former Cardinals head coach Jonathan Gannon, a light Vikings injury report, and a Packers front missing Micah Parsons and Josh Jacobs. “Kyler Murray could come out, throw for 400 yards and five touchdowns on Sunday, and it wouldn’t surprise anyone,” Forness said. “He also could throw for like 180, a touchdown, and two picks.”

The offensive plan, as they sketched it, is incremental, not a full holster dump. Forness cited Murray’s 2024 split: 0.08 EPA per play in the pocket, 0.16 outside it. Expect bootlegs, floods, and half-rolls so Kevin O’Connell can “get him those confident reps.” Frank Smith’s motion is the other lever. Forness argued O’Connell’s run game has been too bland and that Smith’s Dolphins-style motions can change the math against a Packers edge group without Parsons. Dave wants to see Christian Darrisaw and Blake Brandel (and the whole O-Line) in wide zone. On Justin Jefferson, Stefano’s call was blunt: feature him early “to get Gannon to declare.” Forness’s caution: Gannon may simply refuse to let Jefferson beat him and live with Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings, and T.J. Hockenson.

Defense is one job. “You gotta stop Jordan Love.” Fantasy Points data they aired: Love’s intermediate-right window (10–20 yards, right of the hashes) was 96th percentile and 99th percentile in EPA per dropback at 1.105. Favorite concepts were outs and hitches. The counter: interior pressure, cross-dog linebacker games, contain from Andrew Van Ginkel and Dallas Turner so Love cannot escape and hit the scramble drill. “Get pressure up the middle, keep him in the pocket, and collapse on him.” Harrison Smith’s communication is the back-end glue. Forness’s bottom line: “This feels like a game that the Vikings should be able to win rather convincingly.” Will they? That’s the variable.

Key Points

  • Vikings injury report: Jacob Thomas (ankle), Jakobe Thomas (illness), Caleb Tiernan (ankle)
  • Packers questions: Zach Bako-Bewele, Aaron Banks, Jordan Morgan, Javon Hargrave, Devonte Wyatt; Parsons and Jacobs out

item.title: Opponent Analysis and Schematic Breakdown: Boston College Edition
item.description: Looking Deeper at What Boston College Showed On Tape and How Rutgers Can Counter Them Best
item.content:encoded:
Bringing back one of my favorite series of last year, I wanted to take a deeper look at Boston College’s game against Cincinnati and what the Scarlet Knights can do to win this pivotal football game on Friday night in Chestnut Hill. Both teams are coming into this game off of highly disappointing losses and will be looking for a huge bounce-back win for bowl and season morale purposes.

This will not be a film room series with live clips embedded, but I will do my best to break down what I saw from the game highlights and carry that forward in what Rutgers needs to do on either side of the football to best counter the Eagles on both sides of the football.

Game Analysis: Boston College vs. Cincinnati

Watching the extended game highlights, the first thing I noticed is that Boston College looked to quickly establish the run and struggled in pass protection. Boston College transfer quarterback Mason McKenzie made some nice and timely throws in the short and intermediate areas of the field, but he really made a difference with his legs by picking up third and longs on the ground. He ran the ball 20 times for 78 yards, and had elite bursts of speed, not only taking what the defense gave him, but also what was not given at times.

Before the end of the first half, the Eagles appeared to score a touchdown, with the tight end appearing to catch and fumble the football before recovering it in the end zone, but it was ruled as an incomplete pass. On the next play, McKenzie attempted to zip a pass to Colgate transfer receiver Reed Swanson, but double coverage saw that pass sail incomplete. The ensuing field goal kick from Luca Lombardo was no good, leaving the Bearcats up 10-0 at halftime. UC would go on to lead 24-0 and 34-8 before a late BC touchdown closed the margin to 34-15.

On defense, Cincinnati quarterback JC French was similar to McKenzie in his limited passing and rushing ability, if not even more so, going 10-14 for 77 yards through the air while rushing for 52 yards on 10 carries. The BC defense mightily struggled against the run, with running back Gi’Bran Payne going for 108 yards off of just 14 carries, an average of 7.7 yards per carry.

Rutgers Offense vs. Boston College Defense

The big question is how will AJ Surace perform in his first collegiate start, and first for Rutgers? In the lone drive he came in last game, he instantly made solid throws, moved the chains, and had a nice deep ball down the sideline to KJ Duff before capping it off for a touchdown.

Surace seemed more willing to take shots down the field, as opposed to Lonergan’s tendency to dink and dunk, and that capability could prove to be a big difference-maker against Boston College. KJ Duff is a matchup nightmare for almost any secondary in college football with his size and ability to haul in contested catches, but the real differentiator could be in the run game.

Cincinnati ran the ball at will, and if Rutgers looks to pull out this game in Chestnut Hill, they must exploit the same formula. Antwan Raymond is one of the top backs in the Big Ten, but he struggled to get going behind a shaky offensive line that also left Lonergan vulnerable to rushed throws, sacks, and hits, eventually getting injured in the fourth quarter due to the accumulation.

If the offensive line can properly protect AJ Surace, and Rutgers can control clock by running the football, they should have enough offense to give their defense a chance. This will be paramount especially given the fresh face at quarterback; Rutgers should not immediately put it on Surace to win the game on his own.

Rutgers Defense vs. Boston College Offense

Boston College will lean on using their running backs, as well as feature Mason McKenzie as a rusher, which is probably his greatest attribute. The defense kept the Eagles in the game, put pressure on French at times, but struggled to defend open areas in the field, and mightily struggled in the run game, which is where Rutgers should take advantage. In addition, BC will be sure to feature their tight ends, as is tradition.

It appeared evident that the Eagles did not fully trust McKenzie with his arm just yet, although he was able to make timely throws when the team needed. If not for miscues, the Eagles could have gone into the locker room down 10-7 at halftime and the second half could have played out differently, but BC was challenged greatly by Cincy’s defense.

However, the Cincinnati defense is likely far better than what Rutgers showed against UMass last week. The Scarlet Knights posed no pass rushing threat, severe limitations in tackling, and lapses in coverage that led directly to Minutemen touchdowns. If the Knights repeat that defensive performance, the offense that looked incapable against the Bearcats could look very good against the Knights.

Prediction

I am not too certain on a Rutgers win, but if they execute their game plan perfectly, and AJ Surace is immediately the quarterback that was advertised, the Knights could steal one in Chestnut Hill, especially with KJ Duff looking like an NFL wide receiver. However, given how lackluster they looked and the issues at nearly every defensive position, it will be hard to imagine a complete 180 on that side of the football.

While I think the offense starts to gel, it will not be enough to overcome a new quarterback, a shaky offensive line, and a defense that struggled in every facet of defending against UMass. Boston College and Rutgers likely have the same formula to win, but the Eagles execute the run-the-ball, stop-the-run strategy better and come away with a narrow victory, possibly between three and seven points.

item.title: Packers got help from long-time OL coach Harry Hiestand in camp
item.description: Matt LaFleur had another voice in the OL room this summer.
item.content:encoded:
The Packers’ offensive line got some additional help from a long-time college and pro offensive line coach.

According to reporting from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel’s Tom Silverstein, Harry Hiestand spent training camp with the Packers in what appeared to be a consultant-style role.

Hiestand is about as decorated as an offensive line coach can be, boasting success and connections to significant players at just about every stop in his multi-decade career. Dating back to the 1980s, Hiestand coached with eight different college programs and one NFL team, the Chicago Bears, in two different stints. From 2005 through 2009, Hiestand worked with the Bears under head coach Lovie Smith, then returned to Chicago under Matt Nagy in 2018, staying through the 2019 season. 

In between those two tours with the Bears, Hiestand had stops at Tennessee and Notre Dame, and the latter appointment probably explains how he ended up in Green Bay. His time with the Fighting Irish overlapped with Matt LaFleur’s one-year stint there, so Hiestand’s role with the Packers turns out to be not that much of a surprise. In football, even more so than other businesses, it’s about who you know as much as what you know.

So what’s Hiestand up to in Green Bay? That’s not exactly clear, as Silverstein laid out. He characterizes Hiestand as a “consultant,” but it might be more complicated than that:

The well-respected Hiestand coached on the field during training camp, taking over some of the duties Butkus, Gordon or a quality control coach would normally handle. It meant, instead of having one offensive line coach in charge, under the supervision of the offensive coordinator and head coach, the Packers had three line coaches, plus an offensive coordinator who used to be a line coach, in the linemen’s ears.

Hiestand isn’t listed in any official capacity on the Packers’ website, and Silverstein reports that he may still be offering some kind of insight to the team during the season, but his exact role, if any, is a mystery.

Still, with as many questions as the Packers are facing on the offensive line, having another voice in the room hardly seems like a bad thing. Whatever pointers Hiestand can offer are probably worth whatever trade offs arise when you shake things up a bit.

item.title: 5 Questions with Dawgs By Nature: Containing KC Concepcion is Priority No. 1
item.description: Gain intel on the enemy as the Jaguars prepare to face the Browns in Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Cleveland Browns in Week 1, we exchanged questions with Chris Pokorny of Dawgs by Nature to learn more about the opposing side.

Question 1: The Browns have a brutal QB situation and traded away a legendary defender. Do you expect Cleveland to still be competitive this season, or has the race for Arch Manning already begun?

If the Browns had just received draft picks only, then it would have been a clear signal that the race for Arch Manning (or whatever quarterback) has already begun. But, the fact that Jared Verse was part of the deal was huge, and reportedly the only reason Cleveland agreed to it. Granted, Myles Garrett is in a league of his own as a two-time defensive MVP, but the fact of the matter is that Cleveland consistently had losing seasons even with his talent. Verse allows the team to still maintain a solid presence at his vacancy, and the defense in general still has the rest of the pieces that has made it successful over the years, including not allowing a 300+ yard passer in…I think it’s been 45 games? Cleveland’s defense will allow them to be competitive on any given Sunday, but the big question mark is how the offense will perform, which I’ll try to touch on more in your other questions below.

Question 2: If we disregard final standings/draft order, what would a successful 2026 season look like for the Browns?

A successful season for Cleveland would be if the offensive line builds some chemistry together, the young wide receivers look worthy of the draft spots they were taken, and the team has crystal-clear clarity as to how their quarterback situation will be handled next offseason. That could involve Shedeur Sanders (at some point) getting a chance to start and blowing people away, or it could involve Deshaun Watson continuing to be a liability and everyone confirming that “Cleveland is right there in terms of contention, but now we can use as many draft assets as we need to for drafting a quarterback in 2027.”

Question 3: What are your expectations for first-time head coach Todd Monken? Have there been any positive or negative signs this offseason?

Todd Monken seems to be in a unique position where this is going to be his only shot at being a head coach in the NFL. Even if he doesn’t say it, he knows that Cleveland could be transformed with a new quarterback next year, so if he wants to be part of that, the team needs to play relatively well. The quarterback play holding the team back will not be a red mark on him. If he makes dumb coaching decisions and the team loses motivation quickly, then he’ll be kicked to the curb and there will be no qualms about starting over next offseason.

In general, he’s been fine this offseason. We’ve seen elements of the Ravens’ offense incorporated, and he’s inheriting a solid defense. He often talks candidly and has fun stories to listen to. The only thing that somewhat irked me earlier this offseason was during the quarterback competition, Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders would alternate first-team reps every other practice. Prior to one practice, Monken clearly said Sanders was going to get the first-team reps that day, but then when practice started, Watson got all of the reps instead, which made the media go into a frenzy about what it meant. The next day, when Monken was asked about it, he essentially said he changed his mind to balance things out and didn’t need to update the media. Which, on one hand I understand, but it just seems weird to switch it up so close to practice starting — like, shouldn’t that have been well-decided already?

Question 4: What problems could the Browns pose for the Jaguars this week?

The Swiss Army knife utilization of KC Concepcion can be a problem. Taken in the first round, we heard some good and bad things about him. But, through all of training camp and the preseason, this guy looks like he has that “it” factor. He has caught everything. He is effective on jet sweeps. He can be used on any route, he can stretch the field, he can return punts. He looks like the type of player who could be an instant Pro Bowler, and he was having success in camp regardless of what quarterback is throwing him the ball. Watching him is by far the No. 1 thing I’m eager to see at the beginning of the regular season, because we’ve seen this tremendous offseason, and now I want to see that it transforms to regular season action.

Cleveland’s defense is also poised to remain a problem. Their defensive front has several top-tier players, and their secondary remains consistent. Having a new defensive coordinator, we still don’t know if the unit will suffer any dropoff from that, but I’m banking on them remaining a well-oiled machine.

Question 5: Do you expect the Browns to cover as 8.5-point underdogs, and do you have a favorite player prop for the game?

There are times when Cleveland can fall apart later in games from a snowball effect of negativity, but for as bad as they were last year, they still remained highly competitive in a lot of games. The Browns’ entire offensive line from last year is either retired, out of the league, or a backup on other teams in 2026, and the Browns went out and got five new starters. That could be a disaster in terms of chemistry, but also, it can’t get any worse than last year. With that improvement, plus a significant upgrade at wide receiver, the Browns have more pieces to be a better team than they were a year ago. The quarterback position might continue to hold them back from being a playoff team, but they should easily be right in these games, so I’d take the Browns to cover the 8.5-point spread.

With how much I hyped up WR KC Concepcion above, I think it’s a solid bet to take the over on the 33.5 receiving yards for him.

item.title: Week 1 Prediction: New Orleans Saints vs. Detroit Lions
item.description: The 2026 season kicks off for the Saints Sunday afternoon.
item.content:encoded:
There’s no easing into the 2026 season for the New Orleans Saints.

They will open the season on Sunday afternoon on the road against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field, facing a team that is very eager to put last year’s disappointing 9-8 record behind it.

For the Saints, it’s an opportunity to show just how much progress they’ve made entering Year 2 under head coach Kellen Moore.

New Orleans finished 6-11 a year ago, but the team closed the season with four wins in its final five games and enters 2026 with considerably higher expectations. Quarterback Tyler Shough has emerged as a leader, while the Saints made several offseason additions designed to give him more help.

But the Saints will have their work cut out for them Sunday.

Detroit is a difficult place to open a season, and the Lions have plenty of firepower on both sides of the football. Aidan Hutchinson is coming off a career-high 14.5-sack season, establishing himself as one of the NFL’s top edge rushers and earning second-team All-Pro honors.

The Saints also won’t have a completely healthy roster.

Running back Alvin Kamara is expected to miss the opener with an MCL injury, meaning offseason addition Travis Etienne will be taking on a significant workload. First-round wide receiver Jordyn Tyson will also miss the first four games after landing on injured reserve with a hamstring injury. Defensively, New Orleans will be without defensive tackle Bryan Bresee and possibly defensive end Cam Jordan.

Still, there are several reasons to believe the Saints can make this interesting.

Detroit will also be without two key defensive backs, Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who are on the PUP list and will miss at least the first four games. That could give Shough some opportunities to attack a secondary that isn’t at full strength.

The biggest question for New Orleans may be whether the offensive line can protect Shough and whether the Saints can establish enough of a running game to keep Hutchinson and the Lions’ pass rush from taking over.

If they can, I expect this to be a competitive game into the fourth quarter.

Detroit has the home-field advantage, a talented offense and a defense capable of creating problems for a young New Orleans offense. The Lions are favored by 6.5 points entering the week, and I think they find a way to make enough plays late.

Prediction: Lions 27 – Saints 24

However, if Tyler Shough proves capable of making the big throws in a hostile environment, New Orleans could quickly make it clear that this is a very different team from the one that finished 6-11 last season.

item.title: Gabe Jacas shows improvement in regular season debut
item.description: Jacas recorded his first career sack in the opener.
item.content:encoded:
New England Patriots second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas played 19 defensive snaps in his NFL debut Wednesday night. For the most part, head coach Mike Vrabel liked what he saw.

“Continues to improve. I thought he was active, set some good edges in the run game. Good to see him make a nice play for a tackle for a loss,” Vrabel said. “Some good things. Some things we’ll have to coach and correct, and fix things on special teams. Thought it was an improvement.”

Jacas showed his motor by chasing down Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock for his first career sack in the second quarter. Coming out of halftime, Jacas flashed his athleticism by getting into the backfield for a tackle for loss.

But another play caught the eye of his head coach, with Jacas diagnosing a run play against an unbalanced look and chasing down the ball carrier to record a tackle.

“Thought his most instinctive play since he’s been here was the unbalanced play in the red zone,” Vrabel explained. “They went for a speed break, tackle over in a little bunch to the boundary. They tried to block down on him and he just kind of reacted across the guys’ face and made a tackle for just a few yard gain.

“That was probably the play I was most pleased with. Said this a guy just out here playing.”

After missing the entire spring and start of training camp due to a procedure and contract dispute, things were expectedly moving quickly for Jacas upon his return. That included some consistent issues in the preseason when it came to play recognition.

The struggles left many wondering if Jacas’ Week 1 role would be diminished. But those inside the building noted that the extra preparation time ahead of the season opener was beneficial to Jacas and other younger players across the roster. Jacas felt similarly.

“The preseason definitely helped. Then coming into the game, the preparation that we had, like a week or two to prepare for this game. I was comfortable out there and just playing football,” he said post game.

The Patriots edge group — which currently features just four players on the active roster — was the position with the most question marks on the roster ahead of the season. The group got off to an overall strong start as free agent addition Dre’Mont Jones impressed in his Patriots’ debut, leading the team with seven pressures.

The early flashes from Jacas were then promising, and the 23-year building on that performance would be a welcomed development for the edge group.

“Not bad. I mean, there’s a lot of stuff I can clean up,” Jacas said of his performance. “First sack, first game. Not too bad, just look at the film when I get back and work on the things I need to work on. You know, just continue to improve as weeks go on.”

item.title: OC Matt Nagy will call plays from upstairs Sunday vs. Cowboys
item.description: Nagy chooses the “calm” of being away from the sideline.
item.content:encoded:
After experimenting during the preseason with calling plays from the sideline and upstairs in a booth high above the field, New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said Thursday he will work from upstairs Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys.

“I’m excited about it. I think that I’ve always been down on the field. When I was a quality control coach, I was up in the box for one year,” Nagy said on Thursday. “So, I wanted to experiment with that in the preseason, and I was able to do that. I really liked it. You can see a lot more from up there.”

The tradeoff, of course, is giving up the personal interactions and feeling the game from the sideline.

“It takes away a little bit of the on the field element of being able to communicate and talk all the time, but there’s a calm in the box,” Nagy said. “And for me, first time in this role as a play caller, OC being up in that box, I just feel like I can see things a lot better and then have the ultimate trust in the staff and being able to see things so that they can communicate to me what they’re seeing. And we’ve got the telephone, too, so I can always jump on the phone with (quarterback) Jaxson (Dart) if I need to. But I’m excited about that opportunity.”

Here are more takeaways from Nagy’s Thursday media availability.

On the Giants’ offensive scheme …

“What I would say to that is, we talk about, Coach Harbs (Head Coach John Harbaugh) talks about principles and methods and what that means and you can relay that to an offense is, I learned this game through Andy Reid, (former NFL coach) Marty Morningweg when I was in Philadelphia. And I learned that foundation of this offense and that offense for me. Took it to Kansas City, took it to Chicago, and now here I am. And again, this opportunity that I have is a first for me. So, being here to be able to take some of the things that we do as a staff and make it ours, that’s been some of the times for me selfishly, it’s been fun just putting this thing together. So, I’m excited to see how this thing goes this year, because I think you’re going to see it’s our offense. It’s no other offense from prior history. You know, it’s ours.”

On what he wants to see from Jaxson Dart …

“We want Jaxson to be able to play fast. We want him to be himself. He’s a special talent. And it’s our job as coaches to take all this time that we’ve had to do it. And that’s what we’ve put together is a game plan that we think is to his strengths. But at the same point in time too, we got to make sure that there’s going to be times in the game where we just got to let him cut it loose and continue to build every week. This isn’t, there’s going to be good plays, there’s going to be bad plays, but how does he keep that up? It’s going to be an emotional time. Sunday night football against the Cowboys, a lot of emotions going on. He’s a competitor. So, I want him to stay calm, extremely confident, play fast and execute and just be a complete leader, but also just be himself, man. Cut it loose and have fun.”

On where Dart has grown …

“Probably just the confidence and understanding of the concepts that we’re doing, both run and pass. There was probably some frustration early on because sometimes you don’t know, it’s the first time you’re running a play, you don’t really know the play. And now when we’re out here, he knows the play, he has multiple reps. And so, we can build off of that. We can teach off of that. Now we’ve got to transfer it to the game and some unscouted looks. And so, I think for him, again, his growth, and he’s so mature for being 23 years old and having limited experience in the NFL, super mature, very calm, but he’s really good. So, we got to make sure we use his strengths.”

On Odell Beckham’s acceptance of his role …

“He hasn’t brought that up at all as far as that part of it, which is probably hard. Odell has come to me at times and we’ve had some good conversations where he’ll almost come to me like I’m the conduit between him and Jaxson because he wants to be careful and gentle with how much he gets in Jaxson’s ear, with how he, he’s played a lot of football. He’s seen a lot of things. And so, what I can do is I can balance some of the questions he has and filter it to Jaxson. And then the other times he goes to Jaxson. But what I find really professional about Odell is that he doesn’t want to put too much on Jaxson’s plate mentally. And I think he’s in a good spot too. You guys see what he can do. He can do a lot of good things, but we also have a lot in this offense and there’s details. So, every now and then, if he screws up an assignment, the biggest thing we say is don’t do it again. And he’s done a good job with that.”

item.title: Andy Reid reaffirms the Chiefs’ confidence in rookie Kahlil Benson
item.description: On Thursday, Kansas City’s head coach and quarterback discussed a curious impending lineup decision.
item.content:encoded:
When the Kansas City Chiefs host the Denver Broncos on the season opener of “Monday Night Football” to close Week 1, all indications are that rookie Kahlil Benson will start at left tackle.

Starter Josh Simmons has been out of action since midway through training camp with a lower back ailment. Simmons missed this week’s initial practice on Thursday.

The decision is curious in that Benson went undrafted in April — and only signed with Kansas City after trying out at the team’s rookie camp. Also, the former Indiana and Colorado talent never took a snap at left tackle in college. Benson has played almost exclusively on the right side both at tackle and guard.

Speaking before Thursday’s practice, head coach Andy Reid expressed confidence in Benson’s ability to hold down the fort for Simmons. Reid also defers to his own years of experience and that of the coaching staff.

“He’s done a nice job for us,” Reid remarked of the rookie. “He’s obviously shown us that he has the ability to play, and we wouldn’t put him in there if we didn’t think that.

“We’ve all been through that. I think when we first got hired, we thought we probably were pretty good at it. So, I want his confidence to be that and go out and play and just use his abilities and write a good story.”

Benson will be tasked with protecting star quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who is expected to see his first game action on Monday since tearing multiple knee ligaments in December. A decade of NFL experience has taught Mahomes to be ready when backups are on the field. He trusts that Benson will get the job done — and the possible downgrade on the offensive line does not change his own responsibilities.

“Either way,” said Mahomes on Thursday, “you’ve got to roll. That’s the beauty of football is that it’s next man up, and you have to go up there and compete. These guys have gotten a ton of reps in training camp. They’ve gotten a ton of reps throughout their entire life, and they’re going out and living their dream as well.

“So, I’ve got trust in anyone that the coaches put out there, because I know that they’ve worked their tail off to be at that spot. There’ll be mistakes here and there, but at the end of the day, you’ve got to go out there and trust those guys and make the plays whenever the plays need to be made.”

item.title: 5 points: The important Cowboys-Giants storylines
item.description: What storylines will you be following during Sunday’s game?
item.content:encoded:
Football is back, and so is the five points column. Last year, this article came after the Dallas Cowboys played to break down what went right or wrong, and boy, a lot went wrong last year. I’m sorry if a lot of it came off as complaining. This year will hopefully be different.

Instead, this year it will come before each matchup to help set the table on both sides and highlight the key factors to watch for each week. Some points will be a little more on the nose, while others may be a little more obscure.

This will be the 13th season the Cowboys will begin the year with a game against the New York Giants. The Cowboys are 11-1 in the previous 12 games. History would dictate Dallas walking out of MetLife Stadium with a win, but the Giants have overhauled their team the same way the Cowboys have.

It should be a game that’s more competitive than people think. Here are five points to watch for on Sunday.

First Point: Did Dallas build their wall with sticks or bricks?

If you don’t believe in an over-the-hill Odell Beckham Jr., or Jaxson Dart to take the next step as a quarterback, be fearful of what the Giants defensive line can do to the Cowboys offense. Headlined by Brian Burns, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Abdul Carter, and rookie first-round pick Arvell Reese, New York has reimagined a slew of pass rushers that mirror how they won their Super Bowl matchups against the New England Patriots.

Dallas’ offensive line is young but growing quickly through continuity. However, Tyler Guyton needs to carry over his offseason bump to the regular season, Terence Steele needs to hold off Broderick Jones, and T.J. Bass has to fill in for All-Pro Tyler Smith for the next month or more.

A second-year leap from Carter could be the key to the Giants’ pass rush Sunday night, especially if they move him all over the defense similar to how Micah Parsons played in Dallas. When Carter was on the field, the Giants generated quick pressure on 18.6% of opponent dropbacks, which would have been the second-highest mark of any defense on the season, per NFL Pro.

How Dallas neutralizes the Giants’ pass rush will unlock whatever they want to do on offense. They can do that early by establishing the run and limiting the damage on the outside.

Second Point: Jaxson Dart prefers his eggs scrambled

If you have watched enough Cowboys football over the last decade, you understand the problem that’s plagued the Dallas defense has been the mobile quarterback. Rob Marinelli’s old saying of “keep the quarterback in the well” echoes every time an opposing QB scrambles for seven yards a carry.

New York’s second-year signal caller was one of the best at getting out of the pocket last year. Dart had 18 explosive runs last year, tied with Patrick Mahomes for most in the league, and a 61.6% rushing success rate, per NFL Pro. That was the highest among QBs with at least 35 carries last season, and the fourth-highest career mark among QBs with at least 75 carries in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016).

The Cowboys’ defense gave up the third-most rush yards per game (23.4) and the most touchdowns (8) in the league to quarterbacks running. Having the league’s worst defense will do that.

If Christian Parker wants to put his stamp on this defense, it’ll be keeping them disciplined and not allowing Dart to run all over the field for first downs. Maybe someone like Caleb Downs can be used as a spy on Dart to make sure that if he leaves the pocket, he’s there to clean it up before it reaches seven to ten yards downfield.

Dallas no longer has a Micah Parsons on the outside to put Dart in pressure situations. Collapsing the pocket from the inside will bode well for Dallas’ defense. They need a big night from Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark.

Third Point: Calling your Schott

Brian Schottenheimer defied expectations placed on him last season as a play-caller. The Cowboys had a top-ten offense in almost every major category, along with career seasons from Dak Prescott, Javonte Williams, and George Pickens.

The one black mark against the unit was how they fared in the red zone. Dallas finished 18th in red zone efficiency at 56.9 percent. Still middle of the league, but not good enough for an offense with this much talent. How Schottenheimer responds with his play-calling in year two, especially in the red zone, could be what puts Dallas over the top as a true NFC contender.

The Giants’ pass rushers can be mitigated Sunday night by how Schottenheimer calls the game, so the sequence of play calls and how in tune he is with Prescott will matter in Dallas winning Week 1.

Fourth Point: Passing the buck(eye)

Before the NFL draft, Cowboys fans had sugar plums dancing in their heads of what life could be like with Caleb Downs falling to them and pairing him with Christian Parker. All along, it felt like a pipe dream. There’s no way Downs would not fall past the New York Giants, who picked twice in the top ten.

John Harbaugh called Downs a generational talent at safety, almost tipping the internal feelings around the national champion. Then the unexpected happened. The Giants didn’t pass on Downs just once, but twice. The Cowboys traded up with the Miami Dolphins to pick 11, and the rest is history.

Schottenheimer talked about how they felt heading into draft weekend; there was no chance they would be lucky enough to land their No. 1 player, but that’s what makes it so fun—the unknown.

Downs will be making his professional debut as a member of the Cowboys on Sunday Night Football with all the eyes of the world on him—and yet he seems unfazed by it all. You wonder if there will be any extra motivation for someone who already plays with a chip on his shoulder, facing the team that passed on him twice.

Players have talked in the past about how things like this can give them extra motivation in a game. Hopefully, for the Cowboys’ sake, it could bring out the very best in Downs in primetime.

Fifth Point: Under-the-radar players

There are a few guys who have not been talked about as much this offseason that could be key to a Cowboys victory:

  • Cooper Beebe – The Cowboys center has had a quiet offseason. For the center position, that’s a great thing. Dexter Lawrence is no longer in the picture for the Giants, leaving veterans DJ Reader and Shelby Harris to fill the void. Both players are nowhere near the same level as Lawrence, so Beebe should have some favorable matchups. How he fares against some of the edge rushers who line up on the inside will be the biggest challenge.
  • Javonte Williams – The $24 million man is looking to carry the success from a breakout 2025 season into this year. Williams had 1,201 yards rushing and 13 total touchdowns. From a fantasy angle and production angle, his career year flew under the radar over the offseason. As the unquestioned bell cow for Dallas’ offense, Williams should have success running up the middle without Lawrence on defense.
  • Tyler Booker – The second-year man out of Alabama had a great rookie season. He should be even better in his second year, with a full offseason and NFL acclimation under his belt. There’s a chance he could earn Pro Bowl honors when it’s all said and done.
  • Jalen Thompson – It’s not often a team’s most expensive outside free-agent acquisition goes unnoticed, but Thompson has done just that. Unfortunately, he dealt with a lot of nagging injuries from mini-camp to training camp, so he didn’t see the field as much. However, the excitement around him and the type of player he can be for a Christian Parker defense shouldn’t be overlooked.

item.title: NFL survivor contest picks, predictions, advice, strategy: My favorite Week 1 selections
item.description: NFL survivor pools are back and Matt Russell runs through Week 1, giving his favorite picks to help you advance.
item.content:encoded:
You've got a better chance of stepping up into the hole against Derrick Henry than you do of stopping the momentum of NFL Survivor contests in the current football betting landscape. 

The world's largest (legal) contest, hosted at Circa Sports in Las Vegas, has over 20,000 entries for its guaranteed $20 million pool, and it's not even the biggest prize available in the space for this coming season.

The siren's song of "just" needing to pick one winner per week in America's most dissected sport makes everyone believe they can navigate the perils and potholes that the unpredictability of football supplies, but there's more to it than just "pick and pray."

Upgrade to Fantasy Plus and gain your edge in player projections and much more

Of course, you don't need to play in a high-roller edition of survivor. You, your friends, and family can play along as well here at Yahoo Sports, but a smaller pool of participants also changes the calculus when it comes to strategy. After all, the fewer the entrants, the less conceptual risk is necessary. 

Each week (until we've exhausted all reasonable paths of survival), we'll look at the Survivor Contest landscape and the best options available while understanding that it matters who you've already taken and what you might be giving up by burning a team that week. 

Week 1 moneylines

How likely is a team to win and you'll advance? The betting market provides the answer to that each week with the moneyline, which we can convert to an implied win probability.

Market power ratings

It's not as simple as picking the team most likely to win, because once you use that team, you can't use them again. What is simple is that if you're going to make it through the 18-week season, then you need to use 18 teams. That means, at some point, you'll be trusting the 18th-best team in the NFL — an unnerving thought. 

Here's a list of the current top 18 teams (with help from the betting market), and an estimation of their value to the point spread: 

  • Rams: 19.7

  • Seahawks: 18.1

  • Bills: 17.8

  • Ravens: 17.3

  • Lions: 16.7

  • Chargers: 16.7

  • Chiefs: 16.5

  • Packers: 16.5

  • 49ers: 16.5

  • Texans: 16.5

  • Eagles: 16.2

  • Patriots: 16.2

  • Bears: 15.9

  • Cowboys: 15.7

  • Broncos: 15.7

  • Bengals: 15.7

  • Jaguars: 14.6

  • Vikings: 14.0

Picking the most likely team to win each week, or the highest available team on this list above, means that you're giving up the opportunity to use them again later, and while every week is technically created equal, trusting a team in September is nerve-wracking, but doing so at some point in December is real tension. 

Week 1's top choices

As we look at the best options for Week 1 and onward, we'll be factoring in the decision tree that will sprout from that pick. The implied probability derived from the moneyline should answer any questions about why the favorite should win, but the nuance is found in what you're giving up by using them now and not later (with a projected point spread projection for those matchups). 

Jaguars (78.6%) over Browns 

Jacksonville's not the biggest favorite in Week 1, but you're backing a team that won nine straight games to end the regular season a year ago. 

On the other side, the Browns have tabbed Deshaun Watson as their starting quarterback, but there's nothing we've seen from him in Cleveland — either before he tore his Achilles in 2024 or during this preseason — that would make us think that Cleveland's offense is going to come alive. Plus, with defensive metrics that went from great to terrible depending on whether Myles Garrett was on the field, with the 2025 Defensive Player of the Year in Los Angeles, there's less to worry about for Trevor Lawrence. 

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 10 at Titans (JAX -4.5)

  • Week 12 vs. Titans (JAX -7.5)

It can be a fool's errand to try to project who the easiest matchups will be down the road, when we haven't seen anyone play in the regular season, but the Jaguars do have a pair of games with the Titans — a team that's seen money come against them in Week 1 at home … against the New York Jets. 

Chargers (80.9%) over Cardinals 

For the second spot on this list — generally reserved for a significant favorite — the game with the biggest line (and likely to be the most popular pick) does come with some trepidation. 

Cardinals QB Jacoby Brissett looked more capable last season than, say, Watson has. With legitimate weapons like Trey McBride, Marvin Harrison Jr., the emergent Michael Wilson and a pair of new running backs, combined with some uncertainty around the Chargers breaking in a new defensive coordinator — and a new offensive coordinator — and you could envision more of a sweat than you thought you were bargaining for. 

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 2 vs. Raiders (LAC -8.5)

  • Week 11 vs. Jets (LAC -8)

  • Week 16 at Dolphins (LAC -7.5)

The other reason(s) not to just roll with the chalk are that there are three other spots where the Chargers look appealing, and one is literally next week. 

At the moment, based on lookahead lines, there are two games with bigger betting lines in Week 2, and two nice options for later in the season might be enough for you to save the Chargers. 

Steelers (62.5%) over Falcons 

That the Steelers aren't even considered our "dark horse" pick only tells you how weird things might get for those either brave enough, or who are in a super-deep pool — where it's a necessity to zig while others zag. 

From a matchup perspective, if you're ever going to back a 42-year-old quarterback, doing so when the weather is warm is the time to do it. 

Aaron Rodgers' availability isn't the only consideration on the Pittsburgh side of things. For how long the defending AFC North champions will have a fully healthy defense is anyone's guess. Specifically, T.J. Watt, with whom the Steelers have a considerably better record than without, but also 37-year-old Cameron Hayward and a secondary featuring 31-year-old Jalen Ramsey and 29-year-old Jamel Dean (both older by defensive back standards). 

On the Falcons' side, Tua Tagovailoa will start Week 1, having done very little in the lead-up to the season to take the starting job from Michael Penix Jr., even as Penix Jr. recovers from ACL surgery. 

Rodgers is vulnerable against a formidable pass rush, but the Falcons are without both of 2025's highly-drafted edge rushers: Jalon Walker (season-ending injury) and James Pearce (eight-game suspension). 

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 8 vs. Browns (PIT -3)

  • Week 17 at Titans (PIT -1.5)

Before you think we're irrationally high on the Steelers this season, the fact that the other two weeks where we might consider them come with spread projections shorter than this game with the Falcons should confirm that it might be now or never for Pittsburgh. 

You'll note that the Steelers didn't make our top-18 list above, but:

  1. Pittsburgh just missed the cut, as they're bunched with the Buccaneers and Commanders around the top 20

  2. So, if you're in a contest that requires more than 18 teams selected to get to the end (like, Circa's), then the Steelers become more viable 

  3. Once you get to the top 16-24 teams in power-ranking, the order becomes personal preference

The dark horse: Raiders (61.9%) over Dolphins

There's no darker horse than the Raiders, but if you're looking for a pick with a low selection percentage, you could do worse than backing a team actively trying to win this season versus one that's more "wait-and-see."

Kirk Cousins, healthy and with his old offensive coach from when they were both with the Vikings, provides more certainty on the offensive side than the Dolphins have with new quarterback Malik Willis, who doesn't have the same roster support around him that he had in Green Bay. 

While both teams have new regimes, the Raiders are further along in their rebuilding plan. For at least one game, Las Vegas has the ideal combination of already having its potential quarterback of the future, without dealing with the growing pains of starting Fernando Mendoza just yet.

Estimated Availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 16 vs. Titans (LV -1)

I think you already knew there wasn't going to be another glaring spot to take the Raiders, but at least they might be favored at home against the Titans in Week 16? 

That's not something you'd want to plan for, though, as the Raiders aren't in anyone's top-18, 20, or even 25 teams, by power rating, and will likely have turned the team over to Mendoza by then.

So, maybe, if there's 20,000 other entries in your pool, finding yourself in a virtual "Black Hole," might be the way to play Week 1.

You can find more valuable betting analysis from Yahoo Sports betting contributor Matt Russell at THE WINDOW.

item.title: Vikings will provide an excellent early test for the Packers on Sunday
item.description: Zaire Franklin is ready for the challenge. Are you?
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Vikings are generally not expected to be a front-runner in the race for an NFC North title this season. They have the worst odds to win the division of any of the four teams, and there are questions up and down their roster. However, for a Green Bay Packers team looking to get a good litmus test of where they stand to start the year, a road game in Minnesota might be just what the doctor ordered.

You want to figure out your offensive line? You’re going to have to do it quickly in this game against Brian Flores’ tough, creative defense. You need to figure out who you can count on at defensive tackle and edge? A matchup with an offensive line that looks questionable (especially on the interior) should provide some opportunities. Your new defensive coordinator needs to settle into a groove with his new personnel? Cool, go face the quarterback he just coached for the last two seasons in Arizona and whose tendencies he therefore knows extremely well.

At least one Packers defender is eager for the challenge of a road game against a divisional opponent for the opener. As fans, maybe we should take a page from Zaire Franklin and embrace the challenge that awaits the Packers as well.

Jordan Love, passing weapons will lead Packers to 11-6 record | Packersnews.com
I appreciate that Pete Dougherty doesn’t waste time and puts his record prediction in the headline. That’s right about where I’m at, but we’ll see where APC readers’ poll results land later today.

Career reboots: Vikings’ Murray faces Packers’ Gannon | ESPN
Gannon and Murray worked together in Arizona for the last two years. Which one knows the other’s weaknesses better? We should get a good idea on Sunday afternoon.

NFL Week 1 uniforms: Vikings rocking throwbacks, Bengals go orange | ESPN
As a uniform classicist, I appreciate Minnesota’s throwback threads, and I appreciate it even more when they wear them against the Packers. It gives me nostalgia for the look and feel of the matchups between these teams in the mid-90s.

Three Matchups That Will Decide Packers’ Week 1 Game at Vikings | SI.com
Surprise, surprise: the line of scrimmage when the Packers are on offense is the biggest one. If the Packers’ offensive line can’t hold up, they’ll need some magic from Jordan Love to win.

Kamal Hadden, Anthony Campbell learned to dream big at ‘Dream U’ | Packers.com
This is an incredible story: Hadden and Campbell were juco teammates at Independence Community College in Kansas back in 2019.

Packers LG Aaron Banks expecting to be game-time decision vs. Vikings | Packers Wire
He said that in the locker room on Thursday, so don’t be surprised if we see Jager Burton getting significant snaps in his rookie debut.

Ryanair boss ‘disputing’ account of passenger partially sucked out of window | Belfast Telegraph
Look, the passenger was only sucked “towards” the window, not out of it! Everything is fine!

It’s not hard to see why Franklin is already so well-liked in the Packers locker room.
