item.title: Week 1 Best and Worst WR, TE matchups: Garrett Wilson set to smash, Xavier Worthy faces tough test
item.description: A breakdown of how secondaries handle slot pass catchers and boundary receivers.
item.content:encoded:
It’s always a popular question — or string of questions — during my Friday live streams on the NFL on NBC YouTube channel: Which slot receivers have the best matchups? And which outside (boundary) wideouts are in good spots?

While it shouldn’t be the deciding factor in how you make your weekly lineup decisions, knowing if a pass catcher has a particularly good or bad matchup is valuable information that can sometimes serve as a tiebreaker for your most vexing start-sit decisions.

This season I’ll use this space to break down the best (and worst) matchups for pass catchers operating from the slot and those lining up primarily on the boundary. Some pass catchers, as you know, split their time between the boundary and the slot, making this little exercise more complicated. I’ll do my best to pinpoint the most appealing (and unappealing) weekly matchups, at first with data from the 2025 season, and then -- after a week or two -- with 2026 data.

RotoPat’s Week 1 Fantasy Football Rankings
Ranking and evaluating all of Week 1’s top plays at quarterback, running back, receiver, tight end, kicker and defense.
  • Patrick Daugherty,

Slot Matchups

Falcons vs. Steelers: Pittsburgh’s struggles against slot pass catchers should be something of a boon for Kyle Pitts, who last season ran 36 percent of his routes from the slot (and 44 percent from the in-line position). There’s reason to believe Pitts will see his slot usage increase — even moderately — in Kevin Stefanski’s offense. That popgun-armed Tua Tagovailoa targeted Pitts heavily in the preseason (and reportedly during 11-on-11s in training camp) is another plus for the tight end.

Eagles vs. Commanders: DeVonta Smith last season led the Eagles in slot rate. You don’t need another reason to start Smith though. This is more about Dallas Goedert, who ran half of his 2025 routes from the slot and was among the NFL’s most efficient tight ends while doing so. Goedert’s 21 percent first-read target rate from last season is bound to rise with A.J. Brown dispatched to New England. Goedert might be overlooked in a solid matchup, with the Eagles headed into the season opener with a 24.5-point implied total. The same goes for rookie Makai Lemon, who should run from the slot more often than not.

Jets vs. Titans: Tennessee’s secondary last year was tormented by enemy slot guys. It’s why enjoyers of my Friday live stream targeted the Titans with slot pass catchers for much of the season. While head coach Robert Saleh has made some adjustments that could make the Titans slightly better against slot receivers, I think we’ll need to see it before we believe it. Mason Taylor in 2025 ran 34 percent of his routes from the slot and could play a surprisingly big role in the New York passing offense while Kenyon Sadiq recovers from offseason hernia surgery. Isaiah Williams, listed as the Jets' starting slot wideout, ran 68 percent of his routes from the slot in 2025, and could be a (very) deep league option for Week 1. This matchup is mostly about Taylor as a streaming tight end option though.

Raiders vs. Dolphins: Miami’s secondary was cooked last season from the slot, giving up the league’s fourth-highest completion rate over expected on slot throws. Michael Mayer, with Brock Bowers (knee) sidelined as usual, could be the main beneficiary of this juicy matchup. Mayer in 2025 saw a target on a decent 23 percent of his routes in the disaster we called the Vegas offense, and in games without Bowers he saw a target on a borderline-elite 26 percent of his routes. Mayer has a real chance to cook against Miami in Week 1. I wouldn’t blame you for playing Mayer over options like Jake Ferguson, Travis Kelce, or Mark Andrews.

Commanders vs. Eagles: It could be something of a rough start for Stefon Diggs if he runs primarily from the slot in the Washington offense. That Eagles coverage unit was a nightmare for slot guys in 2025 (and 2024, for that matter). Last year they allowed the sixth-lowest completion rate over expected on slot targets along with the fourth-lowest yards per game from the slot.

FLEX Finder Week 1: Where to find value before roles take shape
Rivers McCown comes up with a list of players he hopes will defy their low cost to be fantasy football heroes for Week 1.
  • Rivers McCown,

Boundary Matchups

Giants vs. Cowboys: The Dallas defense, which was gouged last season for the league’s fourth-highest dropback EPA and the third-highest passing success rate, is going to be better this season. The addition of Caleb Downs, if nothing else, all but guarantees that. I wouldn’t read too much into the Cowboys being burned on the perimeter last season as they head into their Week 1 matchup against John Harbaugh’s Giants. Malik Nabers, in case you were wondering, ran routes from the boundary at a 76 percent clip last year before his season-ending injury. And don’t get cute with Malachi Fields in this spot.

Jets vs. Titans: Between the slot metrics and these boundary numbers it seems Garrett Wilson is in a pretty good spot for the Jets’ opening game. Only two teams allowed a higher completion rate over expected to boundary wideouts than the Titans in 2025, and only four secondaries gave up more yards per game (118) to outside receivers. Wilson sure looks like a Week 1 smash.

Vikings vs. Packers: Jordan Addison last year had a grand total of one catch for eight yards in two games against Green Bay. Maybe we can be generous and write that off as part of the failed JJ McCarthy Experiment. That Addison operates from the boundary on around 80 percent of his pass routes could translate into an interesting matchup in Week 1 against the Pack. Addison, who has reportedly worked extensively with Kyler Murray this offseason, should be in lineups this week. You probably knew that already.

Chiefs vs. Broncos: It’s a nightmare Week 1 for Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton, and whoever else is going to run pass routes from the boundary. Denver’s elite coverage unit obliterated opposing outside receivers last season, allowing just 90 total yards per game to boundary pass catchers. That should mean more target funneling to slot pass catchers, namely Rashee Rice — who last year ran about half his routes from the slot — and Travis Kelce.

item.title: Five Good Texans questions with Buffalo Ramblings
item.description: Matthew Bynum of Buffalo Ramblings joins BRB for five questions
item.content:encoded:
The NFL scheduling has its quirks and in one of those quirks, the Texans and the Bills match up for the third season in a row. The Texans owned Josh Allen in the first two matchups, but we will have to see if that happens yet again. A new season also marks a new opportunity to catch up with our comrades at the other sites. Matthew Bynum has always been a joy to work with. We caught up with him to check in on the Bills before Sunday.

Battle Red Blog: The Bills achieved a lot of success under Sean McDermott but it ultimately wasn’t enough. Why do you think he came up short?

Matthew Bynum: Sean McDermott accomplished so much as head coach of the Bills that it feels a bit unfair to say he came up short. But he did, simply because his teams never did win an AFC Championship Game, nor play in or (better) win a Super Bowl. It’s a small but significant list of items McDermott didn’t check off after nine seasons.

McDermott and general manager Brandon Beane built teams to take down the Kansas City Chiefs. Yet every time they faced KC in the playoffs, they lost despite Josh Allen playing out of his mind most of the time. McDermott came up short because he was never the best coach in playoff games against the Chiefs.

That’s enough, and a lot, but that’s not all there is to it. A very demanding coach, McDermott’s defensive scheme relied on intelligence, both individually and as a unit. Players had to be system sound in their assignments at all times, or else disaster would strike. Yet there was also a focus on a player’s RAS score. That meant trying to make it all work with two often diametrically unique types of player skill sets — the heady leader, and the instinctual athletic freak. Sure, anyone coaching an NFL team would welcome superlatives from both arenas, but McDermott relied on players being able to excel from both buckets whether or not they were capable.

Too often, McDermott’s defense proved to be the team’s playoff Achilles heel. Not always, and in no way is the offense’s failures in more than one playoff game’s final drive overlooked. But the head coach was a defensive mind and his units faltered in the biggest moments.

Time also worked against McDermott. Nearly a decade at the helm is a long time in the NFL. The reason people remember long NFL tenures is because it’s so rare. But McDermott-coached teams hold the best regular-season record in that span. You don’t just move on from a guy because he didn’t get lucky enough to play and win a Super Bowl. Well, at least not until missing out becomes a trauma-filled trend.

The Bills have a large number of catch phrases attached to their worst moments, and McDermott owns many of them. When someone mentions “13 seconds” anyone who follows the sport immediately drifts to Buffalo’s gut-wrenching overtime loss against the Kansas City Chiefs. Many thought a change should have been made after that loss. But a lot of leeway was given simply because it was Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes. It wasn’t yet time.

The trouble is that things didn’t meaningfully improve with time. With Allen, McDermott’s teams were a perennial playoff participant, and a Super Bowl favorite. The postseason was expected, all but guaranteed. Yet McDermott never could find a way toward earning the one seed. His teams were always forced to play on Wild Card Weekend, to the detriment of a severely injured defensive roster.

You’d think that if the playoffs appeared automatic, then a lot of effort would be spent on the team’s second season. But too often if felt like the only one who showed up to play was Allen. That’s unacceptable, no matter how good Allen is. They were dog-walked at home against the Cincinnati Bengals the year after 13 seconds — the same season Damar Hamlin almost died playing against those same Bengals. McDermott managed Hamlin’s trauma well, but that clearly didn’t extend into the postseason. By and large, he should be given a pass for that, but it’s the same game where the Diggs-Allen drama gained legs.

Then there was the home loss to the Chiefs the next season, which saw McDermott settle for a field goal try that wouldn’t have given them a win anyway. Instead, Buffalo missed another kick wide right (yup), and an over-matched defense folded while allowing Mahomes and company to win its first road playoff game.

Whatever a person believes or doesn’t about last season’s loss to the Broncos, the fact is that the Bills were short-handed on defense thanks to McDermott’s decision to play then-rookie cornerback Maxwell Hairston Week 18. That resulted in an injury for Hairston during the closing minutes, which kept him out of postseason play.

Sean Payton diagnosed an obvious weakness following an injury to Tre’Davious White that had Dane Jackson playing for Hairston, and it resulted in a touchdown. It’s not McDermott’s fault that the referees saw things a certain way to call the game as they did. It’s McDermott’s fault that his defense was ill-equipped to overcome injury.

If I had to guess what really happened on an acute level, it’s that McDermott probably lost the locker room. That was perhaps true years earlier (specifically Diggs), but it’s difficult to move on easily from a coach who’s automatic in the regular season. Then there’s what co-owner Terry Pegula mentioned, seeing Allen beside himself. It may be that he’d seen enough and decided the franchise’s most prolific player was beginning to run out of time due to wasted opportunities.

BRB: It’s a new era of Bills football with a new coach and new stadium. What changes are you expecting under Joe Brady?

MB: Well, we’ve been told that the vibe is more relaxed, looser at One Bills Drive. Brady is the youngest head coach in the NFL, and by all accounts he’s a player’s coach who brings a more youthful and energetic swagger. He also comes from Sean Payton’s school of hard knocks (yes, that’s a sleight Payton’s way). No Brady is not a direct clone of Payton, but it would be silly to think he won’t lean on Payton’s leadership example while trying to find his groove. He also has John Fox to help guide him, but Brady’s familiarity with the offense should benefit his transition.

I don’t necessarily expect a huge dynamic shift on offense, and it’s likely we’ll have to wait and see what the offense abandons and adds to know where he and McDermott differed. How much do you change for an offense that just finished top-three in the NFL last season?

I do expect to see running back James Cook III more involved in the passing game. He came out of college dubbed a bona fide dual-threat player, but for the most part his usage there has been as a distant second fiddle. Time will tell if Brady allows Allen to do as he pleases as a run, and if he leans more heavily into the types of west coast scheme Payton teaches.

BRB: Obviously championship windows are about the quarterback. Can you make your best case for Josh Allen to return to MVP Allen?

MB: I guess my move is to offer up that I see zero need for Allen to reascend to an MVP level simply because I still see him playing at that level. Without Allen, the Bills are fighting with the Jets for a spot in the AFC’s basement each season.

Allen raises everyone’s play around him, which included a less-than-stellar wide receivers room last season. All that Buffalo needs is competent play around Allen come playoff time. Otherwise, any MVP-worthy season by Allen will once again be little more than a regular-season award.

But to honor your ask here, I suppose I see Allen winning the MVP if he puts together a season similar to or better than his 2024 campaign, while guiding the team to greater success under a rookie head coach.

BRB: The Bills and Texans have butted heads the last two years. Who are some new Bills that will make a dramatic impact on Sunday?

MB: Hopefully everyone focused on the field at NRG becomes well-versed in wide receiver DJ Moore. He came to Buffalo by way of a trade with the Chicago Bears. To this point, the reviews have been tremendous, where it appears Allen once again has someone capable of playing a role akin to that once held by Stefon Diggs.

Skyler Bell was viewed as a draft steal for Buffalo this past April. He’d battled an injury during the summer, but put together an impressive game in the final preseason tilt. Bell could find opportunities for big plays if Houston commits too many resources elsewhere.

Beyond Moore and Bell on offense, look out for the team’s four-headed tight end room. Each of them were in the building last season, but I like Keleki Latu and especially Jackson Hawes to be bigger parts of the game plan.

Defensively, a lot has changed. The scheme shift sees Bradley Chubb in-house playing edge rusher, while a name familiar to Texans fans — C.J. Gardner-Johnson is set to make a ton of noise in the defensive backfield.

The team’s top rookie this past spring, edge rusher T.J. Parker, isn’t a starter, but he should be given a chance to impact the game in obvious passing situations. Rookie cornerback Davison Igbinosun brings a physical brand of play to outside cornerback, where he’ll likely be used to spell Maxwell Hairston or leveraged based on coverage needs.

The Bills also draft a punter, Tommy Doman Jr., who won the starting job. Is he ready for Week 1? Overall, Buffalo saw nine of its drafted rookies make the 53-man roster.

BRB: Vegas has the Bills as 1.5 point favorites. How do you see the game going? Are there any other bets you feel comfortable recommending?

MB: First off here, I’m a bit surprised at that line. It’s the Josh Allen effect, certainly. Buffalo is marching out a new first-time head coach (prior OC, yes) in Joe Brady, and a new, first-time NFL defensive coordinator in Jim Leonhard, yet they come in as the favorites against a home team with six consecutive NRG wins against them.

Look, NRG Stadium is akin to kryptonite for Allen and the Bills. The team hasn’t won in Houston since 2006, which was 10 matchups and two decades ago. The Texans may present Buffalo with its toughest defensive matchup of the season.

The fact is that we have no idea how the Bills will play, what they’ll look like on offense if it’s different than last season, and how the new 3-4 base defense will fare amid an aggressive mindset.

But there’s one thing in Buffalo’s favor: Let’s talk about Diggs again. Look, that guy is an enigma. He’s (probably still) undeniably talented and a sheer alpha on the football field. He’s also a mercurial cancer who did all he could to sabotage the Bills when things weren’t going his way — and he rarely played his best in the team’s biggest playoff moments.

Why bring him up? Because he’s not a part of this matchup, thankfully. That should help Allen, at least. I still believe that the last time these teams played, Allen forced things in trying to prove to himself and Diggs that the team was just fine without 14. They weren’t, and everyone knew it. As then a member of the Texans, Diggs got in his head and I think that played into Buffalo’s chaotic day in Houston.

I can see this game going either team’s way, to be honest. If history repeats itself, then of course the Bills have no chance at winning Sunday. But Week 1 is its own wild card, and counting out Buffalo due to history may prove foolish. All I have to do is look back to the Bills’ 2025 season opener against the Baltimore Ravens. Late into the fourth quarter it seemed as though Buffalo was heading to 0-1, yet Allen and defensive tackle Ed Oliver had other plans in the closing minutes.

To win, the Bills have to make life uncomfortable for Houston’s offense such that any defensive aggression doesn’t deal a lethal blow. That, and Allen must find a defensive weakness to exploit, even if it’s just taking what the Texans give him.

As for bets, I’m never the person someone should turn to when looking to “invest” in gambling odds. That said, whatever you like for James Cook’s player props, why not bet the over or at least take the easy, favorable odds? Josh Allen is also pretty good at throwing and running for touchdowns in the same game. Might want to look at those options.

We want to thank Matthew for taking the time to answer our questions so thoroughly. Week one is definitely one of those weeks both teams will likely look back on when either celebrating success or lamenting failure. It is finally time to begin enjoying these for real. We want to wish Matthew and the Bills the best of luck this season, but as always we hope the luck begins on Monday.

item.title: Rams' Puka Nacua acknowledges alcohol issues during 'darkest times' of his life
item.description: Nacua entered rehab in March. He could still be disciplined by the NFL during the season.
item.content:encoded:
Puka Nacua told Netflix's Elle Duncan that "alcohol was definitely a thing" as he went through an offseason which he described as the "darkest times I've had in my life."

Prior to Thursday night's Los Angeles Rams-San Francisco 49ers game from Melbourne, Australia, Nacua explained what led him to check into a rehabilitation center in March.

"I was never one to share my fears, my worries," the Rams wide receiver said. "I was always finding different ways to escape from that tension, that stress. I think one, alcohol was definitely a thing for me. Just kind of drowning myself so that the issues and the stress that I was feeling never had the opportunity to be addressed."

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

The 25-year-old Nacua was a 2023 fifth-round draft pick by the Rams out of BYU. He immediately shot to stardom with a 1,400-yard rookie season. In 2025, he was a first-team All-Pro, the NFL's receptions leader and a second-time Pro Bowler after recording 129 catches for 1,715 yards and 10 touchdowns.

Turning into a household name overnight was something Nacua said he struggled to deal with. He was also co-parenting with his son's mother, which led him to isolate himself at times.

Nacua's off-the-field issues this past offseason also included a woman filing a lawsuit against him, accusing him of making an antisemitic statement and biting her shoulder. The woman cited gender violence, assault and battery, and negligence in her lawsuit. Nacua has denied the allegations against him. There were was also several other incidents last season, including appearing on a livestream before a game and agreeing to perform an antisemitic touchdown celebration.

The time in rehab, Nacua said, allowed him to have "open and honest conversations" and he's eager for the future.

"I'm looking forward most to becoming a person that I think my son will be proud of ... and as my son gets older, I can share some of the things that I've learned from the mistakes I've made," Nacua said.

Nacua has practiced with the Rams since training camp opened and caught five passes for 74 yards in the Rams' 27-7 opening game loss to the 49ers. The NFL could still hand out a suspension at some point this season.

item.title: Christian McCaffrey's workload will worry many, but Kaelon Black's usage is what the 49ers and fantasy managers need
item.description: Matt Harmon explains why Christian McCaffrey's reduced workload is actually a good thing for the veteran RB this season.
item.content:encoded:
I regret to inform you that I think San Francisco 49ers rookie running back Kaelon Black seeing the exact usage that we witnessed on Thursday night is smart and ideal for everyone involved. 

There is no doubt that Christian McCaffrey has been a transformative player for the 49ers since he arrived midway through the 2022 NFL season. His ability to bring every rushing concept to the table, alignment versatility as a receiver and overall gravity as a player has brought the offense to life. You can feel how much Kyle Shanahan appreciates his mere presence. You can also feel his pure addiction to just smashing the McCaffrey button over and over, with a complete inability to resist playing him on nearly every snap. 

It was never more apparent than last season, when McCaffrey had an abnormal workload for a running back in the modern era. 

Christian McCaffrey's 480 intended touches (targets + rush attempts) in the regular season and playoffs combined are tied for the fourth-most by an RB in a single season since 2000. pic.twitter.com/Fuu52PGrAH

— Matt Harmon (@MattHarmon_BYB) January 19, 2026

While McCaffrey was a fantasy monster once again thanks to his receiving profile, we can be honest that it clearly took a toll on him as a rusher. McCaffrey ranked 23rd among 33 running backs with over 150 carries in EPA per rush and 28th in yards after contact per rush. Just 8.7% of his carries went for 10-plus yards, 28th out of 33 backs. He was far from one of the most impactful or effective rushers last year, to be kind. 

I will never get it out of my head that McCaffrey described the 2025 campaign as "the hardest year of his life." While it wasn't all about the workload or even football, it was still a strenuous season on his body. It would make all the sense in the world for the team not to grind him into the dust on a weekly basis as he enters his age-30 season. 

As a matter of fact, Shanahan even said himself back in May that it would be smart to not do so again. 

Kyle Shanahan on Christian McCaffrey after insane 2025 workload:

"I want him to have more juice. I want him to be fresher. He doesn't have to take that beating when it's unnecessary. I'm hoping we can have some other guys step up more this year so you don't feel like you need…

— Hayden Winks (@HaydenWinks) May 28, 2026

It was fair to be skeptical that Shanahan would follow through on his statements, considering he's behaved as a man unable to resist the McCaffrey temptation in the past. That doesn't change the fact that it was a perfectly logical desire and even a sharp move.  

I can also understand any skepticism over the idea that Shanahan and the 49ers would actually trust and use a rookie running back they took in the mid-rounds. Especially because Kaelon Black was a surprise Round 3 selection who some evaluators didn't even give a draftable grade. However, his on-field profile quietly fit the exact back they needed alongside McCaffrey. In my guy James Koh's charting of Black's college film, while he didn't find him to be an exciting playmaker whatsoever, he described him "as a viable, workmanlike back" and noted "when you go through the charting, all he does is give you positive plays."

Check out the full profile from @JamesDKoh ⤵️https://t.co/wLkV99ZlKOpic.twitter.com/nFzinIVqrK

— Reception Perception (@RecepPerception) May 7, 2026

Black looked like that exact player on Thursday night: finding holes in outside zone concepts, getting what was blocked to the tune of 14 carries for 65 yards. The 49ers have needed that exact back to be able to take the grinder carries away from McCaffrey. I remember doing shows with Austin Ekeler years ago and he was constantly pleading for the Chargers to find a back like that to pass off some of the work to stay fresh. There's no doubt McCaffrey wants the same at this stage of his career and Shanahan confirmed it was his desire as well.

To the point that it's good for McCaffrey, we referenced the 2025 rushing stats, or lack thereof, earlier. In Week 1, McCaffrey took 20% of his carries for 10-plus yards and averaged 6.8 yards per carry. He looked noticeably more explosive and ran with more aggression on fewer opportunities. McCaffrey also maintained a clear lead in the passing game with 18 routes and a team-high eight targets to 10 and one for Black. 

McCaffrey might not have the absolutely legendary fantasy upside we've seen in his league-winner years if this split continues — which it should. Yet, the risk of injuries and a decline in rushing efficiency are much lower as a result. I don't know about you, but I want McCaffrey here for a long time this season, not just a good time early in the year. I'll take the trade-off. 

From a brass-tacks perspective, the end results here aren't even bad in fantasy. Are you going to turn your nose up at 18 opportunities and 88 yards from scrimmage? I don't think so. People already have way bigger problems with some other fantasy players and we're not even out of the opening slate. This development won't come close to one of the things I'm panicking about most from Week 1. 

If we redrafted today, McCaffrey would still be a fringe Round 1 selection for me. With games against the Dolphins and Cardinals on deck the next two weeks, I can't see myself ranking him outside of the top-five running backs.

Meanwhile, Black becomes one of the best running back stashes and backup insurance policy holds in the game with perhaps some level of standalone value. By the way, to speak to the foreseeable nature of where we are, this was true before Week 1. I added him to the end of my top-150 rankings this draft season after he enjoyed a strong preseason and earned the RB2 gig. Either way, Black should be one of the most-added players heading into Week 2.

item.title: On Paper: Lions vs. Saints preview, prediction
item.description: A statistical preview and score prediction for Detroit Lions vs. New Orleans Saints.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to another season of On Paper, my statistical-heavy Detroit Lions preview that attempts to be as objective as possible.

For those new to On Paper, a brief explanation.

At the heart of On Paper are eight charts that detail each team’s primary units (pass offense, run offense, pass defense, run defense). Those charts are filled with weekly performances that compare it to the opponent’s average. This provides proper context to show that holding the Lions passing offense to 120 yards is much different than holding the Jets to that yardage. Cells that are green indicate a better than average performance, yellow is within 5% of averages, and red means you stunk that week.

Then we compare the units that face off. If there’s one thing about NFL previews that enrages me, it’s when analysts compare units (ie: who has the better offense, defense, QB?). That doesn’t matter. The quarterbacks don’t ever share the field. Instead, it matters how the Lions pass offense matches with the opponent’s pass defense. So after throwing a bunch of stats at you, I provide a key matchup and my overall thoughts on who has the advantage in each matchup—which is graded on a 1-5 scale based on how big the advantage is, how important I believe that matchup is to the overall outcome, and just my overall confidence. This is the only part that is a bit subjective.

At the end, I add up all the advantages, see who has the edge, and provide a final score prediction. In the comments, be sure to give your score prediction. The closest to the actual score will get a shout out in next week’s On Paper.

Now, let’s get to it.

Lions pass offense (6th in DVOA in 2025) vs. Saints pass defense (19th)

Despite a running game that fell apart, significant issues on the offensive line, and an offensive coordinator that just didn’t fit, Jared Goff and the Lions passing offense remained pretty efficient all season. The 2025 season will always be a great counter-example to those who claim Goff needs everything to be perfect around him to be successful.

In 2025, the Lions and Goff finished:

  • 4th in yards per attempt (7.4)
  • 3rd in passer rating (103.6)
  • 7th in dropback EPA (0.167)
  • 9th in dropback success rate (48.5%)

By nearly every metric, this was a top-10 passing offense.

So what has changed this year? Well, in terms of weapons, nothing is really all that different. Sam LaPorta is healthier, Isaac TeSlaa is a year older, and that’s about it.

But the offensive line has been completely revamped. Penei Sewell went from right to left tackle. Rookie Blake Miller takes his spot on the right. Cade Mays Juice Scruggs takes over at center for Graham Glasgow. And Ben Bartch and Christian Mahogany are still battling for the left guard position. Second-year right guard Tate Ratledge? You just stay there and keep being you.

Pass protection was an issue last year. Despite Goff being one of the quickest quarterbacks in time-to-throw (fifth), he also faced the 14th-highest pressure rate, and took a career-high 38 sacks (eighth among all NFL quarterbacks). The Lions also ranked 31st in ESPN’s pass block win rate and 24th in PFF pass blocking grade.

Are the Lions decidedly better on the offensive line in 2026? It’s impossible to know right now, but I’m not entirely optimistic it will look better to start the year given just how many moving parts there are. So some protection issues should be expected early, but Goff should still be able to orchestrate at a top-10 level of efficiency.

The Saints’ pass defense wasn’t good last year, but as you can see from the chart, it got significantly better as the season went on. Part of that is due to playing ONLY terrible passing offenses in their final eight games, but it’s reasonable to think they also improved as a unit down the stretch.

If you didn’t pay attention to the quality of their opponents, the difference between the first and second half of the season would be incredibly stark:

Weeks 1-9

  • 29th in passer rating allowed (107.2)
  • 26th in dropback EPA
  • 27th in dropback success rate

Week 10-18

  • 7th in passer rating allowed (74.7)
  • 5th in dropback EPA
  • 1st in dropback success rate

Those are drastic swings and shouldn’t be ignored completely. It’s very normal for a team to start figuring things out in Year 1 of a new coaching staff toward the end of the season. But… also… just look at those offenses. They didn’t face a single team who averaged a passer rating above 90 in their final eight games.

That makes trying to predict how 2026 will go difficult. The Saints didn’t make a ton of changes on defense this offseason. They lost linebacker Demario Davis but replaced him with a far younger Kaden Ellis. They also bolstered the interior of their defensive line with second-round pick Christen Miller… but they lost Brian Bresee to a season-ending injury and Cam Jordan won’t play this week.

Last year, the Saints were pretty inconsistent as a pass rushing team. They ranked 24th in pressure rate (31.9%), 23rd in PFF pass rushing grade (66.6), and 22nd in ESPN pass rush win rate (35%), but they still produced the 10th-most sacks.

Coverage was a different story. Kool-Aid McKinstry had a bit of a breakout year (17 passes defended, 3 INTs), and the Saints sport a trusted safety duo in Justin Reid (66.7 PFF grade last year) and Julian Blackmon (82.4).

Player to watch: Chase Young vs. Blake Miller. Right, I forgot about Young. Despite playing just 12 games, he produced 49 pressures and 10.0 sacks. Last year, he almost played exclusively opposite the left tackle (529 snaps there vs. just 13 on the right), but I wouldn’t be surprised to see New Orleans change up strategy when the options are Penei Sewell or a rookie in his first NFL game.

Advantage: Lions +1. I’m probably not going to move far from +1s early in the season with very little relevant data to go off of. However, I can feel pretty confident in Detroit here because they’ve been doing it longer and more consistently, and I’m still not sure who the Saints are just because they played a bunch of terrible offenses to finish 2025.

Lions run offense (10th) vs. Saints run defense (8th)

After some inconsistent—but occasionally great—performances early in the season, Detroit’s run offense absolutely collapsed down the stretch, and it was a big part of their downfall—losing four of their last six games.

The season-long stats are not encouraging. Detroit ranked just:

  • 9th in yards per carry (4.6)
  • 23rd in rush EPA (-0.037)
  • 16th in rushing success rate (41.0%)

The only thing that kept Detroit’s stats even mildly afloat were the explosive runs from Jahmyr Gibbs. He ranked ninth in 10+ yard rushes (27), third in 20+ yard rushes (10), and t-second in 30+ yard rushes (six).

The Lions offensive line ranked 13th in PFF run grade, 20th in run block win rate, and 20th in adjusted line yards.

There is hope the offensive line changes and a switch to a more innovative offensive coordinator will help out the run game this year, but that remains a theory, not a fact.

The Saints gave up a lot of rushing yardage last year (2050, 14th most), but that was largely a result of always trailing in games and facing the third most rushing attempts in the league. On a per-play, basis, they were actually quite sound. In 2025, they ranked:

  • Eighth in yards per carry allowed (4.0)
  • 2nd in rush EPA (-0.136)
  • 9th in rush success rate (39.0%)

That’s the bad news for Detroit. The good news? Two of the Saints best run defenders from last year will not be playing in this game. Demario Davis—their leader and best linebacker who posted an 89.3 run defense grade—left in free agency. And veteran defensive lineman (82.1 grade) Cam Jordan is out with an injury. Kaden Ellis, the linebacker they added this offseason, doesn’t bring much in terms of run defense.

So is it reasonable to expect a step back this season? Yeah, possibly. But given this is also Year 2 under a new defense, I find it hard to believe they’ll significantly regress.

Player to watch: Jonas Sanker. The Saints nickel defender could be a liability in coverage, but he’s excellent as a run defender. Last year, he often played in the box as a safety, and he produced an impressive 73.7 run defense grade.

Advantage: Saints +1. I imagine I’ll get some pushback here from Lions fans, but I expect some issues on the offensive line early with a backup center, rookie right tackle, and a potential guard rotation at left guard. While the Saints don’t possess an extremely stout defensive interior, their unit plays well as a whole, including defensive backs who get their nose dirty.

Saints pass offense (27th) vs. Lions pass defense (6th)

Important in this timeline is that Tyler Shough took over in Game 8 against the Buccaneers.

Shough impressed the Saints enough after taking over midway through the year that he became the unquestioned starter for the 2026 season. The advanced stats aren’t as convinced, though. From Week 8 on, Shough ranked:

  • 15th in yards per attempt (7.3)
  • 16th in passer rating (91.9)
  • 27th in dropback EPA (-0.169)
  • 23rd in success rate (44.3%)

It’s not exactly mind-blowing, but it’s clearly an upgrade over what was happening in New Orleans before. The reason why there’s such a dramatic fall off when it comes to the dropback stats is that it includes sacks, and Shough took a ridiculous amount of them. His 2.8 sacks per game ranked fifth-highest in the NFL despite the fact that he only faced a 31.6% pressure rate (11th lowest).

This offseason, the Saints attempted to give Shough more weapons with three drafted wide receivers, the addition of tight end Noah Fant, and even the signing of running back Travis Etienne (at least 35 catches each NFL season). But with first-round pick Jordan Tyson sidelined to start the year, Shough will have an extremely young receiving corps and may have to rely on the security blankets of Chris Olave (100 catches, 1,163 yards last year) and tight end Juwan Johnson (77 catches, 889 yards).

It’s probably hard to believe that Detroit’s passing defense was considered relatively good last year. I’ll admit the sixth DVOA ranking is just flat-out wrong, but there are some other positive signs that you may have overlooked.

Last year, Detroit ranked:

  • 24th in yards per attempt (7.3)
  • 19th in passer rating (92.5)
  • 14th in dropback EPA (0.040)
  • 9th in dropback success rate (43.5%)

When you see a success rate that high, and all of the other stats are bad or mediocre, it means one things: explosive plays. Detroit gave up boatloads of them. The Lions allowed the fifth-most passing plays of 20+ yards and the most 30+ yard passing plays.

That has been a huge focus this offseason for Detroit, and it may not be as big of a problem this week. Last year, the Saints produced just 33 passing plays of 20+ yards (31st) and 14 of 30+ yards (t-26th).

Detroit’s secondary is not good on paper, but it may somehow actually be improved from last year. D.J. Reed, Terrion Arnold, Brian Branch, and Kerby Joseph missed so much of last year, that it left Detroit scrambling. Well, now Reed is healthy and the Lions invested in veteran safeties to help out not having Branch and Joseph.

However, the real improvement happened up front, where the Lions are both healthier (Alim McNeill, Levi Onwuzurike) and deeper (Tyler Lacy, Derrick Moore, Ahmed Hassanein). Whether that results in more and quicker pressure? We’ll see.

Player to watch: Aidan Hutchinson. Saints left tackle Kelvin Banks had an extremely solid rookie season, and he’s likely to be even better in Year 2. But Hutchinson could cause some issues for right tackle Taliese Fuaga, who finished 2025 just 41st out of 58 qualifying tackles in pass blocking grade (66.2).

Advantage: Lions +1. I think some of the Shough hype is a bit premature, but it’s okay to be optimistic about his long-term future, and it’s reasonable to think he’ll take a Year 2 jump with some offensive scheme consistency. But his weapons are young, and Detroit has some real firepower up front. Throw in a raucous Ford Field, and I think it’ll be a tough environment for Shough.

Saint run offense (30th) vs. Lions run defense (19th)

The Saints running game was one of the worst in the league last year, arguably a bottom-three unit. They ranked:

  • 31st in yards per carry (3.7)
  • 31st in rush EPA (-0.155)
  • 29th in rush success rate (36.6%)

But this is also where the Saints put most of their offseason investments towards. They added Etienne and starting guard David Edwards in free agency. Additionally, the Saints dealt with a lot of offensive line injuries last year—ranking 10th in most adjusted games lost on the offensive line. Health alone could improve the unit.

It’s a good offseason strategy to attack the team’s biggest weakness, but it’s hard to know how much a team can fix in one year. I remain pretty skeptical, even though it should obviously look better than last year’s disaster.

Detroit’s run defense began so promisingly. Through the first nine weeks, it looked like they were going to be their dominating selves yet again. However, everything collapsed toward the end of last year, and the Rams, Steelers, and Vikings all ran over them in ways we haven’t seen in years. In the end, Detroit finished:

  • 21st in yards per carry allowed (4.4)
  • 23rd in rush EPA allowed (-0.037)
  • 16th in rushing success rate (41.0%)

At best, they were average for the season.

How did they improve in 2026? The additions and health up front should certainly help, even if the focus was more on pass rush. They did lose Alex Anzalone, though, and there are certainly questions about whether a combination of Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Devin White can make up what was lost there.

The best chance for improvement in 2026 is simply another year in this defense with a healthy front seven, and this team’s deep history of being solid against the run. I have moderate confidence they’ll improve this year, but it is a bit of an overlooked concern, too.

Player to watch: Etienne. I didn’t talk much about what he brings to the offense, but it’s worth noting he was outside of the top 30 in both EPA and rushing success rate with the Jaguars last year. Will he thrive behind what should be a much better Saints offensive line? It’s still hard to find backs with his size and speed, so I’m not doubting it.

Advantage: Draw. I have severe questions about both sides of the matchup here, and therefore no strong feeling on how it looks in Week 1.

This week’s prediction:

After finishing a terrible 7-10 last year with my predictions, I’m hoping to turn things around this year. But these early-season predictions are always the hardest.

In the end, I gave the Lions a +1 advantage, which properly matches my overall confidence in this game. It’s impossible to ignore that all signs point to the Saints finding some improvement this year. But they’re still figuring things out on offense, and have to answer some key losses in free agency (and injury) on defense.

The Lions, meanwhile, have to prove their arrow isn’t pointing down. I’m not convinced the Lions offense will be any better until I see the offensive line clicking—but it likely won’t be worse. And while I’m optimistic about the defense, the late-season trends last year were concerning.

Overall, I expect sloppy, relatively low-scoring football as both teams try to find their identity. Lions 23, Saints 20.

item.title: Here are 3 keys for the Cardinals to defeat the Chargers
item.description: Week 1 is coming up fast
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals are making all the preparations they need as they are getting ready for the 2026 NFL season. Right out of the gate, they are set to open their Week 1 contest on the road against the Los Angeles Chargers. Last year, the Chargers proved they were a very good team with a playoff berth.

A lot of time and effort have been deposited into this Cardinals’ roster ever since Mike LaFleur was hired as the new head coach. There are many exciting aspects from last year, and as with every team, there remain some concerns. Mostly with this year’s version, Arizona will start off their first game with three new starting offensive linemen. The offensive line must be a cohesive unit of five men instead of five individuals.

RELATED:LOVE OFFICIALLY LISTED AS LIMITED

And right out of the gate, the Cardinals must face the Chargers. Last year, they finished 11-6-0 since Jim Harbaugh took the reins. This year, Arizona’s coaching staff wants to run the ball effectively. Last year, LA was ranked #5 in overall defense and averaged just 285.2 combined yards per game on average. That breakdown is #5 against the pass and #8 against the run.

Let’s look at three things the Cardinals must accomplish to defeat the Chargers.

Establish a balanced rushing attack

This new offense has several aspects that LaFleur wants to maintain. A short passing game is one. Usage of multiple tight ends is another. And a consistent rushing attack is paramount. That is why Arizona used the third overall draft pick on a stud running back instead of one of the elite pass rushers that were available.

LaFleur wants to run the ball. Last year the Cardinals were #31 in rushing, averaging just 93.1 yards a game. They were #22 in red-zone scoring at 54.1%. All of that needs to change.  

How were the Los Angeles Rams in 2025, the team LaFleur left as their OC? #1 in total offense, #1 in passing, #7 in rushing, #1 in scoring offense, and #7 in Red Zone efficiency.

This will not happen overnight, but LaFleur has multiple years of running this offense, and it will get there eventually. For now, the Cardinals need to have their running game produce and become a game manager against the Chargers.

Arizona’s offense needs a balanced rushing game. The bulk of carries will most likely come from Tyler Allgeier. If rookie Jeremiyah Love is 100% with his ankle issue, he will get his fair share of carries, but don’t expect a full load. A balanced attack will ease the need to pass the ball often and also help control the clock.  

Now, how will the offensive line react? Already, RG Isaish Adams is ruled out, and rookie RG Chase Bisontis is on IR. This is already a problem. Jon Gaines will take the reins and had a great camp and preseason. LG Isaac Seumalo is also a question mark. So, we’ll see.

Keep out the Chargers’ pass rush

The Chargers have a very good pass rush, and it comes from various spots and players. They generate a great pass rush with LB Tuli Tuipulotu, who actually lines up as an EDGE rusher, and Khalil Mack, who has returned to California.  

To counteract these fine athletes, the Cardinals depend greatly on the skills of RT Elijah Wilkinson and LT Paris Johnson on the corners. The Wilkinson vs. Tuipulotu will become a battle and just might determine quite a few things in this ballgame. What is that called? Baptism by fire?

Mack is a beast and has been for years. He was the “NFL Defensive Player of the Year” back in 2016 but dislocated an elbow last year, which landed him on IR. Mack finished the 2025 season with 11 starts, 32 total tackles, 5.5 sacks, 11 QB hits, 11 hurries, and 23 pressures.

Tuipulotu has a leaner build and was a second-round draft pick. He was exceptional in college at USC and totaled 21 sacks in a tough conference. He led the conference in tackles for loss (22) and sacks (13.5) in his final year. He was a unanimous All-American, a two-time All-Pac-12 recipient, and was named the “Polynesian College Football Player of the Year.”

In the 2025 NFL season, Tuipulotu racked up 13.0 sacks and has 26 for his three-year career. His quickness off the edge and a fast first step are his calling cards. 39 tackles for loss, 52 QB hits, and 73 pressures are why he is such a menace.

Tuipulotu was limited in practice on Thursday, but is expected to play. Can Johnson contain him? Stay tuned.

Attack the Chargers’ receivers

Arizona’s defense has to have constant pressure on Chargers QB Justin Herbert every time he drops back to pass. But he will have time to throw. And when he does, the back end of the Cardinals defense has to be ready. Herbert has a good arm and can’t be allowed to set up and go through his progressions and set up the short passing game.

If Herbert is able to set his feet at will, it will become a very long day. He can throw into tight windows when he has time to survey the field, and can throw long.

Whether the defensive line can rattle Herbert is one issue, but when he does throw, the Cardinals’ defensive backfield has to come through. It is not clear if Garrett Williams will play, or at the very least become limited in his snaps. A guy like Williams is as real as they come and is a critical piece to the pass defense. 

This would mean that Max Melton will become the default starter on the outside with Will Johnson. Denzel Burke will then be moved to the slot corner position. The coaching staff has complete trust in all four players.

Keeping Herbert out of his comfort zone will be a huge plus to this game with containment. The Chargers have a very good receiver corps headed by Ladd McConkey. Also in this group are Quentin Johnston and Tre’ Harris. Rookie WR Brenan Thompson was drafted in Round 4 and is expected to have a decent number of offensive snaps.
