item.title: What can we learn about Mizzou in Border Battle No. 121
item.description: Some burning questions as Mizzou heads to kU for the first time in 21 years
item.content:encoded:
How exciting is this? For the first time since Oct. 29, 2005, Mizzou football is traveling to Lawrence, Kansas to face the ever-hated Kansas Jayhawks. It’s another installment of the revived Border War, one of College Football’s historic and treasured rivalries. 

Last week, we asked some questions and learned a lot. Austin Simmons helped engineer a sharp, effective passing game. Jack Lange had an up-and-down performance in his first start, while we saw a bunch of newcomers take the field (Ex. Elijah Dotson).

But a game against the FCS in comparison to a Power Four rival can tell us so much more. So, ahead of Friday’s game, here are some burning questions for the Tigers for Border Battle No. 121.

How much of a difference will Cayden Green make?

The SEC’s best rushing attack in 2025 looked a bit stale against Arkansas-Pine Bluff. The Tigers rushed for 205 yards on 45 carries (4.6 yards per attempt). In the first half, it was 85 yards on 20 carries. 

Mizzou is still without Ahmad Hardy, and his status to return is still unknown. Fortunately, the team received positive news as left tackle Cayden Green is expected to suit up on Friday night. Drinkwitz mentioned he was a full participant in practice on Tuesday 

“There’s no concern for me in him being able to perform at the level that he needs to. So it’s really good. I mean, that guy bleeds black and gold. He loves his teammates. It’s an impressive thing for him to be back and ready to go on Friday night, I know that,” Drinkwitz said. 

Green brings a significant boost to the Tigers’ offensive line, as Jack Lange and Whit Hafer both head back to being depth options. Kansas held Long Island to one yard per carry, a Sharks team that is 34 spots ahead of UAPB in Bill Connelly’s SP+ rankings. But for the Jayhawks, linebacker Daveon “Bam” Crouch is doubtful per Pete Thamel.

Nevertheless, this is an aspect of the game that will be intriguing to watch. But, Green’s return should provide a boost that was missing in week one. Friday will give us a better indication if this is a long-term concern (Even when Hardy returns) or if this was just a slow start. 

On the opposite end of the front seven, will we see a stronger pass rush and contain Isaiah Marshall?

Mizzou generated nine pressures in week 1, the same amount as the same time last year. Good.

But unlike last year, the Tigers didn’t collect any sacks, and overall, it was a poorer day tackling. Mizzou was credited with 14 missed tackles per Pro Football Focus compared to 9 in the 25 season opener, including one from Darris Smith, and linebackers Nicholas Rodriguez, Robert Woodyard Jr., and Dante McClellan, all part of the primary front seven. 

“We did not do a good enough job of displacing blocks in the backfield and then sacking the quarterback. There’s multiple times the we were there; we had them caged. But we’ve got to disengage and track the quarterback is going to be much bigger challenge this week.” – From Matthew Gustafson’s Tiger Talk Notes and Quotes: Border War Edition.

The quarterback Mizzou is facing is Isaiah Marshall.

The Detroit-area native is a dual-threat quarterback who can challenge a defense with his legs. He carried the ball seven times for 49 yards last week against Long Island, averaging 10.7 yards per attempt in 15 carries a season ago, and has the ability to make defenders miss in open space. It’s a much more challenging test than Jack Schierholz and Garrison Davis. 

But this game also serves as a test to see if the Tigers can turn up the heat in the pass rush. As for Smith and Kitchen, they are replacing over 100 combined pressures between Zion Young and Damon Wilson II. And for the linebacker room, Marshall can create with his legs, so it’s not beneficial to give him extra yardage off of missed tackles.

We’re not asking for 5 sacks; this is not always indicative of a great pass rush. But, if the Tigers can contain and collapse the pocket, it would shine some positive light on the defensive front.

How will the new-look secondary perform against tougher competition? 

But what if Marshall gets a pass off?

Last Thursday, you didn’t really hear anyone be mentioned in the secondary, outside of Elijah Dotson making plays all over the field, and that’s a good thing.

Mizzou’s cornerbacks were sticky in coverage, running side-by- side with wide receivers all night against UAPB. 

For KU, Marshall has an arm. As much as we loved Austin Simmons’ debut, and how smooth the pass game looked, Marshall was just as effective with 12.9 yards per attempt, and a aDOT of 11.9. Simmons’ was a 13.3 and 11.6. 

With three new starters at cornerback this season, we’ll get to see them tested a bit, as his deep ball placement and accuracy were impressive. In throws of 20-plus yards last week, Marshall was 3-of-4 for 112 yards, his most impressive area of the field, with a 96.3 passing grade in that area.

We saw Mizzou’s new-look secondary debut against UAPB, but it was an stress-free night as the Golden Lions quarterbacks could practically do nothing. Now, we’ll get to see names like Chris Graves Jr., Khalil Florence and Sione Laulea be tested with a quarterback that can test them vertically.

Personally, this game is the most important game on the regular season schedule. You don’t lose to Kansas.

Beat KU, and thanks for reading.

item.title: Film Study: Washington State, Apple Cup Edition
item.description: Offensive miscues & crushing defense
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back Husky fans to another season of college football!

Washington enters Year 3 of the Fisch era in an unconventional way, kicking off against the Washington State Cougars for a Week 1 Apple Cup matchup. The team also played in an offbeat way, struggling against their former Pac-12 counterpart and not like the #17 team in the nation. Demond Williams Jr. had flashes of greatness but the offense still struggled, especially behind an underwhelming performance by the promising offensive line. On the flip side, the defense was there to play and showed the makings of a possible top unit in the conference and maybe even country. Backed by a combination of experienced playmakers and young athletes, they were able to force two turnovers deep in Cougar territory (shoutout the new Turnover Space Needle; see below) . Ultimately the Dawgs were able to pull away in the end and hoist up the trophy yet again.

To the film.

Offense: Bumpy Starts

It was pretty obvious that the offense the Huskies trotted out this past weekend isn’t up to the standard, nor expectations, of the staff, the fans, or their own. After a finishing last season with a top 25 offense per SP+, most expected the offense to build off that success. With the QB1, TE1, and 3/5 of the starting OL all returning, plus a 5-star freshman LT and promising rotational RG projected to start, I certainly focused most of my concern on the WRs and RBs during the offseason. Even after Landen Hatchett was announced as unavailable at center, I discounted his absence in part due to Kolt Dieterich stepping into the role as an experienced veteran.

Turns out, the cumulative in experience at three key positions along the OL (at least in experience in those specific positions) was just too much for the offense to overcome. That, plus injuries at RB and WR, led to a surprisingly sluggish performance for most of the game. Granted, the play calling at times didn’t help.

Let’s take a look.

1st Quarter – 11:25 – 2nd & 6

First up, we wanted to give an example of how even the seemingly basic or routine play concepts in this offense can be thrown off if the players haven’t gotten sufficient reps to develop the unit’s chemistry. On this play from early in the game we’re running Inside Zone, which is one of the base run concepts in our primarily Zone-based run scheme. Obviously, this was an unsuccessful play for the offense that resulted in a TFL by a defender right at the point of attack, but before we get into the “why” of the play’s outcome, let’s do a quick refresher on Zone runs.

All Zone run plays are based on a few key blocking assignment rules. At the snap, every lineman takes their first step towards the play side. This initial step helps to establish their “zone”. If there is a defender on the line directly in front of them after they take their zone step, or if there is a defender partially in front of them towards the play side, that is the lineman’s defender to block. In Zone blocking terminology, this is also called being “covered”. However, if there isn’t a defender on the line in their zone, then they are considered “uncovered”. Uncovered linemen will then continue downfield to the second level of the defense until they find a defender in their zone to block.

There are a bunch of other Zone blocking rules that could apply depending on if it’s Inside Zone, Mid Zone, Outside Zone, Wide Zone, Split Zone, etc., but the key takeaway is that each offensive lineman is responsible for blocking whoever is in their zone. The whole Zone scheme is designed to have blocking assignment rules that can account for any defensive front, as well as any thing the defense does, including post-snap. Defensive pre-snap alignment may give the OL clues as to who they’ll be blocking once the play starts, but it’s the blocking assignments could still be fluid post-snap if the defense slants, stunts, or blitzes. Much like how DBs need to keep their scanning the field for incoming receiving threats in zone coverage, offensive linemen need to keep their eyes up even as their engaged with one defender if a new defender comes into their zone. This is often a challenging coaching point when installing a Zone run scheme because linemen have a natural tendency to lock in on beating the defender right in front of them. It’s even harder to master at multiple positions along the line since threats come from different angles and positions depending on if you are a tackle, guard, or center. That is where this play went sideways.

Circling back to the replay above, the run was stuffed for a TFL because of a missed blocking assignment that let the DE come in unblocked at the point of attack on the right side of the formation. If you lock in on Drew Azzopardi (RT, #74), you see him take his initial zone step to the right, recognize that the DE has vacated his zone on a twist stunt, and so he continues up field looking for someone to block. Looking one player in, Champ Taulealea (RG, #73) takes his zone step to the right and is met by the DT slanting into his zone. Champ doesn’t square up on his block, but the DT is more or less accounted for in the blocking scheme.

Where things fall apart is when you get to Kolt Dieterich (C, #55). Kolt takes his initial zone step, and he quickly realizes that he is uncovered. So like Azzopardi, Kolt starts to move up field to find a defender to block. Where his coaching starts to fall apart is in his eye discipline and aggressive movement up field. A major coaching point in Zone schemes is for the OL to largely ignore anything backside from their zone. The priority is always to get blockers on play side defenders because that is where the running back is heading. If all the play side defenders are picked up and a backside defender comes in unblocked, the running back at least has a head start to out run him coming from a chase down angle. In this case, Kolt, instead of maintaining his eye discipline towards the play side, lets his eyes drift towards the mass of defenders towards the backside of the play and completely misses the twisting DE coming from the play side.

I don’t want to beat up on a guy who was playing his first game ever at the center position, but this play highlights why general starting experience doesn’t directly translate to a different position. Hopefully Hatchett can return soon to stead the position.

2nd Quarter – 0:03 – 4th & 1

Next play up we have another similar miscue on a Zone run play, but this time it’s a Zone Slice/Split play in a short yardage situation.

Since this is still a Zone run play, the blocking assignment rules we just ran through in the last play still apply here, but there are specific coaching points that apply when you’re in a short yardage situation running Inside Zone in particular. Things like play side zone steps and blocking assignment priority still apply, but there’s a greater emphasis on double teams and vertical push up the middle.

Taking a look from the overhead angle, you can see the hypothetical pre-snap blocking assignments a bit better. Yes, I know I just told you that Zone blocking assignment rules are fluid from pre to post-snap, but this gives you a decent idea of what I’m talking about when it comes to how double teams and downhill push off the line is achieved on an Inside Zone play. Anyways, since the play is Zone Slice/Split (depending on scheme to scheme terminology), the backside EDGE is left unblocked by the OL and is the TE’s responsibility to cut off as diagramed above. This leaves the 5 OL to focus on the remaining 3 DL and any other second level defenders who come in to stuff the run.

As I said earlier, a key coaching point on Inside Zone plays in short yardage is to get double teams and vertical push. This is done within the Zone blocking rules by instructing the OL to engage the closest defenders towards their play side, get push on them, and then keep their eyes scanning while executing the double team in case a second level defender comes into their zone that they need to peel off to block. Ideally, by the time a second level defender comes into play for one of the double teaming OL to pick up, they’ll have pushed the DL off the line and built forward momentum for the now solo blocker to continue driving them up field. In this case, that’d mean that Kodi Greene (LT, #76) and John Mills (LG, #72) are double teaming #98, Kolt and Champ are double teaming #52, and Azzopardi is left on a solo block against #6 as his closest defender on the line.

As you can see from this mid-play snip, there are two OL miscues/good plays from the WSU DL that blow this play up. First, the DE on Greene’s side takes a very tight angle to crash in on the run while the DT #98 slants towards the center. This catches Greene off guard, and I think he panicked a little bit. Instead of trusting that Decker DeGraaf (TE, #86) would pick up the DE on the Slice block, Greene tries to get a piece of the DE before helping Mills on the double team. However, by attempting to do so, Green ends up whiffing on both. This has the unintended effect of leaving Mills left solo blocking the DT and unable to block both the DT and the incoming LB up the A-gap.

The other miscue was on the right side of the line. The other DE, #6, is left unblocked after Azzopardi takes his zone step and starts looking wide for a defender to block. My guess is that he was looking to block the stand up defender, not realizing that Rashid Williams (WR, #3) was already blocking him. You could argue that it also looks like Azzopardi was expecting Champ to pick up the DE, but it still wouldn’t have made sense for Azzopardi to be looking as wide as he is on the mid-play snippet above when it’s a short yardage Inside Zone call where a DL was directly in front of him pre-snap to at least get a quick chip block on.

2nd Quarter – 12:26 – 1st & 10

Finally on offense, we wanted to touch on our struggles through the air for most of the game. We talked extensively last season about Jedd Fisch’s tendency to emphasize the downfield and perimeter passing game with Demond behind center, and it hasn’t changed much at the start of this season. The problem now is that opponents have a full season of Demond tape to game plan with, and it doesn’t seem like Fisch has a strong counter to those defensive adjustments.

On this play, from the edge of the red zone, Fisch has a Four Verts concept called with a play action protection tagged that involves pulling Kolt to the right side of the formation to sell the run fake. In theory, 4 Verts can work against any coverage with enough option route tags and route adjustments, but generally speaking, it works best against Cover 2 and Cover 3 where there is a downfield numerical advantage. Based on the pre-snap alignment though, it looks like WSU is running Cover 4 based on the 2 high safeties and both corners 6+ yards off the line. Cover 4 is designed to take away the deep ball, like the Four Verts concept, but WSU was also regularly rotating or shifting safeties post-snap to disguise coverages, so maybe we were rolling the dice that that was the case yet again.

If we we’re expecting WSU to rotate out of a 2-high look, we guessed right because the Cougs ended up in a Cover 3 Cloud look with a zone blitz underneath. The design of the play, especially the pairing with the nickel zone blitz, really threw a wrench in the offense’s plans despite giving a favorable Cover 3 look. In Cover 3 Cloud, the defense uses two safeties and one corner for its deep coverage while there are four zone defenders underneath, this makes it an ideal variation of Cover 3 to run out of a disguised 2-high look. By shifting the safeties towards the field post-snap for the Cover 3, the defense is also able to provide high-low bracket coverage against UW’s lone receiver to the boundary side. This boundary receiver is often an alert read in Four Verts if there’s a favorable match up, and you can see in the replay that that’s where Demond’s eyes go to first. However, with the EDGE dropping underneath to takeaway the passing lane, Demond needs to quickly move to his next read.

That next read is between the TE and slot running up the seams. The defense takes these away through a combination of dropping underneath zone defenders and pressure. With the nickel blitzing from the slot, Demond’s internal clock gets rushed as he sees an incoming defender right in his face as he scans towards the slot waiting for his inside receivers to get open. By this point in the play, the pocket is collapsing and Demond narrowly avoids a sack or intentional grounding penalty while taking a big hit.

Again, in theory this play design isn’t terrible against the coverage call, but it has become predictable enough that WSU had the right tweaks to underneath coverage and pressure design that they were ready for it despite being in a Cover 3. If this is something we can expect from future opponents, Fisch has to really consider giving Demond more check down options and emphasize more short and intermediate passing to keep opponents honest.

Defense: Lights Out

The defense was lights out this past week. I think a lot of UW fans had high expectations for the defense this season, but I don’t think I was expecting this type of physical, smothering defense in year two under DC Ryan Walters. Last year’s defense finished the year strong, but with an infusion of young talent and a largely rebuilt DL room, there was some level of curiosity with regards to what the next evolutionary step the scheme would take. Turns out, it was a lot of what worked best last year, just supercharged with talent.

1st Quarter – 2:32 – 3rd & 10

First play up we have a sweet blitz design that got Jacob Manu (LB, #9) his first sack of the season. At the end of last season, Walters started to lean into our defense’s strengths in zone coverage and started to mix in more creative zone blitz designs to get our versatile and physical DBs more involved near the line of scrimmage. This play builds on that foundation.

Like many of last year’s zone blitz designs, we’re lined up pre-snap with tons of bodies on the line. This is a foundational play design concept in Walters’ scheme as it forces the OL to account for as many potential pass rushers as possible, even if not all of them end up rushing. This in turn limits the number of protection calls that the offense can utilize and makes it easier for Walters to design pressures that can exploit them. Putting 6+ bodies on or near the line also gives Walters more options to mix and match rush and coverage assignments with.

Last year, we often utilized a Double Mug front with LBs walked up into both A-gaps as the starting alignment that got 6 defenders on the line. Against WSU, we debuted the “BOSS” front as a new front to deploy Walters’ pressure schemes out of. BOSS stands for “Bigs On Same Side”. It’s a bit tough to see the formation on the TV angle clip above, so here’s a clearer example from the the NFL below.

Basically, a BOSS front with 4 DL shift the two DTs to one side of the center. This leaves an open A-gap and B-gap for the two LBs to walk up into pre-snap. Aside from the BOSS front being something else to throw at an offense, it also does an even better job at forcing the offense’s hand when it comes to setting their protections. Most offenses design their protection calls to prioritize having OL block DL if at all possible, a.k.a. “big-on-big”. By overloading one side of the front with the bigs via the BOSS front, you can bait the offense into sliding their OL consistently towards a predictable side of the formation. From there, you can exploit the more predictable protection call with the pressure design.

As you can see in the clip at the beginning, or the diagram above, on this play we have our bigs towards the field side to get the OL to slide towards the field. We also have both ZRS (LB, #23) and Manu up in the gap in the front. We had already brought the LBs up onto the line several times already with them blitzing and dropping at various times. e brought Alex McLaughlin down towards the line in a coverage alignment over the TE closest to the OL.

This alignment puts up to seven defenders in play as a potential pass rusher that the offense has to consider. They’re going to want to slide at least the center, RG, and RT towards the field since that would keep big on big protection principles, and they’re going to want the LT locked into man blocking against Logan George (EDGE, #12) to maintain big on big on the left side. This leaves the LG as the only unknown blocking assignment since the RB will typically pick up blitzers on the backside of the slide. However, since ZRS is occupying the left A-gap and is an immediate threat, the LG will likely slide to the field as well to make sure the interior gaps have OL blockers.

This is where the craftiness in the blitz design shines though. With the front and alignment doing so much heavy lifting pre-snap to bait the OL into a predictable protection call, Walters doesn’t need to bring numbers to get pressure. Instead, he has Ramzak Fruean (EDGE, #11) drop into underneath zone coverage to takeaway field side check downs while our 2 DTs occupy the entire right side of the OL. Then, we have George, who is lined up extra wide to the boundary, take a wide and deep rush angle to play contain and to draw the LT extra wide as well. This leaves a blitzing McLaughlin and Manu in extra wide space against the LG and RB.

The final wrinkle in the design is Manu’s “coffeehouse” blitz. By feigning a coverage drop, the sliding LG moves his eyes towards the blitzing McLaughlin, who is coming in so fast from depth that the RB is already selling out to block him. Manu then blitzes untouched after the fake coverage drop into the now vacated space that the LG left for a huge 3rd down sack.

Much like how offensive formations can do a lot of heavy lifting pre-snap to set up a successful play, defensive alignments can too, and on this play Walters puts on a master class in designing pressure while only rushing five and still playing conservative Cover 4.

2nd Quarter – 12:31 – 3rd & 7

Next up we’ve got another big play off of another Walters pressure design. Like the last play, everything is set up by the pre-snap alignment baiting the offense into predictable protections.

On this play, we again put our 6 DL and LBs on the line in our Double Mug front (2 LBs in the A-gaps) to force the offense into accounting for all 6 as potential rushers. Pure speculation, but I suspect that the defensive staff locked in on Kirby Moore offenses tending to emphasize the big on big protection philosophy because yet again we’re calling a pressure design that exploits their big on big call. With 6 on the line but the DL split 2 and 2 over the guards and tackles, WSU would have to call a split protection or all man protection to account for at least 5 potential rushers. In a split protection, half the line (including the center) would slide to one side and use zone pass protection rules and the other two OL would be locked in man-to-man blocking assignments against the DL bigs on the other side. Alternatively, in an all man protection, the guards and tackles would pick up the DL bigs with the center picking up one of the two LBs if they rush. Either way, we’ll get at least two of our DL bigs matched up against OL in man-to-man blocking assignments.

We end up dropping our LBs into underneath coverage in what ends up being a rather vanilla Cover 4 call, but their pre-snap alignment already set up the pass rush. We have E-T (End-Tackle) stunts called on both halves of the DL to take advantage of the likely man-to-man protection call. On an E-T stunt, the Ends crash inwards toward the B-gaps to create a “pick” while the DTs loop around the outside, hopefully unblocked. This type of pass rush stunt is very effective against man-to-man protection calls because the OL is often so focused on blocking their predetermined defender that they don’t effectively hand off blocking responsibilities once the looping DT crosses pash rush paths behind the end.

Fruean and Derek Colman-Brusa (DT, #5) execute their stunt perfectly and get heavy pressure on the passer (and likely a tip), sending the ball fluttering into Jeron Jones’ (CB, #24) hands for the INT.

2nd Quarter – 4:01 – 3rd & 5

Next up we have a great run stuff from Jacob Manu on a 3rd down. We picked this play for Film Study because it highlights three things:

  1. Our continued use of the 5×1 “Penny” front
  2. Our improved personnel allowing us to use the Penny front in a wider variety of situations
  3. Our improved ability to utilize man coverages and still be able to stop the run

At this point, we’re probably all familiar with the 5×1 Penny front, but we’ll give a quick refresher. Like we used under Belichick a couple years ago, as well as last year under Walters, our version of the Penny front utilizes our typical 4-2-5 personnel to create a 5-man front with one LB at the second level. We do this by shifting our DTs and one EDGE over the iOL and then rotating one of our two LBs down onto the line in a stand up rusher alignment like you can see in the snip below.

In the past, we’ve utilized this look selectively in obvious passing or running situations. Kind of like the last two plays where we put 6 defenders on the line, the Penny front forces the OL to simplify their blocking calls. On a pass play, we have the option to rush all five and potentially get five 1v1 pass rush matchups against a base 5-man blocking front (just the OL with no TEs attached). Against a run play, particularly Zone run plays, having that many defenders up on the line prevents the OL from getting double teams since they’d need to get blockers on defenders immediately at the snap.

However, there are a few weaknesses to the Penny front that forced its utilization to be limited in the past. One major drawback is that by placing that many bodies on the line and just the sole LB at the second level, we can be left far more susceptible to a big run if the LB missed the tackle in the hole. This year though, at least in our one game so far, that seems to be a less risky proposition. With an improved DL anchoring the line of scrimmage, it’s going to be a lot harder for the offense to pick up our lone LB. On the replay you can see Elinneus Davis (DT, #90) stone wall the lone double team the OL could generate against our front, and none of the rest of our DL got pushed past the line in their respective 1v1s. This left just one gap for our lone LB, Manu, to plug, and Manu is an elite run stuffer. He has a natural feel for run fits and he’s a big hitter when coming down hill on the RB. If our DL can continue to keep him free to attack the runner, he’ll be a perfect fit for the role of clean up tackler in this type of front and can allow us to deploy this front more often.

The other drawback to the Penny front is related to coverage. With one LB committed to one side of the formation in a stand up rusher alignment, we have fewer options in where we can drop players into underneath zone coverage (as compared to our BOSS or Double Mug fronts). Zone coverage has been the primary coverage scheme we’ve utilized since the second half of last season because it was easier to install and was more forgiving to our young LBs and CBs and it kept more eyes in the backfield who could help in run support. If we couldn’t run our full complement of zone coverages out of Penny front and, at the time, be certain that the run defense wouldn’t be gashed without the zone coverages, we needed to be careful when we utilized the front. However, with an improved front in run defense this year, particularly in the Penny front, we may see its usage grow now that we can pair it with man coverage, like on this play.

3rd Quarter – 4:17 – 1st & 10

Finally this week we have a play that highlights the 3-high look that first got deployed last season and has become an even more important look in our defense this year.

As you can see in the pre-snap snip above, we’ve got a base 4-man front with Manu and ZRS at the second level and the trio of Rylon Dillard-Allen (S, #4), Rashawn Clark (S/Nickel, #2), and McLaughlin deep. We initially used this 3-high look last season for two key reasons:

  1. It allowed us to play Cover 3 while keeping our physical CBs near the line to help in run support
  2. It allowed us McLaughlin, usually playing as the middle safety, to seamlessly transition post-snap between deep post safety, middle robber underneath, and box run defender

The limiting factors to its usage last year were our inability to consistently stop the run without McLaughin as a consistent extra box defender and that it creates a soft spot in coverage in the slot because we move our nickel into deep coverage to create the 3-high look. However, I think we’re going to see a lot more of this look in the 2026 season because those concerns have been addressed with our improved play in those areas.

ZRS, now in his second season, is a promising athlete in coverage and can hold his own playing coverage in the slot more than any of our other LBs in the rotation. He might not provide the same type of coverage ability as a nickel DB, but he’s certainly not a liability at this point. This frees up Clark to play up in the 2-high look more often. Up front as you can see in the clip, our DL’s improvement holding the line, even while moving laterally on the toss play, plus Manu and the CBs’ tackling ability, indicate to me that McLaughlin playing in the box is no longer an absolute necessity when it comes to stopping the run. Dylan Robinson already proved last season that he’s a positive contributor in run support, and Karnley is as well, as he showed here turning the run back inside to the oncoming DL and LBs.

Expanded use of this coverage look, now that some of last season’s limitations have been mitigated, could allow for more creative usage of McLaughlin in underneath robber coverage, as well as an enhanced ability to play bracket coverages on both perimeter receivers without weakening our overall deep and underneath coverage structure.

Awgs’ Bonus Play(s) of the Week

We’re also going to start the season unconventionally and give this week’s honors to the ref for dodging this knockout celebratory punch by Derek Colman-Brusa (shoutout DCB for avoiding the penalty too)

item.title: Washington Commanders vs Philadelphia Eagles Week 1: Five Questions with Bleeding Green Nation
item.description: Is it good or bad to be playing the Eagles early in the season?
item.content:encoded:
It’s week 1 of the NFL season and the Washington Commanders will be facing an Eagles team on the road at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA on Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET. The Eagles have now done the improbable and won the NFC East Championship two years in a row, though they flamed out of the playoffs last postseason to an injury-riddled 49ers team in the Wild Card round. Still, the Eagles are the most accomplished team in the division in recent years and the betting favorites to win the division.

On offense, the Eagles have switched OC again after an underwhelming stint from OC Kevin Patullo last year. The Eagles offense this year will be helmed by OC Sean Mannion, formerly of the Packers. Similar to Washington’s OC David Blough, Mannion was a player as recently as 2023 and only served a couple of years coaching QBs for the Packers before being hired by the Eagles to run their offense. Mannion is expected to run a Shanahan-style outside-zone run game with heavy use of under-center formations and play-action fakes. It is also an offense that typically features an emphasis on passes to the middle of the field, though this seems to conflict with the preference of QB Jalen Hurts, who threw just 28 times between the hashmarks last season. This was both a career high for Hurts and the fewest amongst QBs who played 14+ games in 2025. Hurts seems to prefer to throw to the sidelines, an area where X-receiver AJ Brown thrived. Brown was traded away in the offseason, but former 1st-round pick DeVonta Smith will try to reprise Brown’s role and become the boundary X. Meanwhile, 2026 1st-round pick Makai Lemon (who battled hamstring injury during training camp, but is now fully healthy) will try to fill that important between-the-hashes role.

On defense, the Eagles are in their third year with Vic Fangio at DC. Fangio typically runs a 3-4 front and 2 deep safeties to limit explosive plays. He also typically runs a light box, relying on stout defensive linemen to stop the run, while dropping most of his players back into coverage. It is a defense designed to limit big plays and slowly suffocate offenses into punting. Quite frankly, the Eagles defense is well coached and stacked with good or great players at multiple levels. It will be in contention for best defense in the NFL this year and should be comparable to last year, when it was ranked 13th in yards allowed and 5th in points allowed. However, if it has a weakness, it seems to be at the safety position, which has received little attention in the offseason.

I asked Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation five questions to better understand the state of the Eagles and what to look for in this game.

1) Jeff Stoutland was one of the all-time great OL coaches in the NFL and retired this offseason. What does this mean for the Eagles and what do you expect to be different in the Eagles’ OL blocking this year?

“Retired.”

The Eagles purportedly wanted him back … but only as their offensive line coach and NOT their run game coordinator, which is a title he was granted after the Eagles’ Super Bowl LII win.

It would be disingenuous for anyone who previously talked about how great Stout was to now act like it’s no big deal that he’s gone. The Eagles likely downgraded at offensive line coach this offseason.

That said, the early returns on his replacement — Chris Kuper — seem to be positive. We saw the Eagles’ run game have success in training camp settings, for whatever that’s worth. The Eagles’ young backup offensive lineman seem to be developing nicely.

Multiple Eagles offensive linemen have expressed excitement about the new offense as it relates to making their jobs easier. Lane Johnson has talked about how he’ll have more help now as opposed to almost always being on an island at right tackle. Johnson and Jordan Mailata have also discussed how the new scheme is going to make their offense less predictable. Of course, it’s easy for players and fans to look on the bright side before the games actually start.

I do think the Eagles’ offensive line will be better than it was last year because they should be healthier. The entire group isn’t coming off the massive 2024 rushing workload that clearly took a toll on them. Cam Jurgens in particular seems to be removed from the back injury that tanked his 2025 season. I do have some concerns about Landon Dickerson, who doesn’t look back to his Pro Bowl form based on what I saw in training camp, but there are worse starting guards in the league.

To be determined if schematic tweaks help or hurt the o-line, if they even make a big difference at all.

2) What will the Eagles offense look like being run by Sean Mannion? How big of a change is that from last year?

Great question! It’s not easy to know exactly what to expect, both in terms of aesthetic and the extent to which it is effective.

We did see enough in training camp to lead one to believe there will be meaningful differences from the past. There was much more under center play-action usage. There was a good deal of pre-snap motion. Jalen Hurts seemed to throw over the middle of the field more frequently than he has in the past.

Do these tweaks guarantee that the offense will be a lot better than it was in 2026? I don’t think they do. But they could certainly help. I mean, it’s hard to get worse than last year’s offense that led the league in three-and-out percentage.

But there are still a lot of questions here. Mannion isn’t only a first-time play-caller, he’s entering the third year of his entire coaching career. He’s inexperienced. I already touched on Stoutland above. A.J. Brown is gone, that’s a pretty big loss.

It’s also not like the Eagles are the only team trying to reinvent their offense to some degree. Offensive coordinator change has become the norm in the NFL; the longest tenured play-calling OC is from 2025! Most seem to be chasing the Sean McVay/Kyle Shanahan systems, which is where Mannion draws experience from. But while teams understandably covet those influences, it remains to be seen which (if any) disciples can effectively enact their visions. And if these teams might be too late to a trend.

The thinking here is that the Eagles’ offense could have some success early on since they begin the season with games against the Commanders and Titans. But things might get bumpy after that and I tend to think that progress might not be linear for this offense. There could be some ups and downs before they hit their stride, if they ever do.

3) What are your thoughts about the Eagles’ trade of AJ Brown and how it will affect the team? 

I think it’s a bummer because Brown is an awesome player (not was, still is) and Eagles fans should ultimately remember the Super Bowl LIX champion as a big contributor to the most successful sustained stretch in franchise history. But it’s not quite that simple because Brown clearly didn’t put his best foot forward for the Eagles in 2025. Keeping him moving forward clearly wasn’t an option; the Eagles were never going to get the motivated version of Brown in 2026 that the Patriots will be getting. And that’s a shame, for a lot of reasons.

I do think the Eagles did reasonably well to get a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick for him. But I also think they’re going to miss Brown. Similar to what I said about Stoutland earlier in this correspondence, I think it’s silly for people to espouse Brown’s greatness during his time in Philly only to then act like replacing him is no big deal.

I’m not concerned about DeVonta Smith at all; I think he’s going to have a great season as the Eagles’ undisputed top target. But I do have questions about the other Eagles receivers. Dontayvion Wicks had an encouraging summer and he’s poised to be the No. 2. I think he’s a solid starter. Beyond that? 2026 first-round pick Makai Lemon missed most of the Eagles’ offseason practices and hasn’t done much to inspire confidence when he has been on the field. Then it’s Elijah Moore, Darius Cooper (a player I’m very high on), and Hollywood Brown. I don’t know how much they’ll play but they could rotate in.

The Eagles also have questions at tight end, which is arguably their weakest position on offense. So, there are some concerns about the passing attack as a whole with Brown gone.

4) What have been your biggest takeaways from following the Eagles through training camp and the preseason?

I already touched on the offensive uncertainty so I’ll go with something different and more positive from an Eagles perspective: the strength of this defense.

I’m feeling really good about the Eagles’ defensive front. Jalyx Hunt looks like he might be a superstar and his strong summer shadowed positive progression from 2023 first-round Nolan Smith, who had a lost season in 2025 due to injury. Jonathan Greenard is back at practice and, while it’s currently unclear if he’ll play in Week 1, he should be a major contributor to this defense if he’s healthy. A.J. Epenesa and Arnold Ebiketie are very credible rotational contributors at edge rusher. And then there’s the Eagles’ interior, which is anchored by a healthier version of Jalen Carter, an improving Jordan Davis, and a Moro Ojomo who looks poised for a big season before leaving the Eagles in free agency (much like the 2024 Milton Williams trajectory). The Eagles have one of the best off-ball linebackers in the NFL in Zack Baun, who makes plays in coverage that you just don’t see from most players at his position. He’s joined by 2025 first-round pick Jihaad Campbell, who may be worse than Nakobe Dean right now, but offers a high ceiling.

The Eagles also might have the league’s best cornerback trio. Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean (thanks for him, Adam Peters!) were All-Pro players in Year 2 and I’m fully expecting them to be pretty swell again in Year 3. Whereas the Eagles were starting Adoree’ Jackson on the outside last year, they now have Riq Woolen. There could be some volatility with him but I tend to think he’s going to make more big plays than he’s going to give up.

Safety is the Eagles’ weakest position group on defense but I haven’t seen anything from them that leads me to believe they’re going to be a massive liability. Especially since they should benefit from the talent elsewhere on the defense. And I trust Vic Fangio to make it work; he’s inarguably earned the benefit of the doubt.

5) How should Washington go about game-planning this matchup on both sides of the ball?

If I’m the Commanders, I’m looking to test the Eagles’ safeties, especially Marcus Epps (No. 29). He’s usually pretty sound in coverage but he’s not exactly a playmaker. I’d also look to go after Woolen because he might give up some big plays, especially on outbreaking patterns. I’d also look to get Daniels involved as a runner and work in some screens to try to keep the Eagles’ pass rush honest.

When it comes to the Eagles’ offense, I think Philly is really going to try to run the ball a lot. Keying in on Saquon Barkley is easier said than done, especially for the Commanders over the past two seasons. But that’s where I’d start. Try to dare someone other than Barkley and DeVonta Smith to beat you.

A companion article to this with my answers to Brandon’s questions can be found here.

Thanks again to Brandon Lee Gowton for taking time out of his day to answer our questions about the Eagles.

item.title: Scouting the Enemy: Kansas City Chiefs
item.description: The Denver Broncos open their 2026 regular season on Monday Night Football against the Kansas City Chiefs. Here is a deeper look at their Week 1 opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos kickoff their 2026 gridiron campaign defending their AFC West title against their longtime rival Kansas City Chiefs. For the first installment of Scouting the Enemy this year, we will take a look at how the Chiefs performed in 2025, their key offseason additions and departures, as well as their X-Factor players on offense and defense for Monday Night Football.

2025 Kansas City Chiefs Season Review

The Chiefs finished last season with a 6-11 record. It was the first time they had missed the playoffs since 2014 and their first losing season since 2012 when Romeo Crennel was head coach.

2026 Kansas City Chiefs Offseason Additions and Departures

The big addition for the Chiefs over the offseason was signing running back Kenneth Walker III in free agency. They also brought back cornerback L’Jarius Sneed, who had spent the past two years with the Tennessee Titans. Kansas City also traded a late 2027 draft selection to bring in former first-round quarterback Justin Fields to be the backup to Patrick Mahomes.

The biggest departure came via trade, with the GM Brett Veach trading two-time All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie to the Los Angeles Rams. Additionally, cornerback Jaylen Watson and defensive lineman Charles Omenihu both signed with the Washington Commanders in free agency.

With extra selections after the McDuffie trade, the Chiefs focused on shoring up their defense. Kansas City moved up to get Mansoor Delane at the six slot in 2006 NFL Draft. The former LSU standout was touted as the best cover corner last April. Additionally, they added versatile Clemson defensive lineman Peter Woods late in the first round.

To bolster their pass rush productivity, the Chiefs picked R Mason Thomas out of Oklahoma in the second round. I also liked their fourth-round selection, Oregon slot cornerback Jadon Canady. Their fifth-round picks, running back Emmett Johnson and wide receiver Cyrus Allen could be situational players for them as rookies.

Offensive X-Factor: Running Back Kenneth WalkerIII

All eyes are on the health of Patrick Mahomes and how he will return from an ACL injury last season. If he can revert to prior form, the Chiefs are likely title contenders. However, my X-Factor for them in Week 1 is free agent addition Kenneth Walker III. Last year’s Super Bowl MVP, Walker inked a 3-year, $34 million dollar deal this offseason to bolster their rushing attack.

Walker had a productive 2025 season with 221 rushes for 1,027 yards, and 5 touchdowns. He added 31 receptions for 282 yards as a receiver out of the backfield. The creative playcalling of Andy Reid coupled with Walker’s skillset will be a big challenge for the Broncos.

Limiting his impact will be critical to not only win the time of possession battle but also come out of Arrowhead with a victory. The Broncos can’t afford to let Walker run wild. Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his defensive front seven certainly have a tough challenge in the opening game.

Defensive X-Factor: Cornerback Mansoor Delane

The Chiefs opted to do a little bit of reshuffling in their defensive backfield this offseason. Their general manager has a history of trading away cornerbacks right before they are set to earn mega-extensions. Sending off McDuffie to the Rams was emblematic of that.

That means rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane will have to play a huge role for them this season. On Monday night against the Broncos, he will certainly have his hands full. With Denver adding Jaylen Waddle into the mix, Delane will be tasked with not just covering him, but also having to battle longtime veteran Courtland Sutton as well.

Both wide receivers have unique skill sets which will certainly test his abilities. Delane’s talented merited such an early selection, but I don’t see Bo Nix and the Broncos being shy about throwing in his direction. I expect them to test Delane early and often.

How the Broncos can secure a victory over the Chiefs

The Chiefs are a tough draw for the Broncos in Week 1, but I’m confident the Broncos can find a way to victory. As noted above, slowing down Walker will be a huge part of that. With it being a road game, slowing him down and finding a way to win the time of possession battle will be crucial.

Not only that, but finding a way to force some turnovers on defense will be huge if Denver wants to earn a victory. That’s been a focal point of theirs over the course of the summer. Now it’s time to put their plan in action on Monday Night Football.

On offense, the Broncos will need to limit their miscues and be efficient on the ground and through the air. The team’s rushing attack needs to hit the ground running, and Bo Nix needs to dial up a good game and find a way to get some explosive plays against their defense.

Hart’s Prediction: Broncos 24, Chiefs 17.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings, Week 1 find the Buffalo Bills favored to begin 2026 season
item.description: Where do NFL writers, experts, and analysts rank the Buffalo Bills heading into Week 1 against the Houston Texans?
item.content:encoded:
Despite the fact the NFL has only played two games of the 2026 season thus far, nothing was going to stop analysts and prognosticators from revealing their first Power Rankings of the regular season. Some call it “Week 0” and use the endeavor as a means to discuss expectations and rank accordingly. Others? It’s it’s their own version of the wild west borne out of quota needs.

That doesn’t mean we should focus only on those that are observably button-up, since sometimes the off-the-beaten-path offerings are far more entertaining. If you’ve followed along with me in prior seasons, you’ll know I try to remain consistent in sharing the same group of “rankers” each week. You may see some outfits join in or drop off, depending on vibes. That’s to be expected because we all know how important it is to give such an opinionated exercise the level of seriousness it deserves.

One thing’s clear in looking over this batch: Everyone LOVES the Los Angeles Rams. We get it, they have the reigning NFL MVP in Matthew Stafford, made a massive trade for edge rusher Myles Garrett (injured, mind you), and someone convinced a well-retired Aaron Donald to come back and play defensive tackle. Plus they have some guys who are good at catching the football.

Los Angeles is the easy pick. Well, it was until they took a flight just to mail in a game in Australia. Someone has to be crowned the premiere team (The Athletic crowned them a “superteam”), and the Rams made the most sense. But their Week 1 effort should serve as a reminder that crowning a champion in September is foolish.

In a similar way, any success a team finds early in the season should be dealt with in measured praise. Though quick to pass in our timeline, it’s a long season and very little reveals itself until after the Turkey (maybe Tofurkey or even lobsters) is (are) carved. We saw this play out last season when the Bills beat teams the experts didn’t view as a real threat. They wanted to see more out of Buffalo, only content to buy in once the playoffs began. Well, we know what happened on that front.

Anyway… power rankings. It’s not that serious. Or is it? Seriously, power rankings are fun! We’re at almost 2,700 words with this one — featuring 20 outlets (plus one) — so this article should help dissolve away some of those Friday office blues in no time. This list may shrink in any given week, but this season’s first at-bat is swinging for the fences. No one aggregates Buffalo Bills power rankings data like Buffalo Rumblings!

Let’s get to it, to see where the experts place the Buffalo Bills, shall we?

SB NationNFL

3 via: 2027 Super Bowl Chances by James Dator and Mark Schofield
4 via: Tim Lynch with Mile High Report
4 via: Brandon Lee Gowton with Bleeding Green Nation

NFL.com: 4

“The vibes are generally high in Buffalo, although receiver Khalil Shakir’s health status is worth monitoring prior to the season opener in Houston. The potential for a honeymoon campaign with WR DJ Moore — oh, and the commencement of Joe Brady’s first season as a head coach — begins against an elite defense, which should inform us on where the Bills stand offensively.— Nick Shook

The Athletic: 3

“(Austin) Mock’s projected win total: 10.8”

The defense is undergoing a significant change, entering a 3-4 scheme with six new starters, and that’s part of the reason for hope. The other is a fresh start with coach Joe Brady that could get this team over the hump and into the Super Bowl. Even if last season didn’t go as planned, it’s hard to keep a Josh Allen-led team out of the top five entering the season.” — Chad Graff/Josh Kendall

ESPN: 3

“Milestone to watch:Josh Allen surpassing Patrick Mahomes for the most combined passing and rushing yards by a quarterback in his first nine NFL seasons.”

“This would take Allen close to the end of the season, but it is well within reach. Allen is 3,782 yards away from eclipsing Mahomes (38,604), and Allen has not missed a start since his rookie season. He averages 590.1 rushing yards and 3,762.8 passing yards per season, so he could pass Mahomes with multiple games to spare. Breaking records is a common occurrence for Allen, and with new No. 1 receiver in DJ Moore added to the mix, he’s primed to set many marks yet again.” — Alaina Getzenberg

Sports Illustrated: 5

“Perpetually a team embodying the Atlas statue, the questions for the Bills are myriad. Can Josh Allen continue to play his style of football and get through a season relatively healthy? Will new head coach Joe Brady represent the right kind of vibe switch for Buffalo? Is Jim Leonhard’s defense finally going to provide Allen with some teeth on the other side of the ball and lessen the burden on his back? This is a team that we can almost assuredly believe will be there at the end of the year, though getting over the hump remains the eternal obstacle.” — Conor Orr

FOX Sports: 7

Ralph Vacchiano is smart listing his rankings in descending order, that way you have to scroll all the way down to see who’s the top dog. No one scrolls an entire article to read who’s holding court in the basement, right? You do? Oh. Moving on…

Vacchiano’s comments on Buffalo should serve as a warning, at least enough to give you pause about what president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane built. However, most teams can’t endure the amount of injuries to one position that the Bills managed with their wide receivers this summer.

“Summer injuries to WRs Keon Coleman and Khalil Shakir were a dangerous reminder that receiver is still a problem for this team. Man, if they can properly address that position, look out.” — Ralph Vacchiano

Bleacher Report: 5

We’re good with B/R these days, no? I am. They’ve come a long way, and to be clear they offer a very slick power rankings presentation. That’s the most important thing in all of this, yes? Well, it’s close to the most important thing. Remember, we’re having fun, folks!

Gary Davenport makes a lot of key points about the Bills that fans of the team are woefully aware of, and which some are fearful may never change. He’s pretty spot on here, revealing that once again that most of this won’t matter if they lose in the postseason.

“There isn’t a team east of Los Angeles more in Super Bowl-or-bust mode than the Buffalo Bills.

The Bills dismissed their highly successful coach because he couldn’t get the team over the hump. They are led by Josh Allen, who has more playoff wins than any quarterback in NFL history without a Super Bowl appearance.

The good news is the team should be in the thick of it in the AFC. The offense has the league’s reigning rushing king and a new No. 1 wide receiver in D.J. Moore. The defense ranked seventh in the league last year.

The bad news is that the Bills have been in the thick of it for the better part of a decade, but for whatever reason they come up short in the postseason. — Gary Davenport“

The Ringer: 5

With genuine and obvious applause to SB Nation and Buffalo Rumblings: Find a better overall sports-focused digital website better than The Ringer, I dare you. The Ringer looks and reads like one of those glossy European-specific car magazines short on advertisements, and that cost $30 dollars in a famous bookstore.

It’s true that The Athletic’s playoff odds/playoff simulator can’t be beat (here are both from last season/if you’re curious), but that’s about the only place The Ringer comes up short. I get nothing for such endorsements, mind you. I’d be shocked if either outfit even knew I existed.

As Dante Lee points out, their rankings will come monthly, which means we won’t see them again in these spaces until October. Lee’s thoughts on Buffalo, should they pan out, would leave little doubt about the Bills’ ability to get where it wants early next year. It won’t be long now before we learn more about what Brady brings to the table as the guy tabbed with doing what Sean McDermott could not accomplish. No pressure!

“Of all the teams that have made major coaching or personnel changes, the Bills seem to have kept the lowest profile in the lead-up to the regular season. After the disastrous press conference that team owner Terry Pegula and team president Brandon Beane gave this offseason (in the wake of firing Sean McDermott), the Bills quietly went about trading for receiver D.J. Moore, adding depth on both sides of the ball, and handing the defense over to highly reputable coordinator Jim Leonhard.

Last year felt like a step backward for Buffalo; it lost the division to New England and beat itself against the Broncos in the postseason. Now that coaching changes have been made and Josh Allen has a no. 1 receiver again, I want to see Buffalo leave no doubt about its place in the NFL hierarchy this year. That means winning at least three of its first four games (against the Texans, Lions, Chargers, and Patriots), looking like a well-oiled machine around Allen, and making it clear that it should be discussed with the same kind of certainty that we have about Los Angeles and Seattle. If this team stumbles out of the gate and starts the year under .500, first-year head coach Joe Brady may be bound for disappointment, and the pressure will ratchet up.” — Diante Lee

CBS Sports: 4

Pete Prisco is back with his succinct musings about where each team stands entering Week 1. Though I’d argue that Brady isn’t the key aggressive mind to focus on here, the point, in general, is understood.

“New coach Joe Brady will bring a much more aggressive approach to this team. That’s something that is badly needed.” — Pete Prisco

USA Today: 4

Nate Davis pulls no punches in his endorsement for the Bills, offering the following ahead of Week 1 in Houston:

“The feel-good vibes in Western New York are hard to ignore, even amid all the changes for what’s become a perennial AFC power … and, perhaps for the first time in more than three decades, the AFC’s preeminent force.” — Nate Davis

Pro Football Focus: 3

The Bills find themselves near the top of Bradley Locker’s rankings to begin the season. Will they prove him right, and eventually finishing as the top team in the AFC?

“Odds to make the playoffs: 77%”
“Odds to win the Super Bowl: 8%”

“For the first time since 2017, the Bills will have a leader other than Sean McDermott — but promoting former offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach should retain Buffalo’s hyper-efficient offense with Josh Allen and James Cook. All eyes are on Jim Leonhard as the Bills’ new defensive coordinator, looking to round out a unit with question marks but talent at all three levels. Buffalo enters the season with the highest division odds (56%) of any team, with a weaker AFC East making the Bills seem like a near-playoff lock for the eighth straight season.” — Bradley Locker

Sportsnaut: 6

It’s difficult to disagree with Matt Johnson saying that no team is under more pressure to win it all. Bills Mafia has only been waiting for a Super Bowl win since they were known as Bills Country — back long before anyone was even thinking about the world ending at midnight of Y2K.

“No team in the AFC is under more pressure than the Buffalo Bills. Brandon Beane wasn’t just spared being terminated for the team’s repeated playoff failures; he was promoted to president of football operations, and offensive coordinator Joe Brady was named head coach. It’s great to see Buffalo finally add a viable pass-catcher in DJ Moore to support Josh Allen, and there’s ample intrigue in Buffalo surrounding defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. Allen and Co. could easily be the AFC’s representative in the Super Bowl come February, but we just like the Ravens and Texans slightly more head-to-head.” — Matt Johnson

The Sporting News: 2

No one has the Bills ranked higher this week than Vinnie Iyer, who sold on Joe Brady being the right hire as head coach. Finding out if he’s right will take some time. Regardless, Iyer is on Buffalo’s wagon right now thanks to the “shakeup” at One Bills Drive. Failing to do anything wasn’t the answer this season.

“The Bills pushed the right buttons in keeping Joe Brady to lead the offense while also staying as head coach and flipping to a more aggressive defense under Jim Leonhard. Buffalo’s shakeup can pay off big-time in Josh Allen’s prime.” — Vinnie Iyer

yahoo!sports: 3

Dalton Kincaid is the focus here, with Frank Schwab recognizing how important a healthy Kincaid is to the Bills’ passing game. No argument there!

“The biggest news of August for the Bills was that tight end Dalton Kincaid was healthy. Injuries have cost Kincaid eight games over the past two seasons. Kincaid had a scorching 2.7 yards per route run last season, a fantastic mark for a tight end. Now he just needs to stay on the field to run more routes with Josh Allen.” — Frank Schwab

theScore: 4

Addressing questions about the wide receivers and defense overall doesn’t weigh Buffalo down much here thanks to Josh Allen.

“Buffalo has lingering questions throughout the defense and at wide receiver, even after adding DJ Moore to the roster. Still, as long as Josh Allen’s under center, the Bills have a chance to finish the season hoisting the Lombardi Trophy.” — theScore Staff

NFL Trade Rumors: 9

Here’s a site that’s terrible. Awful, in so many ways, really, but often unavoidable due to the nature of their content. The pop-ups and copy gatekeeping (don’t even think of right-clicking) are circa 2005-era internet levels, so they’ll begin the season here on a very short leash. I struggle even linking to their page, but journalistic integrity prevails for the effort by Ethan Woodie and their “website’ish.”

Thankfully a dual-monitor setup makes referencing their content here a breeze (though I’ve removed the extra space between sentences, because… so 2005). Here’s the rather interesting take that Woodie had to say about Buffalo’s somewhat low ranking:

“The Bills lost in overtime to the Broncos in the divisional round last year and moved on from longtime HC Sean McDermott, promoting OC Joe Brady in his stead. Buffalo might have the best offense in the league this year, with QB Josh Allen getting an upgrade at receiver with D.J. (sic) Moore. The defense, however, leaves much to be desired. The Bills have serious questions at linebacker, defensive tackle, and safety. Allen could run roughshod through the league all year then get let down in the playoffs by his defense once again.” — Ethan Woodie

Computer Cowboy/Ben Baldwin: 4

Look at the rest of the AFC East!

View Link

“The Rich Eisen Show”: 5

Do we love Rich Eisen still? I think it’s a yes, and I for one enjoy his annual “Run, Rich, Run” 40-yard dash for charity during the NFL Draft. Eisen’s fun, but he’s also a bit unhinged in the way he ranks teams. His brand of unhinged works, unlike select others who’ve seen fit to rank teams based on their fans’/random social media posts in past seasons (or worse, a zero effort from PFT’s Mike Florio). Eisen also doesn’t bore folks with the bottom two-thirds-plus of the league.

“I have them winning the AFC, the Buffalo Bills are here… …Listen, if I’ve got ‘em winning the Super Bowl, I mean in the Super Bowl, I can’t have ‘em not on my power rankings… I’ve come around on it. Josh Allen’s my MVP choice, I’ve bought in.”

Interestingly, Eisen has the Denver Broncos at three despite saying the Bills will win the AFC and play in the Super Bowl. Power rankings: fun and games!

That’s it for this edition of Buffalo Rumblings’ Bills power rankings round-up.
