item.title: 6 NFL players with the most to prove in 2026
item.description: These NFL players are feeling the heat this year.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL is at a major pivot point for many teams around the league. We’re hitting make-or-break time for a lot of players from the 2022 and 2023 NFL Drafts, as well as some guys who might have more runway — but still haven’t lived up to expectations and need to prove something.

In 2025, we went from a prevailing feeling that most teams were set at quarterback to a sense that many teams might be dipping their toes in the water once more. The pressure is on not just for teams to get over the hump, but for individual players to prove they’re worthy of faith beyond this season.

No. 1: C.J. Stroud, QB — Houston Texans

There’s no way to sugarcoat Stroud’s 2025 season. Not only was he mediocre during the regular season, but a disaster in the playoffs as the third-year QB finished two playoff games completing barely over 50% of his passes, throwing two touchdowns and five interceptions in an effort that dismantled a potential Cinderella run for the smothering Texans defense.

We’re in a position where Stroud has regressed for two straight seasons. His breakout rookie campaign feels a mile away, and while there are fair excuses to be made about the lack of protection from the Texans’ line, it’s also fair to note that Stroud has not seen pressure well, adapted effectively, or found a way to get the ball to his receivers in spite of it all.

There are no more excuses. Stroud needs to step up this season and prove he’s a franchise quarterback, not just a decent passer. That’s what’s at stake for 2026.

No. 2: Marvin Harrison Jr, WR — Arizona Cardinals

There’s no question that sometimes there are draft busts, but it’s very, very rare that we see a player who everyone thought was a lock for greatness, only to watch him struggle. There’s been nothing special about MHJ since he entered the league, and while we initially thought it was just rookie nerves, we’re now entering year three of him playing like a second or third receiver, not the game-breaking No. 1 we assumed him to be.

Quarterbacking has been garbage in Arizona, but that doesn’t excuse his lapses in concentration, lazy work in and out of his routes, as well as simply having mental errors that shouldn’t be popping up with a player of his pedigree. Even without an elite QB in 2026, Marvin Harrison Jr. still has a lot to prove.

No. 3: Kyler Murray, QB — Minnesota Vikings

There’s been a symbiotic relationship between Kyler Murray and the NFL ever since he was the No. 1 pick that has meant the league has been unfair to him, and he’s been unfair to the league in kind. Questions about his effort and demeanor in Arizona saw the Cardinals decide to go in a different direction, with Minnesota being his final stop to salvage his NFL career — at least as a starting quarterback.

This can definitely happen with the Vikings, where he will land on a talented roster with an abundance of weapons, meaning there are really no excuses not to make this work. It’s not like Murray needs to be a Top 10 quarterback this season, but at least he needs to show that he can still be an effective starter. At this stage he’s on a one-year prove-it deal, meaning he needs to prove it. If that doesn’t happen he’s destined to ride the bench, or potentially try to make it in baseball.

No. 4: Kayvon Thibodeaux, EDGE — New York Giants

It’s honestly surprising the Giants didn’t decide to move on from Thibodeaux after drafting Arvell Reese, but there’s some method to their madness. At this point Thibodeaux’s value is in the toilet, and there was no reason to force a deal just to get a day-three pick — so instead New York will have a deep pass rush rotation in 2026.

Thibodeaux is on the final year of his rookie contract, meaning that he is fully in “prove it” mode at this point. This year will determine if he’s a rotational pass rusher for the remainder of his career, or if he can prove that he has the potential to be a long-term starter.

No. 5: Jalen Hurts, QB — Philadelphia Eagles

I’m really in two minds about including Hurts here, because he’s a very odd case study. Hurts is neither as good as Eagles fans believe, nor is he as bad as 31 other fanbases think he is. Ultimately he’s an above-average QB who is exceptionally good at running Philly’s system, but he’s not elite in comparison with other QBs around the NFL.

The “something to prove” factor comes from the weight of expectations. The Eagles are routinely a team that should be contending for Super Bowl appearances with the weight of their roster, so when they fall short it’s only going to raise questions about whose fault that is. One of these has been Hurts’ consistency in the playoffs, where he very often looks like a shadow of himself — and that talk was stoked by A.J. Brown being angered that he wasn’t getting the ball enough.

In many ways Hurts has nothing to prove, but he also has everything to prove in 2026.

No. 6: George Pickens, WR — Dallas Cowboys

The breakout of Pickens last year was a mammoth jump for the Cowboys, and it not only justified trading for Pickens, but also established him as a top receiver in the NFL. One season wasn’t quite enough to justify a long-term extension, with Dallas being up against the salary cap and wanting to see more maturity — which led to the franchise tag.

This season will shape Pickens’ future. Either he’ll show out once more and become one of the highest-paid receivers in the NFL, or it will fall apart, and he’ll likely get short-term contracts as teams wait to see whether or not he can be relied on. This is a mammoth season for him.

item.title: Super Bowl 2027 expert picks from 13 football writers
item.description: Let’s make our Super Bowl picks.
item.content:encoded:
Preseason Super Bowl predictions are usually good for absolutely nothing, but they still serve as an important barometer on expectations heading into the new year. A year ago, the Seahawks were 19th in the preseason Super Bowl odds, and the Patriots were 21st. It’s only natural for many fans to believe the Los Angeles Rams will waltz to a championship this year as the preseason No. 1 in the power rankings, but this is the NFL, and anything can happen.

Only three of our 13 experts picked the Rams to win the 2027 Super Bowl in this piece. Four writers picked the Buffalo Bills to win it all. Two people picked the Chicago Bears. There were six different champions picked from the staff members we polled.

Who do you think is winning the 2027 Super Bowl? Leave a comment on this story, and we’ll revisit it at the end of the season. No one could have predicted a Seahawks-Patriots Super Bowl at this time last year. Will this season be more chalk? Time will tell. For now, here are our preseason Super Bowl picks heading into the 2026 campaign.

Rams 28, Ravens 17 — Mark Schofield

Ah yes, the annual preseason Super Bowl prediction that is sure to be wrong.

After all, I’m fairly certain I have predicted the Lions versus the Ravens each of the past two seasons, and you can see how that has worked out for me.

I would say that the third time is the charm, but I’m skeptical about both teams even winning their respective divisions, let alone making it to the Super Bowl. So we are going to change things up. Out of the AFC, I think this is the year that Josh Allen and company finally get over the hump.

And in the NFC, I’ll go with a chalky pick and predict that the Rams get to Super Bowl LXI out of the NFC.

As for a winner? Let’s send Matthew Stafford out on a high note.

Rams 31, Ravens 10 – James Dator

I am ready to be yelled at for a prediction that totally flies off the rails midway through the season.

There’s going to be some chalk, however – because I’m also picking the Rams. When I look at that team there’s just too much veteran strength, too many areas where they’re without weakness, and adding Myles Garrett was an obscene addition. I think this is the year they’re going to head back to the Super Bowl, and hoist the trophy when it’s all done.

As for the other team, I’m resisting an urge to pick the Bills (who I’m not 100% sold on) and instead picking the Baltimore Ravens. I really like a lot about that football team, and Jesse Minter was one of my favorite new coaching hires of the cycle. In addition, there’s a lot to be excited about offensively with the Ravens, as Sean Payton protege Declan Doyle takes over, which gives me faith he can engineer something creative with Lamar Jackson.

When the dust settles on this season I just can’t help but feel like someone is just running towards the Rams meat grinder. Never say never, but they just look too dang good.

Eagles 31, Chiefs 20 – Shamus Clancy

The every-other-year magic of the Eagles’ offense will return under new play-caller Sean Mannion. With a healthier offensive line reinvigorating the run game in tandem with Saquon Barkley, to say nothing of a vaunted, star-filled defense, the Birds will return to the Big Game for the third time in the Nick Sirianni-Jalen Hurts era. 

Why don’t we just make this Super Bowl matchup Eagles-Chiefs III for the theatrics of it all?

Philadelphia wins the rubber match and brings the Lombardi Trophy, once more, back to Broad Street. 

Bills over Cowboys – Kyle Thele

The Bills look like the best team in the AFC and I think it’s finally the year they stop falling over themselves in the postseason. Josh Allen gets his ring by beating an overmatched Cowboys team. Dallas will be the team that just gets hot at the right time and makes a run, but they just aren’t as good. 

I’m tempted to put the Rams in there, and on paper they are probably the best team in football. But they are one important injury away from being a team that at best gets a Wild Card bid. I’m not willing to believe a 38-year old quarterback with an injury history can stay upright long enough to finish the season.

49ers over Broncos – Ricky O’Donnell

I was torn between the 49ers and Cowboys coming out of the NFC. I went with the Niners because it feels like they’re a safe bet to win double-digit games and make the playoffs every year under Kyle Shanahan, and I just feel like if you continue to do that you will eventually get the luck you need to break through. As a Bears fan, San Francisco’s win last season in a primetime Week 17 shootout sticks with me if they can get the defense together. I pick the Ravens every year out of the AFC, but I’m switching it up this year. Denver has a truly elite defense, and I feel like Sean Payton can cook up enough offensively even with a limited quarterback in Bo Nix. The Niners might be cursed, but their top-end talent and coaching is strong, and that’s enough for me.   

Bills over Lions – Beth Maiman

I feel strongly that the Bills can finally get over the hump and make it to the Super Bowl out of the AFC this season. I think the new stadium, Josh Allen’s new journey to fatherhood and other AFC foes not being at full strength are all factors shaping up to be a storybook season for the boys in Buffalo. The NFC pick was a harder decision for me, so I went with my bias of watching too many NFC North games and I am going with the Lions. I think Detroit has a lot of opponents on its schedule the Lions should beat. Picking up a handful of wins this season could help the team with confidence as the season progresses. Head coach Dan Campbell and quarterback Jared Goff have an opportunity to silence the doubters this season by making it all the way to the Super Bowl. If the Bears are one of the biggest teams standing in Detroit’s way during the season, I think the Lions core returners and experience will give them wins against Chicago. Interestingly enough, Buffalo and Detroit  happen to face off in Week 2 of the season at Highmark Stadium. 

49ers 30, Chargers 23 – David Fucillo

I’m a sucker when it comes to picking my 49ers. They’re considered by many as the third team of the big three in the NFC West, behind the Rams and Seahawks. I think LA wins the division, but I think we see the 49ers finally get over the top under Kyle Shanahan. They stay healthy enough for the first time in a long time and the talent is there to get them to the mountaintop.

And why not a rematch of Super Bowl 29 and against one of their former head coaches? The Chargers seem to get overestimated every year, but I think the addition of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator is going to move this offense into elite territory.

Bears over Bengals – Jeanna Kelley

It’s so hard to realistically project Super Bowl winners before a real regular-season snap of football is played. But the Bears locked up the NFC two-seed last postseason, and they lost a very close Divisional Round matchup against the Rams. Given the Bengals offensive talent in particular, I always feel like they should be in the mix for the postseason, and given that their fans have suffered disappointment after disappointment since the Bengals lost to the Rams in Super Bowl LIV, it feels like this year might be time for those fortunes to change. 

Texans over Seahawks – Mookie Alexander

I will confess to being a homer in picking the Seahawks to return to the Super Bowl. Why can’t they? Still don’t think Sam Darnold is good? Still think Mike Macdonald is touring with The Doobie Brothers? This is a well-balanced, well-coached team that should see the passing offense get even better and offset what I think will be a small decline in performance from last season. The Rams coronation sounds cool but I think Macdonald outfoxes Sean McVay’s superteam in the NFC Championship again.

I’ve been burned by the Texans as recently as two years ago, but I’m back on the bandwagon. C.J. Stroud was dreadful last postseason but I think opinion of him has swung too far against him. He’s still a good quarterback who needs a more effective run game and better offensive line, which I think Houston will have this year. Their defense will be the NFL’s best, so much so that they’ll topple Josh Allen and the Bills in the AFC Championship. DeMeco Ryans will not only thwart Seattle’s repeat bid, he’ll finally bring a Lombardi Trophy back to Texas. Stroud bets on himself and cashes in.

Bears over Bills – RJ Ochoa

The Bears took a massive step forward during Ben Johnson’s first season, and I fully expect them to build off of that in his second. Caleb Williams has full and total control of the offense and right now the division is Chicago’s (or Indiana’s, I guess) to lose. The proper things will have to break their way for them to get to the Super Bowl, but when they do they’ll run into a Bills team who finally got over the hump… just to fall short in the final moment yet again. 

Bills 31, Rams 27 – James Brady

The Bills can’t be normal about anything, but persistence will finally pay off for them. This time around, the offense will show up in the postseason and they’ll make the big plays when they’re supposed to. The Patriots, Ravens, Chiefs, and Chargers will all be great teams, but Joe Brady helps Buffalo get it done to get to the big game.

It’s so very tempting to pick the 49ers, even after the tumultuous offseason they had. It’s tempting even with all of the injuries and the dysfunction. They keep getting so close despite those things, but until they’re not a factor anymore I just don’t feel comfortable picking them. So I’m going with the Rams, an absurd team that keeps landing absurd players. If injuries aren’t a major factor, I just don’t see how anybody can reliably beat them in the postseason. But the Bills will do it anyway, finally.

Bills 42, Rams 40 – Matt Warren

This has to be the year the Bills get over the hump, right? Joe Brady is going to be more aggressive on both sides of the ball and it’s going to pay off for Buffalo when it matters most. The defense they have built under Jim Leonhard will take a couple months to gel, but by January they will be locked in. They have the best QB in the NFL alongside an unleashed playcaller-turned-head coach. Josh Allen will set the record for most playoff games by a quarterback before his first Super Bowl but like the previous record-holder Peyton Manning, it will be worth the wait. 

I have the Rams, 49ers, and Seahawks kind of clumped together atop the NFC. The Seahawks have the SB hangover, the 49ers have every distraction imaginable and injuries galore, and the Rams are just plugging along. That L.A. defense is going to put some NFC quarterback in a blender in the NFC Championship Game.

These two face off in Week 5 of the regular season and two years ago put on a gem in L.A., with the Rams squeaking out a 44-42 win. Despite what I anticipate to be two solid defenses, the offensive gurus on either side light it up again with MVP QBs battling it out. 

Rams 24, Ravens 21 – Jared Mueller

For a Browns fan, our former team (ripped from our hearts in 1995) versus our former superstar (Myles Garrett) is not exactly a dream scenario. It’s a nightmare. At some point, Lamar Jackson is going to take the Ravens to another level, or the two sides might just be parting. Why not this year?

Given the additions of Aaron Donald and Garrett, anyone not picking the Rams is probably struggling with that decision. Health, given Matthew Stafford’s history, Garrett’s knee and foot history, and Donald sitting out for a couple of seasons, is really the key variable that could derail the season. A major injury to Stafford or Garrett (with Jared Verse on the Browns) could change everyone’s prediction immediately.

item.title: Eagles News: Saquon Barkley poised for another big season
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 9/11/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Saquon Barkley looked pretty good in training camp this summer. The Eagles’ offense was uneven as a whole but they looked their best when they leaned into the running game. It’s not hard for me to envision Barkley having another big season. Obviously not easy to project him to reach his 2024 numbers. And him looking good won’t matter if the blocking doesn’t hold up, as we saw last season. But I tend to think things will come together in the run game more than they did in 2025.

Can Saquon Barkley recapture his 2024 dominance? – ESPN

Not only is the offensive line in a better place but Barkley is as well. He shot past his career high in carries (345) during the regular season in 2024 and added 91 more rushes in the postseason. That number fell to 280 last season. And while the wild-card playoff exit against the San Francisco 49ers was disappointing for the Eagles, it gave everyone more of a physical and mental break this offseason, including the 29-year-old Barkley. “Huge,” said running backs coach Jemal Singleton, on the benefits of the longer layoff. “He could take the time from the offseason and get his rest but then come back and start working. So I feel like he’s in a really, really good place now. … It’s going to be exciting to kind of see him go.” Singleton can see it most in the conditioning part of it where Barkley, who shares a backfield this season with a pair of capable backs in Tank Bigsby and Will Shipley, has stayed on the field for more plays during long drives while looking “explosive.” Put the fresh legs with a revitalized offensive front in this run scheme, and there is optimism Barkley can ascend to the top of the running back class once again. “Being a better playmaker,” Barkley said on what he wants to improve from last season. “That’s why I was brought here, that’s what I feel I’m one of the best in the league [at] and just bringing that back.”

Can Saquon Barkley defy the RB age curve? His favorite back’s best season came at 29 – The Athletic

The Eagles made a major scheme change this offseason that will be apparent in the running game. Quarterback Jalen Hurts will more frequently line up under center. The Eagles installed a wide-zone running scheme. Barkley said he’s “always been intrigued with this kind of system” while observing the success of players from afar. He spoke to Peterson about the depth he should align before the snap, ranging from six yards to eight yards. The landmarks in the running game are different. Barkley said he must be more of a one-cut runner. He believes the protection is friendly to a running back. “I feel like I have a chance to be really good in this system,” Barkley said. “I feel like it’s going to open things that I may have not been able to show in my career.” “He can be good in any system, let’s be honest,” running backs coach Jemal Singleton added. “But I think this is one that allows him to do some things that I think is going to be fun. It’ll be fun to watch him work, and he’s one of those guys that dives into everything. He reaches out to former players that have played in the system like this.” Barkley connected with Todd Gurley, who was offensive coordinator Sean Mannion’s teammate in Los Angeles. Gurley’s two best seasons came in this offense, making first-team All-Pro both years. (Gurley is also an example of a running back who did not age as Barkley intends; Gurley’s final season was at age 26.) Singleton, who coached in this system elsewhere, raved about Barkley’s offseason. Barkley has made cuts in practice that left new teammates dumbfounded. For old teammates, it’s a reminder of Barkley’s 2024 greatness. “We kind of take that stuff for granted a little bit,” Singleton said. “It’s like the ‘wow’ factor. It’s Saquon Barkley. Let’s not forget, and he’s done some amazing things, and he still can.”

Eagles vs. Commanders Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 1 enemy – BGN

The Philadelphia Eagles are beginning their 2026 season with a home game against the Washington Commanders. Nick Sirianni and Jalen Hurts are aiming to reach 6-0 in Week 1 games together. In order to preview this NFC East matchup, I reached out to our enemies over at Hogs Haven. The affable Andrew Y kindly took the time took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers.

NFC East Mixtape Vol. 188: Week 1 Preview – NFC East Mixtape

We have FINALLY reached Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season and to start things off we have all four NFC East teams taking on another member of the division. Which two will emerge as winners? Which two will hate everything and want to start over? RJ Ochoa and Brandon Gowton discuss in true Mixtape fashion… plus Big Blue View’s Ed Valentine joins for perspective on the G-Men! You can see that we have a BRAND NEW NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel so make sure to subscribe as the show will live here exclusively in video format.

Lots of Questions – Iggles Blitz

So the experts have the Eagles missing the playoffs, as a wild card team or making it back to the Super Bowl. That’s quite a range of outcomes. The lack of faith in the Eagles is all about the offense. AJ Brown is out and a new scheme is in. People have doubts about how good Jalen Hurts will be in the new scheme. It is absolutely fair to have concerns about the offense. I’m buying the Eagles as a contender because of Saquon Barkley, better OL play and an elite defense. That is a winning formula. Hurts should have time to grow into the new offense and for his receivers to work into their roles.

Why Sean Mannion decided to call plays from the booth this season – NBCSP

While Mannion explained that there are pros and cons of both locations, the 34-year-old ultimately decided to head up to the booth as he enters his first season as the Eagles’ offensive coordinator. “When you’re in the box, obviously you have a little bit more space,” Mannion explained on Thursday afternoon. “You’re not pacing around. You have the tablet. It’s a little bit like sitting at a desk, but I think just the vision is a little bit unique there, the higher vantage point. “Honestly, I felt comfortable with both, and really, I just felt like the vision type of thing really led me to the decision. Ultimately, the other part of it is we have a great staff. They communicate really well on the sideline. There’s been constant lines of communication, and I think all of that led to the decision.” This decision is a departure from the way the Eagles have done things for a long time. Franchise quarterback Jalen Hurts noted earlier this week that this will be his first time with a play caller upstairs since his days in college. It can make communication a bit tricky between Hurts and Mannion because it’ll have to be over the red phone on the sideline.

Is Sean Mannion ready for his big moment with the Eagles? He’s been preparing for it for years. – Inquirer

Mike Riley and Sean Mannion were having one of their catch-up calls when Mannion, who played quarterback at Oregon State under Riley, told his former coach the latest project he was working on during the nascent days of his own coaching career. Mannion, the most prolific passer in Oregon State history, told Riley that he was putting together and digitizing all of the passing concepts he could find dating back to the 1960s. “This is what he does in his spare time,” Riley explained recently. Mannion is just 34 years old and only three years removed from his playing career. He has never called plays in the NFL before and now is tasked with turning around an Eagles offense that was too stagnant in 2025 under another first-year coordinator and first-time play caller Kevin Patullo. Nick Sirianni said in February that he was looking for someone who was detailed and had “conviction in what they believed and why they believed in it, and the vision and conviction of how they went about it.” Those traits seem to describe Mannion, whose father, John, called him “a saver” who took and saved detailed notes at every stop along his football path and even has comprehensive notes on concepts that pre-date his own life by some 30 years. Eagles quarterbacks coach Parks Frazier raved recently about Mannion’s attention to detail and his ability to recall and reference something he has learned along the way. “He remembers every detail about all of those things and he’s constantly applying it to what he’s doing moving forward,” Frazier said. “He has extreme, detailed, categorized notes and film of everything he’s been through.”

I did a poor job as a coach of just taking him under my wing and having this confidence with them. That’s on me. That has nothing to do with Tank.”

item.title: Matthew Stafford rarely succeeds on quarterback sneaks, but Rams tried one anyway
item.description: With the Rams facing fourth-and-goal at the 1-yard line on Thursday night, Matthew Stafford attempted a quarterback sneak.
item.content:encoded:
With the Rams facing fourth-and-goal at the 1-yard line on Thursday night, Matthew Stafford attempted a quarterback sneak. It did not go well: Stafford took the snap and fell into the line, going nowhere and ending what had been an excellent drive just short of the goal line.

That raised an obvious question: Why was a quarterback sneak the play call? Stafford isn't Jalen Hurts or Josh Allen. He's a 38-year-old who attempted two quarterback sneaks last year and failed on both of them, and who didn't gain as much as a single rushing first down in 17 regular-season games last year.

Rams coach Sean McVay said after the game that he viewed failing to score at the end of that 12-play, 72-yard drive as the moment the wind went out of the Rams' sails.

"We go right down the field and then we don't get in on the QB sneak, and things got out of hand from there," McVay said.

Given that, McVay needs to look in the mirror at his own play-calling decision. Stafford confirmed that the sneak was a called play and not something he did on his own.

"I've just got to find a way to get in," Stafford said.

If McVay wanted to sneak it in from the 1-yard line, it would have made more sense for the Rams to snap the ball to a tight end or running back, which many teams with aging or immobile quarterbacks do. Or McVay simply could have called another short-yardage play. McVay's decision to go for it on fourth-and-goal was a good one, but the play call was a bad one.

item.title: What we learned from Rams' ugly opening loss vs. 49ers
item.description: The Los Angeles Rams finished the offseason as winners but did not start the season with a victory. Here's the latest.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams finished the offseason as winners, following the addition of Myles Garrett and the return of Aaron Donald, while also being viewed as the favorite to win the Super Bowl at SoFi Stadium again this season.

The Rams won’t come back home with that same successful feeling, after the team’s short trip to Australia was unsuccessful.

The team’s travel itinerary will be viewed as a disaster, with a late arrival likely being viewed as a reason for the 27-7 loss to the NFC West rival, San Francisco 49ers.

“I know there’s gonna be a lot of narratives that appropriately put the blame on me, and then we’ll move forward the right way," Rams coach Sean McVay told reporters after the game. "… I don’t believe (the travel plan) is why we didn’t play well enough. I really don’t.”

The travel decisions will continue to be a topic of discussion in the coming days, but there are several other factors that could be attributed to the loss.

Myles Garrett will benefit from Aaron Donald’s return

Garrett has proven throughout his career that he can be the primary focus on a defense and still produce. He spent some time matched up against 49ers standout lineman Trent Williams and did not have a good showing by the defenders' standards, finishing the game without a sack or tackle.

"We got to be better, myself especially,” Garrett said. “We didn't execute how we want to ... we have to do more. There's a lot more that this team can get done, and it starts with us as leaders.”

He had missed some time away from practice in recent weeks. He did not produce a tackle or sack in 39 snaps against the 49ers.

Garrett produced 23 sacks last season before winning the NFL Defensive Player of the Year award for the second time in his career. 

When Donald takes the field, his presence alone forces defenses to either double-team Donald or Garrett or leave both in man-to-man situations.

Rams secondary had highs and lows 

The defense had few positive moments outside of safety Quentin Lake’s second-quarter interception. It served as the first turnover for the team this season, but it was also the only one for the game.

He jumped 49ers tight end George Kittle and caught 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy’s pass with 12:04 left in the second quarter.

It was the only memorable moment for the Rams as the secondary allowed three touchdowns after that.

What’s wrong with Matthew Stafford?

Quarterback Matthew Stafford did not finish the game, fueling speculation that he may have been injured.

Stafford left the game in the final minutes of the fourth quarter and was replaced by Stetson Bennett.

The Rams’ seven-point performance is the fewest points scored in a game with Stafford as the starter.

Stafford did not appear injured and was removed by McVay with the game clearly out of hand. The veteran quarterback was seen on the broadcast running off the field after the game.

He completed 15 of 25 passes for 155 yards and an interception. He did not throw a touchdown in the game.

Stafford was recorded as having a one-yard loss on two carries, one of which came after a failed quarterback sneak attempt on 4th-and-goal.

item.title: Here’s how the Colts can start 1-0
item.description: It won’t be easy, but the Colts can get it done.
item.content:encoded:
1-0 is a great sight for NFL fans. It is the validation that your hopes and dreams might be well placed. It also starts a team on the right track statistically to make the postseason and avoids the dreaded 0-2 hole to start the season. It isn’t a panacea, as things can go sideways, but it feels pretty good. Here is how the Indianapolis Colts can get it done.

The Ravens are a good team, so it won’t be an easy task. The Colts have some advantages, however. The home crowd will be back and ready. It hasn’t always translated into Week One wins, but the confines of Lucas Oil are much more advantageous than a road opener. The Colts are also trending towards good health. Daniel Jones is back, and Alec Pierce should be ready as well. The bumps and bruises of camp are also healing for Tyler Warren and Josh Downs. Jonathan Taylor is the bell cow, and the Ravens will have their hands full trying to contain him. If the Colts can establish the run game early, Taylor may prove to be too much for the Ravens late. 

A lot of Sunday’s success will come down to how well the defense contains Lamar Jackson. Jackson is electric. If they can keep him in the pocket, though, that electricity falls a few wattages. Speaking of a bell cow, Derrick Henry is in the backfield for the Ravens. Stopping the dual threat of he and Jackson will be tough, but it’s also the key to victory. The defense has some question marks. Veterans have returned to form, but the effectiveness of the line remains in the air. Young linebackers will be tested as well. If those units rise to the occasion, they can keep the Colts’ offense in position to win.

Looking back at Week Ones for the Colts is troubling, so let’s not look back too far. How about one year? The Colts got off to a hot start by using the momentum of a win to start the season. The offense needs to find the footing that was lost in the back half of 2025, and the Colts need to control the line of scrimmage on defense. Do those things and the Colts will start 2026 with that coveted 1-0.

item.title: Patriots injury analysis after season opener vs. Seahawks
item.description: Analyzing the Patriots’ injury situation after their Week 1 loss.
item.content:encoded:
Their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks did not go the way the New England Patriots would have hoped. Not only did they let a 10-0 lead slip out of their grasp behind a three-interception performance from their starting quarterback, they also lost one of their most important offensive skill position players to what projects as a multi-week injury.

Obviously, all eyes are on A.J. Brown and his sprained ankle coming out of the game. But as a look at our weekly injury analysis shows, he was not the only Patriot to get banged up during the 13-10 defeat on Wednesday night.

Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 1

CB Carlton Davis III: Davis was shaken up midway through the first quarter while helping to blow up a run play. He remained down on one knee, but jogged off with members of New England’s training staff shortly thereafter. Following a brief stay in the blue medical tent, he returned to the sidelines and eventually reentered. the contest on the next defensive series.

TE Hunter Henry: Henry took a hard hit on the first play from scrimmage in the second half, landing on his back after a 13-yard reception. He left the field under his own power and entered the medical tent for further evaluation, but returned to the game a short time later.

WR A.J. Brown: The big one. Brown remained on the ground after an incomplete third-down attempt, with medical personnel and even head coach Mike Vrabel checking in on him on the field. He limped off the field into the medical tent, and later gingerly walked back to the locker room albeit under his own power. Follow-up evaluation done on Thursday found out that he had suffered a high-ankle sprain.

C Jared Wilson: The Patriots’ starting center had to be evaluated on the sideline after suffering an apparent cut on his right snapping hand during the first series of the second half, the same that saw Henry and Brown get shaken up. He ended up playing all 71 offensive snaps.

RT Morgan Moses: During his Monday press conference, head coach Mike Vrabel listed Moses among other players suffering injuries in the game. There was no obvious moment an injury might have occurred, however, and he did end up playing 100% of New England’s offensive snaps.

What this means for the Patriots

Losing A.J. Brown just 31 snaps into his Patriots debut is an obvious blow to an offense that already had a hard time stringing consistent plays together versus the Seahawks with him on the field. Now, the unit will have to find a way to operate with Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism as its primary wide receivers — a group that will be in the spotlight over the coming games.

Based on Wednesday and his role throughout the summer, Williams in particular should see an uptick in reps as the primary X-receiver. Hollins, who does have some good chemistry with Drake Maye, also will continue to be heavily involved.

For how long Brown will be out remains to be seen. According to reports, the expected recovery range for his type of sprain is somewhere between four and six weeks. This means that short-term injured reserve, which would sideline him for a minimum of four weeks, appears to be a realistic if ultimately disappointing possibility.

As for the other players listed above, they do not appear to have suffered any long-term issues.

“Morgan Moses was able to return. Hunter Henry was able to return. Carlton Davis III was able to return,” said Mike Vrabel on Thursday. “Probably some bumps and bruises, but I do not think anything that would keep anybody out. A.J. Brown is one we will have to monitor.”

Coming off their season opener, the Patriots will enjoy a 10-day break before their home opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers.

item.title: Plaschke: Sean McVay's travel gamble turns Rams' Australian opener into a jet-lagged flop
item.description: The Rams' decision to leave late for Australia coupled with Sean McVay making a bad play call at a critical moment all add up to a humiliating loss.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams did worse than arrive late.

They didn’t show up at all.

Amid a weeklong barrage of criticism, the Rams didn’t land in Melbourne for their season opener Thursday until 28 hours before kickoff while the San Francisco 49ers had been there all week.

Turns out, the 49ers were smart, and the Rams were sorry.

The 49ers were terrific, and the Rams were terrible.

The 49ers energetically dominated in a 27-7 victory while the Rams exhaustedly despaired in front of more than 100,000 fans at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, a venue that hosts Australian rules football games that aren’t this ugly.

What idiot recently wrote that these Rams were going to go undefeated?

Read more:Star-studded Rams humbled by Brock Purdy and 49ers in Australian season opener

This idiot, and don’t dare say you thought that prediction wouldn’t last one game. One game?

Who knew that football’s super team was capable of being super bad?

Who could have guessed that football genius Sean McVay would be so badly outplanned, so badly outcoached, and so unimaginably wrong on the game’s transformative play?

Who could have predicted that defending league MVP Matthew Stafford would throw high, throw short, and basically throw an array of balls that landed down under?

Who knew that star offseason addition Myles Garrett would get pushed around, thrown down and eventually turned into human Vegemite?

G’night, mate!

“This is a humbling day for us,” said McVay, who knows what’s coming. “There’s going to be a lot of narratives that appropriately put the blame on me.”

As if being ripped nationwide for his travel plans wasn’t painful enough, McVay will also be skewered for a baffling decision on a third-quarter play that could have rescued the Rams but instead doomed them.

With the Rams trailing 17-7, they marched to the 49ers’ one-yard line, where they faced fourth-and-goal.

Do they pass to football’s most prolific red-zone receiver in Davante Adams? Do they run the ball with scoring machine Kyren Williams?

Neither. McVay called a quarterback sneak for 38-year-old Stafford, despite the fact that he had not scored a rushing touchdown in four years and was 0-for-2 on fourth-down sneaks last year.

The 49ers unsurprisingly held and promptly drove 99 yards to score on a 15-yard pass from Brock Purdy to Deebo Samuel between three confused defenders to clinch it.

”The first thing I look at is where can I improve?” said McVay, admirably accountable as always. “Where can I put our players in better positions to have successful outcomes?”

Stafford blamed himself, saying, “I’ve just got to find a way to get in.”

It’s hard to fault Stafford for not making a play that his body just can’t make, but it’s fair to wonder if the travel and short turnaround impacted his worst big game in several years.

He was held under 10 points for just the second time in his last 85 starts. He missed on seven of his first 11 passes, threw for just 155 yards and had no touchdown passes with one interception.

“Obviously not the way you want to start the season,” he said.

While it seemed obvious that he was jet-lagged, Stafford rejected the notion that the Rams’ unique travel schedule — engineered to keep their body clocks on California time for a 10:35 a.m. Melbourne start — was the reason for his malaise.

Read more:NFL Week 1 picks: Texans prevail over Bills; Broncos beat Chiefs

”When the ball was kicked off we were ready to play,” he said. “We just didn’t do it at a high enough clip today.”

Many critics have called the Rams crazy since they announced the schedule last week. This is even though a similarly quick stop in London last year led to a waxing of the Jacksonville Jaguars.

But, bottom line, this game proved those critics — and the early-arriving 49ers — right.

“I don’t believe that’s why we didn’t play well enough, I really don’t,” protested McVay. “They outplayed us in every phase.”

Perhaps nobody was outplayed worse than Garrett, the two-time Defensive Player of the Year who was arguably The Most Irrelevant Player Of This Game.

He had no sacks or quarterback hits. He was shut out in those two categories for only the third time in two years. He was so invisible, his name was never called and the TV cameras never focused on him until he was standing on the sidelines.

No, Garrett also wouldn’t publicly say that the trip timing was a factor despite loads of evidence to the contrary.

“I don’t doubt the decision making of my coach and organization, I think they did what was best for us and we didn’t execute on the field when we needed to,” he said.

To add injury to insult, Garrett acknowledged he was affected by a sore left knee that apparently isn’t healing.

“This was the worst version of myself that I put out there,” he said. “I’ve got to find a way to recover and get back to the player I can be.”

Recently un-retired star Aaron Donald didn’t make the trip, but here’s guessing he’ll be by Garrett’s side in 11 days for the home opener against the New York Giants, so that will help. The extended rest afforded the team will also help.

The Rams aren’t this bad. In fact, they’re still loaded and worthy of their status as Super Bowl favorites.

But this will be forever known as a day when football’s smartest organization got outsmarted, when football’s best coach fumbled and when the San Francisco 49ers turned football’s giants into so much shrimp on the barbie.

item.title: Five bold predictions for Bills 2026 season
item.description: Joe Brady's era is on, and here are my five bold predictions for the Bills' 2026 season
item.content:encoded:
Josh Allen just finished as the second-highest ranked player on the NFL’s Top 100 list for 2026, trailing only Myles Garrett and sitting ahead of every other offensive player in the league. That alone tells you where the conversation around this team should start. But this year’s Bills are also walking into Week 1 with a new head coach, a new defensive identity, and a roster that looks meaningfully different than the one that has been bounced from the playoffs six straight times. With training camp in the rearview and Houston up first, here are my five bold predictions for the 2026 Buffalo Bills.

Josh Allen wins his second NFL MVP

Not so bold, right?

The league already told us where it stands on Allen entering this season. He’s the No. 2 overall player on the NFL Top 100, the highest-ranked offensive player in the sport, and Sports Illustrated’s most recent quarterback comparison had him at the top of the position as well, ahead of Patrick Mahomes. Dalton Kincaid even said out loud what a lot of people around the league seem to think — that Allen should have been No. 1.

He’s also getting what might become the best supporting cast of his career. DJ Moore arrives via trade to reunite with new head coach Joe Brady, who was Moore’s offensive coordinator in Carolina back in 2020 and 2021 — the two best statistical seasons of Moore’s career. Allen himself has said the fit already feels seamless. Pair that with a difficult schedule that will force Buffalo to play its best football just to stay in the AFC East and wild-card race, and you have every ingredient for an MVP case: the talent, the weapons, the opportunity, and the motivation.

Maxwell Hairston finishes with five or more interceptions

Hairston’s rookie season was more about flashes than volume, and for a fair reason — a training camp knee injury cost him the first six weeks, and an ankle issue ended his year before the playoffs even started. He still finished with two interceptions and five pass breakups in just 11 games and three starts, good enough to tie for third among all rookie defenders in picks and to land him on both ESPN’s and The Athletic’s All-Rookie teams.

The tape backs up the ceiling. In just his second career game, Hairston picked off Patrick Mahomes and led every Bills defender in PFF grade that day at 91.1, the highest mark on the field. His 4.28 40-yard dash gives him the recovery speed to play aggressive, ball-hawking coverage rather than just survive downfield. Now entering year two as an expected full-time starter across from Christian Benford, and hopefully healthy heading into the season, Hairston should get the reps and consistency his rookie year never allowed. I think he takes that leap into being one of the better young corners in football. My friend Raphael Sattamini, from the “SattaMiniCast”, has him leading the league in INTs!

Terrel Bernard returns to All-Pro-caliber form

Bernard and Hairston share the same theme: talent that hasn’t been able to stay on the field. Bernard’s ceiling isn’t in question — his 143 tackles in 2023 ranked 12th in the entire NFL, and he added 6.5 sacks and three interceptions that year. Even in a lesser 2024 campaign as a team captain, he still posted 104 tackles. But 2025 was a step back across the board, with just 65 tackles, zero sacks, and one interception in 12 games as injuries piled up.

Here’s why I think that changes. Buffalo’s move to Jim Leonhard’s 3-4 scheme, with bigger bodies up front designed to occupy blockers, should keep Bernard cleaner than he’s ever been in the NFL. That’s not a new concept for him — he played inside linebacker in a 3-4 under Dave Aranda at Baylor, and Aranda and Leonhard worked together at Wisconsin, sharing a defensive philosophy built around disguised pressure. With the extra defensive linemen and Dorian Williams taking on more of the load absorbing bigger offensive linemen in the new base defense, Bernard gets to play in space again, doing what he does best: making plays sideline to sideline instead of constantly shedding blocks from guards and centers. I think he’s not just healthy this year — I think he’s back to being one of the most disruptive off-ball linebackers in the league, earning a Pro Bowl nod and being in the All-Pro conversation.

The Bills finish top three in the NFL in sacks

Jim Leonhard isn’t walking into Buffalo without a résumé. He spent the last two seasons on Vance Joseph’s staff in Denver, where the Broncos set a franchise sack record in 2024 and led the entire NFL in sacks again in 2025. Before that, at Wisconsin, Leonhard ran defenses that blitzed on over half of all dropbacks across six seasons, touching nearly 72% in 2020. Aggressive is the baseline, not the exception, for this coordinator.

He’s also inheriting more juice than Buffalo’s pass rush has had in years. Bradley Chubb signed a three-year, $43.5 million deal after an 8.5-sack season in Miami and slots in as a starter. T.J. Parker, Buffalo’s second-round pick out of Clemson, adds another true edge threat. Inside, Deone Walker and Ed Oliver give Leonhard real interior push to pair with an outside rotation that also includes Greg Rousseau and Michael Hoecht. After finishing 27th in pass-rush win rate a year ago, this group has the pieces and the coordinator to flip that number completely. I expect it to show up immediately in Week 1 against Houston, and I expect it to hold up over 17 games — this defense finishes top three in the league in sacks.

The Buffalo Bills win the Super Bowl

Let’s be fair about what actually happened over the last six years. Sean McDermott built a genuinely winning culture in Buffalo, and that part of his legacy is real. But it’s also fair to point out that his defenses collapsed at the worst possible moments, over and over. Six straight playoff losses since 2020 for a combined 199 points allowed — the most in the NFL over that stretch. Four blown fourth-quarter leads in five of those eliminations. Zero sacks and one takeaway in the loss to Denver that got him fired. That’s not all bad luck or bad calls. That’s a pattern.

Speaking of bad calls, though — they were real too. The fourth-and-1 spot in the 2025 AFC Championship Game, with Buffalo up 22-21 and 13 minutes left, went against Allen on a quarterback sneak that plenty of people, including cameras from multiple angles, thought he got. Kansas City scored a touchdown on the ensuing drive and won by three. That’s not the only time a Bills season has ended on a coin flip of a spot or a measurement.

Sure, Josh Allen had plays he wanted back, which quarterback, EVER, doesn’t? However, his playoff résumé already speaks for itself: a 101.5 passer rating, 3,915 yards, 29 touchdowns, and only six interceptions across 15 career playoff games. He has nine rushing touchdowns in the postseason, second all-time behind only Jalen Hurts. He’s made the playoffs every year of his career except his rookie season, and he’s one win away from tying Tom Brady’s record of eight straight seasons with at least one playoff victory. Allen has done more than enough to get this team to a Super Bowl. What he hasn’t had is a defense that matches his level in December and January, or the racing luck to go with it.

That’s what’s different now. Buffalo kept the locker room culture and the professionalism that McDermott built, while removing the parts that kept costing them in January. Joe Brady gives the offense continuity instead of a teardown. Leonhard gives the defense an identity that should hold up under pressure instead of folding. Add a fairer bounce or two along the way, and I think this team finally has everything around Allen that it’s been missing. Get the Bills to the Super Bowl, and I don’t think they’ll let it slip away this time.

Those are my five bold predictions for 2026, all positive ones because I won’t be the one bringing on negativity to start the season. Let me know which ones you’re buying and which ones you think are too far off — and drop your own in the comments. Oh, and don’t miss the latest episode of Leading The Charge!

item.title: Zay Flowers upgraded on Ravens’ Week 1 injury report
item.description: The Ravens’ star wide receiver should be good to go for Baltimore’s Week 1 against the Indianapolis Colts.
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens upgraded star wide receiver Zay Flowers to full participation on their second injury report of the 2026 NFL season.

Flowers, 25, was listed as as a limited participant on Wednesday with a hamstring injury. He previously dealt with a minor groin injury during training camp but was quickly back on the field. His upgrade should quell any concerns about his availability in Week 1.

Baltimore’s injury report was otherwise the same as Wednesday’s. Linebacker Teddye Buchanan (knee), defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike (neck), and wide receiver Devontez Walker (groin) were all limited.

The Colts had five status changes on their Thursday injury report. Rookie safety A.J. Haulcy (ankle), depth tight end Drew Ogletree (neck), and backup center Sedrick Van Pran-Granger (illness) were all upgraded from limited to full participation. Quarterback Anthony Richardson (illness) was listed as a full participant, while defensive tackle Grover Stewart (rest) did not practice.

The only constant for Indianapolis was wide receiver Alec Pierce (heel), who remained limited as he works his way back to 100%. Head coach Shane Steichen said earlier in the week that he is expecting the 26-year-old to take the field on Sunday. However, if he is out of the picture, the Colts’ wide receiver corps will be led by Keenan Allen and Josh Downs with former Raven Laquon Treadwell elevated to the No. 3 role.

Neither Allen nor Downs particularly impressed in 2025; both averaged just 6.4 yards per target. But the former is still a crafty route-runner who will find the soft spots in zone coverage, and the latter can be a dangerous threat with the ball in his hands.

The Colts’ offense was one of the best in the league before Daniel Jones’ injuries last season, including a 38-point, 401-yard outburst against the Chargers’ Jesse Minter-led defense. Pierce had nine catches for 98 yards in that game, so his potential absence could make a difference on Sunday.

item.title: Cowboys news: Rising stars get new contracts before start of the season
item.description: Here is today’s Dallas Cowboys news.
item.content:encoded:
We are just days away from the Dallas Cowboys kicking off their 2026 season on the road, taking on a division rival, the New York Giants.

Before the Cowboys go wheels up to New York, they took care of some business, inking tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford to a three-year contract extension to remain in Dallas. Spann-Ford has been one of the biggest risers for the Cowboys over the offseason, and his development was rewarded with a brand new three-year extension. They also took care of wide receiver Ryan Flournoy with a 1-year extension.

Brevyn Spann-Ford agrees to terms on extension with Cowboys – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com

Brevyn Spann-Ford is expected to make a big leap in 2026. Before doing so, the Cowboys lock him in for three more years ahead of week one.

FRISCO, Texas — The Cowboys and tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford have agreed to terms on an extension.

Spann-Ford, who was set to be a restricted free agent after the 2026 season, will now stay in Dallas through 2029.

During training camp, Spann-Ford grew into Dallas’ TE2 role behind Jake Ferguson, contributing as one of the offense’s best in-line blockers at the position and a key player on special teams.

With three days to go until the Cowboys kick off the NFL season, Spann-Ford now gets added comfort long-term with Dallas being confident in what he can bring to the offense.

Cowboys, WR Ryan Flournoy agree on 1-year extension worth up to $6M – RJ Ochoa, BloggingTheBoys.com

Another deal indeed.

Just before the league’s second game of the season kicked off in Australia, it was reported that Dallas agreed to a 3-year extension with tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford. That was great to see.

About 5 minutes after the San Francisco 49ers polished off the Los Angeles Rams… news of the same variety broke. This time it is Ryan Flournoy.

For Cowboys rookie Caleb Downs, opener vs. Giants offers opportunity for extra motivation – Joseph Hoyt, The Dallas Morning News

The Dallas Cowboys first-round pick Caleb Downs is ready to make his NFL debut. From the sounds of it, it seems like he has a little extra motivation heading into New York.

Now, instead of playing for the Giants, Downs will play against them in his NFL debut when the Cowboys open the season against New York on Sunday Night Football. There’s already a lot of excitement for Downs about getting the chance to live his NFL dream. Considering the Giants’ interest and their decision to pass on him not once, but twice, is there also some added motivation?

Downs downplayed the notion when asked Thursday. 

“I’m just trying to win on Sunday,” Downs said. “That’s about it.”

The Dallas Cowboys are getting mixed signals from the Giants as star player’s availability is getting seriously confusing – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports

One of the biggest questions coming into Sunday Night Football is will Malik Nabers play? The Giants are doing a great job of keeping that information all in house ahead of their home opener.

The Dallas Cowboys got hit by major injury news when they were forced to place All-Pro guard Tyler Smith on Injured Reserve. But other than that, their starting lineup looks ready to go. The biggest injury mystery ahead of Sunday Night Football is on the New York Giants’ side of things.

That’s because Giants top wide receiver Malik Nabers is raising questions about his Week 1 availability despite being a full participant in practice in back-to-back days.

Despite Nabers’ participation in practice, the Giants have been non-committal on his status for Sunday. That’s mostly because of Nabers, who claims the organization is letting him make the call.

“I’m just focusing on today, had a really good day at practice,” Nabers told reporters. “I’ll let God tell me [when it’s time to return].”

How the Cowboys offensive line matches up with the Giants front

The Cowboys offensive line was going to have it’s hands full with the Giants pass rush before the Tyler Smith injury. With T.J. Bass in and Tyler Smith out, those problems could get louder on Sunday Night Football.

The biggest concern for the Cowboys offensive line this week is not difficult to find. New York can send Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux after Dak Prescott, and Dallas enters the season with questions at offensive tackle.

That matters most on the right side. Terence Steele allowed 52 pressures last season, the most among qualifying offensive tackles according to PFF, while his 54.9 pass-blocking grade ranked 76th out of 89 tackles. Dallas trading for Broderick Jones just before the season and immediately putting him into competition with Steele tells its own story about how the Cowboys view the position.

Daily discussion question: Are you more confident or nervous about this week?

item.title: Illustrating a Pete Golding quote about coverages
item.description: Let’s take a look at one (of many) coverage busts from the Louisville game.
item.content:encoded:
If you can allow yourself to go back to the Louisville game, you may recall the seemingly endless instances of Cardinals receivers running alone due to yet another coverage bust from the Ole Miss secondary.

It was a less-than-ideal time for everyone involved and watching, minus Louisville. They looked like they were having fun with it.

The most egregious of these busts came with just under 5 minutes left and Ole Miss leading 38-24. Given the amount of time left and a two-score lead, all Ole Miss needed to do was not give up explosive plays and force Louisville to eat clock on long drives.

Instead, on third and 6, Louisville quarterback Lincoln Kienholz hit a WIDE WIDE WIDE open Lawayne McCoy for a 54-yard touchdown. Again, given the situation, a worst case scenario for Ole Miss in terms of seeing the game out comfortably.

On Monday at his weekly press conference, Golding referenced the disaster when asked about coverage issues:

It doesn’t matter if you’re playing Louisville, Charlotte, or Delta State. If you call Three Cloud, and they don’t roll to Cloud, it’s going to be a touchdown.

And that’s what we’re looking at today. What happened on the back end to give Louisville that easy score.

After the touchdown on the ESPN broadcast, Greg McElroy (who I think is perfectly fine at his job) broke down the coverage, but he mistakenly thought Ole Miss called Cover 3.

As you’ll see below, Ole Miss shows a pre-snap look of two-high safeties (FS and SS), meaning they want Kienholz to think he’s looking at either Cover 2 or Cover 4. However, as soon as the ball is snapped the coverage will change.

If Ole Miss called standard Cover 3, the responsibilities on the back end would be as follows:

Free safety Edwin Joseph would rotate to the middle of the field to take the middle third, corner Jaylon Braxton (top of screen) would take the right third, and corner Jalyn Crawford (bottom of screen) would take the left third. In the middle of the field, strong safety Joenel Aguero would rotate down and follow his coverage responsibilities from there.

But, as Golding said on Monday, he didn’t call Cover 3, he called Cover 3 Cloud. What’s the difference? A great question!

In Cover 3 Cloud, both safeties make up 2 of the 3 players in the Cover 3.

Joseph (FS) and Crawford (CB bottom) have the same responsibilities as in standard Cover 3, but Aguero (SS) should roll to the right third, with Braxton (CB top) sitting down. With Braxton sitting down, Cover 3 Cloud is designed to take away an easy access throw to one side of the field. In this case, Braxton’s side.

However, as you’ll see below and remember from the game, Aguero didn’t roll to the right third, and that’s what Golding meant when said not rolling to Three Cloud. And we know Aguero should’ve rolled because of what Ole Miss did underneath. Braxton (CB top) sits in a line of five underneath players after Blake Purchase (edge at bottom of screen) drops out.

If executed properly, Kienholz should’ve been throwing into an 8-man coverage with five players at an intermediate level and three players deep.

Golding didn’t say Aguero by name because he’s not a jerk, but, to hit on another point he made on Monday, 10 guys got the call right and one didn’t for whatever reason.

Joseph and Crawford rolled into deep coverage, five players sat at intermediate depth, and Aguero rotated down to help in an area where help was not needed. That created the massive hole in the defense that Louisville exploited.

The good news, as Golding also noted, is that blowing coverages is much more fixable than not having talented players. Ole Miss has the big, fast, and strong boxes checked, but there is work to be done in not losing those advantages due to catastrophic mistakes.

item.title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 2 Days Remaining
item.description: We continue our countdown to the Panthers opening the 2026 season against the Chicago Bears
item.content:encoded:
Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial.

#2. Julius Peppers

It is the penultimate entry in our list of top 100 Panthers of all time. We’ve hit lots of fan favorites and players that were good to great. Now we’ve reached the best of the best. The best player to ever suit up on the defensive side of the ball for the Panthers comes in at number two on our list, defensive end Julius Peppers.

Peppers is a Carolina kid through and through. He grew up in Bailey, North Carolina, about 30 miles east of Raleigh. He didn’t play football growing up, but his sheer size and athleticism caught the eye of the coaching staff of his high school, and he quickly turned into one of the most dominant players in the state on both sides of the ball. He received a scholarship to play football at UNC and also walked on to the basketball team. He was a reserve forward for the basketball team while we was assembling an elite resume as a defensive end for the Tar Heel football team. He was considered a generational talent entering the 2002 NFL Draft.

The Panthers had the number two pick in that draft with the first overall pick going to the expansion Houston Texans. Fortunately, the Texans elected to take David Carr with the first overall pick to be their franchise quarterback. That meant Peppers was sitting right there for the Panthers at the second pick.

Peppers delivered on the hype. He registered 12 sacks, five force fumbles, and an interception en route to Defensive Rookie of the Year honors in 2002. He added a modest seven sacks in his sophomore season before fully breaking out as an elite defensive end. He earned his first of six All Pro nominations in his third season with 11 sacks and two interceptions, including a 97 yard pick six. He would spend five more seasons in Carolina after that, accumulating double digit sacks in all but one season in which he was uncharacteristically ineffective.

The Panthers elected to let Peppers test free agency after the 2009 season, and Peppers opted to leave to sign with the Chicago Bears. He spent four seasons there before hopping over to the division rival Packers. He spent three years before making a return to his home state. He tallied 11 sacks in his first season back in Carolina despite being 37 years old. He added five more sacks in his age 38 season before announcing his retirement at the end of it.

Peppers finished his career with 159.5 sacks, fourth most in NFL history (0.5 sacks behind Kevin Greene for third). 97 of those came with the Panthers, 29.5 more than any other player to wear the black and blue. He scored six defensive touchdowns and blocked 13 kicks, showing just how much of a menace he was in every facet of the game.

The two seasons that Peppers spent in Carolina to end his career did a lot to improve his standing with the fan base. During his first stint, there was a perception among parts of the fan base that he wasn’t always giving full effort despite his dominance, and his even keeled persona was often misconstrued as apathy. Those frustrations further boiled over when Peppers refused to re-sign with the team and ultimately left in free agency. Some time apart allowed for a storybook ending, with Peppers returning home to become a fan favorite to end his career and ultimately ending up in the team’s Hall of Honor.

Peppers was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2024 and became the first player to spend the majority of his career in Carolina to earn that honor. The end of his career quashed any beef between he and the fan base, leaving him as the inarguable best defensive player to play for the Panthers. For that, he comes in at number two on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

item.title: Can the 2026 Bears Measure Up to the Greatest Scoring Offense of All-Time?
item.description: Comparing Chicago’s Playmakers to Bears Greats, Previous Ben Johnson Players, and the 2013 Denver Broncos
item.content:encoded:
With the start of the 2026 NFL season upon us, it’s time to set the stage for a project spanning the entirety of the season. That’s right, folks – I’m back to Benchmark Da Bears once again! Each week, I’ll be taking a look at Chicago’s offensive playmakers, tracking their production, and comparing their statistical output against a comparable player from Ben Johnson’s past.

New this year, however, is the introduction of some additional milestones that hold historical significance either to the Bears franchise or even to the league as a whole. Both Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams have expressed a desire to field the most productive offense of all-time, so we’ll naturally have to keep one eye on the 2013 Denver Broncos (led by Bears legends John Fox and Adam Gase), who hold that distinction, having scored an average of 37.9 points per game.

But without further ado, it’s time to name our players and the comps that have set the standard we will hold them to throughout the 2026 NFL season:

Quarterback

Caleb Williams, 3rd NFL season

Comp Player: 2022 Jared Goff (Detroit Lions)

Goff’s 2022 Statline:

We’re starting off with a repeat, but truthfully, Caleb Williams is simply a player who is difficult to compare. Couple that with limited candidates (really just Goff and Caleb himself) and we’re left to select Goff’s first year under Ben Johnson’s direction once again. That said, Caleb is a very different quarterback than Goff, and these statistical benchmarks will serve as more of a measuring stick than the more literal comparisons we will find among some of the following players.


Milestones: 4,000 passing yards; 29 passing TDs (franchise record – Kramer); 5,477 passing yards (2013 Peyton Manning); 55 passing TDs (2013 Peyton Manning)

Running Backs

D’Andre Swift, 7th NFL season

Comp Player: 2025 D’Andre Swift (Chicago Bears)

Swift’s 2025 Statline:

Kyle Monangai, 2nd NFL season

Comp Player: 2024 David Montgomery (Detroit Lions)

Montgomery’s 2024 Statline:

While it was tempting to go with a “Sonic & Knuckles” duo for comparison here, Swift is too unlike Gibbs for that particular comp. Instead, I’ve chosen to compare Swift to his own performance from last season, which was arguably the best of his career to this point. Monangai, in his second season, should be expected to elevate his game and with that in mind, the Montgomery comparison feels apt as the more powerful runner in Johnson’s two-headed backfield. Note: franchise records are likely out of reach at this position for obvious reasons


Milestones: 1,597 combined rushing yards (2013 Broncos RBs); 15 combined rushing TDs (2013 Broncos RBs)

Tight Ends

Colston Loveland, 2nd NFL season

Comp Player: 2023 Sam LaPorta (Detroit Lions)

LaPorta’s 2023 Statline:

Cole Kmet, 7th NFL season

Comp Player: 2021 T.J. Hockenson (Detroit Lions)

Hockenson’s 2021 Statline:

I know some will wonder about the absence of rookie Sam Roush, but ultimately, I think it will take some time for him to grow into his role. Even then, there is a ceiling on his production with all of the mouths to feed in this offense. As far as Loveland and Kmet go, the comps here are extremely familiar as they are the same as last year’s. Loveland’s ascension in the latter part of the 2025 season should align him more closely with LaPorta’s fabled rookie season in 2026. Kmet (like all of the 2025 Bears TEs) had extremely limited production to start the year, but Hockenson is still a closer comp than most Johnson-coached products, even if this was during Johnson’s stint as the Lions’ TEs Coach.


Milestones: 1,076 receiving yards (franchise record for TE – Ditka); 12 receiving TDs (franchise record for TE – Ditka); 90 receptions (franchise record for TE – Bennett); 14 combined receiving TDs (2013 Broncos TEs)

Wide Receivers

Rome Odunze, 3rd NFL season

Comp Player: 2024 Jameson Williams (Detroit Lions)

Williams’ 2024 Statline:

Luther Burden, 2nd NFL season

Comp Player: 2022 Amon-Ra St. Brown (Detroit Lions)

St. Brown’s 2022 Statline:

Kalif Raymond, 10th NFL season

Comp Player: 2022 Kalif Raymond (Detroit Lions)

Raymond’s 2022 Statline:

Zavion Thomas, Rookie season

Comp Player: 2025 Luther Burden (Chicago Bears)

Burden’s 2025 Statline:

I feel that you can make a strong case that this position group is simultaneously the most exciting and puzzling of the four. We largely know what to expect from the players I’ve covered above (albeit with varying levels of untapped potential), but the receivers on the 2026 Chicago Bears seem to be a group that many have opinions ALL across the board on. As far as comp players go, I see Rome Odunze lining up similarly to Jameson Williams’ primary deep threat role, while Luther Burden is set to take on the YAC production responsibility of a young Amon-Ra St. Brown. Kalif Raymond is compared to a past version of himself, but one that held a greater role in the Lions’ offense than in his most recent seasons. Finally, Zavion Thomas is hard to pin down, but Luther Burden’s output from last season seems a fitting measuring stick for another incoming rookie who will need to play himself into offensive snaps.


Milestones: 1,430 receiving yards (2013 Demaryius Thomas); 14 receiving TDs (2013 Demaryius Thomas); 1,508 receiving yards (franchise record – Marshall); 13 receiving TDs (franchise record – Gordon, Kavanaugh); 38 combined receiving TDs (2013 Broncos WRs)

It’s clear that this team will need these players to have some outstanding seasons in order for the Bears to experience success similar to what they found in 2025. To achieve the legendary status that Johnson and Williams have their eyes set on? That may take more than a couple of leaps. Still, a wise man once said, “the ceiling… is the roof,” and I’m hoping to see this team exceed all of our expectations.

item.title: Lions vs. Saints preview: 3 key player matchups
item.description: Our Detroit Lions vs. New Orleans Saints preview identifies three key player matchups.
